units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 Physics is about, how to use these notes, and a map of every unit in First Term.

p: Physics is the science that explains how the world works. It tells us why a ball falls, why a car needs fuel to move, why a stone sinks but a ship floats, and how sound and light travel to us. Everything you see around you in Nigeria, from a generator to a mobile phone to the rain on a zinc roof, follows the rules of Physics.

This is the First Term course of SS1 Physics. It follows the Nigerian curriculum scheme of work for SS1 and prepares you for WAEC, NECO and later for JAMB. In this term you will learn how to measure things properly, how to describe movement, and how to calculate things like speed, acceleration and distance.
Each unit is short enough to finish in one sitting. Read it slowly, one section at a time. Look carefully at every picture, because Physics is easier to understand when you can see it.
When you meet a worked example, cover the answer with your hand, try the working yourself, and only then check. This is the best way to get better at calculations.

At the end of every unit there are practice questions. They do not count towards any mark. They are there to help you check that you really understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit and move to the next one.
Keep a notebook and a calculator close by. Copy the formulas into your notebook in your own handwriting, because writing them down helps you remember them.

sections.h: Tips for doing well in Physics
p: Learn the definitions word for word, because examiners give marks for correct definitions. Always write the unit with your final answer: an answer like 50 with no unit loses a mark. Write the formula first, then put in the numbers, then work out the answer. Practise past WAEC and NECO questions regularly. If a topic is hard, go back to the picture and the simple example first, then try the harder one.

units.title: Physical Quantities: Fundamental Quantities and Units
units.summary: What a physical quantity is, the seven fundamental quantities, their SI units and the instruments used to measure them.

p: A physical quantity is anything about a material or a system that we can measure. Length of a table, mass of a bag of rice, time to boil water and temperature of the room are all physical quantities.
A measurement always has two parts: a number and a unit. When we say a table is 2 metres long, '2' is the number and 'metre' is the unit. A number alone, like '2', tells us nothing. Always give both.
Physical quantities are put into two groups: fundamental quantities and derived quantities.
Fundamental quantities are the basic quantities. They stand on their own and cannot be written in terms of any other quantity. Think of them as the building blocks of Physics.

Scientists around the world agreed to use the same units so that everybody can understand each other. This agreed set is called the SI system (International System of Units). SI comes from the French name Systeme International d'Unites.
There are seven fundamental quantities. In SS1 you will use the first four most often: length, mass, time and temperature.

sections.h: The pictures of common measuring instruments
p: The picture below shows many instruments used in Physics laboratories. Some of them you will meet in this course: the metre rule and vernier callipers for length, the micrometer screw gauge for very small lengths, the stopwatch for time, the thermometer for temperature and the top pan balance for mass. The voltmeter, ammeter and galvanometer are used for electricity, which you will study in later classes.

img.alt: Poster of measuring instruments: micrometer, metre ruler, protractor, vernier callipers, thermometer, stopwatch, voltmeter, ammeter, galvanometer, top pan balance and cathode-ray oscilloscope
img.cap: Common measuring instruments used in Physics.

p: They are independent: you cannot get one of them by combining the others. For example, you cannot get length from mass and time.
Each has a standard SI unit that everybody agrees on.
They are used to build all the other quantities, which are called derived quantities. You will study these in the next unit.

b: Is 'speed' a fundamental quantity? No. Speed is distance divided by time, so it is made from two other quantities. It is a derived quantity.
Is 'time' fundamental? Yes. We cannot write time in terms of any other quantity.

units.activity: Look at the instrument picture above. Choose five instruments and write, for each one, the quantity it measures and the SI unit of that quantity. Example: Stopwatch - measures time - second (s).

units.title: Derived Quantities, Dimensions and Changing Units
units.summary: How derived quantities are made from fundamental ones, what dimensions are, why units matter, and how to convert between units.

p: A derived quantity is made by combining fundamental quantities using multiplication or division. For example, area is length multiplied by length, so its unit is metre multiplied by metre, written m². Velocity is displacement divided by time, so its unit is metre per second, written m/s or ms⁻¹.
Their units are called derived units. Some derived units are so common that they have special names, like the newton for force and the joule for energy.

b: Force = mass x acceleration.
Unit of mass = kg. Unit of acceleration = m/s², which is m s⁻².
So the unit of force = kg x m s⁻² = kg m s⁻². This is given the special name newton (N).
So 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

p: Dimensions show which fundamental quantities a derived quantity is made from. We use capital letters in square brackets: [M] for mass, [L] for length and [T] for time.
To find the dimension of a quantity, write its formula and replace each quantity by its letter. A power tells how many times that quantity appears.

b: Pressure = force / area.
Dimension of force = [M][L][T⁻²]. Dimension of area = [L²].
Pressure = [M][L][T⁻²] / [L²] = [M][L⁻¹][T⁻²].

p: Checking whether an equation is correct. Both sides of a correct equation must have the same dimension.
Working out a relationship between quantities.
Changing units from one system to another.
Standardisation: the same unit is used everywhere in the world, so a kilogram of rice in Lagos is the same as a kilogram of rice in London.
Accuracy: careful measurement reduces mistakes in experiments.
Reproducibility: another person can repeat your experiment and get the same result.
Communication: scientists can share results with each other without confusion.

sections.h: Changing from one unit to another
p: Sometimes the unit given in a question is not the unit you need. You must change it before you calculate. Use prefixes to help you. A prefix is a short word placed before a unit to make it bigger or smaller.

b: Change 100 cm to metres. 1 m = 100 cm, so 100 cm = 100 / 100 = 1 m.
Change 2 hours to seconds. 1 hour = 60 x 60 = 3600 s, so 2 hours = 2 x 3600 = 7200 s.
Change 3.5 km to metres. 1 km = 1000 m, so 3.5 km = 3.5 x 1000 = 3500 m.

units.activity: Find the dimension of density (mass divided by volume) and of velocity multiplied by time. Then convert your own height from centimetres to metres.

units.title: Measuring Mass, Weight, Length and Time
units.summary: Definitions, units and instruments for mass, weight, length and time, with worked examples.

p: Mass is the amount of matter in a body. It is a scalar quantity, which means it has size only and no direction. The SI unit is the kilogram (kg).
Mass is measured with a beam balance, a triple beam balance, an electronic (digital) balance, or a chemical balance when the mass is very small.
Example: a bag of rice has a mass of 25 kg. Your mass is the same on Earth, on the Moon, and in space.

Weight is the force with which the Earth pulls a body towards its centre. Weight is a force, so it is a vector quantity (it has size and direction, and the direction is downwards). The SI unit is the newton (N).
Weight = mass x acceleration due to gravity, or W = mg. On Earth, g = 9.8 m/s² (often taken as 10 m/s² in calculations). Weight is measured with a spring balance or a newton meter.

b: A body has a mass of 5 kg. Find its weight on Earth.
The same body on the Moon, where g = 1.6 m/s², weighs 5 x 1.6 = 8 N. Its mass is still 5 kg.

sections.h: The difference between mass and weight
p: Mass stays the same everywhere. Weight changes from place to place because the pull of gravity is different. That is why astronauts feel light on the Moon but their mass has not changed at all.

p: Length is the distance between two points. It is a scalar quantity. The SI unit is the metre (m). Different instruments are chosen for different jobs.

b: 1 inch = 2.54 cm

p: Time is the ongoing sequence of events. It is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is the second (s). We measure time with a clock or a stopwatch. A pendulum clock is often used in experiments.
Conversions: 1 minute = 60 s; 1 hour = 3600 s; 1 day = 86 400 s.

units.title: Using Instruments Well and Avoiding Errors
units.summary: Common errors in measurement, how to avoid them, and why careful measurement matters.

p: No measurement is ever perfect. A small difference always exists between the reading we get and the true value. This difference is called an error. A good scientist cannot remove all errors but learns to reduce them.

Parallax error: this happens when you look at a scale from the wrong angle. The reading seems to move when your eye moves. To avoid it, always place your eye directly in front of the mark, at eye level, so that your line of sight is at 90 degrees to the scale.

Zero error: this happens when the instrument does not read zero when it should. For example a ruler whose end is worn away, or a balance that reads 2 g with nothing on it. You must either correct the instrument or add or subtract the zero error from every reading.

Instrumental error: the instrument is faulty or was not made or marked properly (for example a stretched spring in a spring balance). Use well-kept instruments and check them against a known standard.
Human reaction time: when you start and stop a stopwatch by hand, there is a small delay of about 0.2 second. To reduce its effect, time many swings and divide, instead of timing just one.
Take readings at eye level.
Make sure the instrument is clean and in good condition.
Always check for zero error before you start.
Repeat each measurement at least three times and take the average.
Write the unit with every reading.

b: A pendulum is timed for 20 complete swings and the stopwatch shows 36.0 s.
Time for one swing = 36.0 / 20 = 1.8 s.
The 0.2 s reaction delay is now shared over 20 swings, so its effect on one swing is only 0.01 s.

p: Measurement gives science its accuracy and lets us compare and predict things. It is used every day in industry, engineering, building, medicine and farming: a nurse measures the dose of a drug, an engineer measures the length of a steel beam, and a baker measures the mass of flour. Accuracy and correct use of instruments give reliable results in any experiment.

units.activity: Use a ruler to measure the width of your desk three times, once with your eye directly above the mark, once from the left and once from the right. Compare the readings and explain what you notice.

units.title: Position, Distance and Displacement
units.summary: The meaning of position, distance and displacement, how they differ, and how to calculate each one.

p: Position is where an object is, compared with a fixed point called the reference point or origin. We usually say how far it is from the origin and in which direction (left or right, north or south).
Example: a student sitting 2 m to the right of the board is at position +2 m. A student sitting 2 m to the left of the board is at position -2 m.

Distance is the total length of the path an object travels, no matter which direction it goes. Distance is a scalar quantity, which means it has size only. It is always positive and its unit is the metre (m).
Example 1: you walk 4 m forward and then 4 m back. The total distance = 4 + 4 = 8 m.
Example 2: you walk 6 m east and then 4 m west. The total distance = 6 + 4 = 10 m.

Displacement is the straight line from the starting point to the finishing point, together with its direction. It tells you how far out of place you are and in which direction. Displacement is a vector quantity: it has size and direction. It can be positive, negative or zero. Its unit is also the metre.
Example: you walk 4 m forward and 4 m back. You are back where you started, so your displacement is 0 m, even though you walked 8 m.
A good way to remember: distance is how much ground you covered, displacement is how far you are from the start.

head: Feature
Distance
Displacement
rows: Yes, if opposite to the chosen positive direction
Only the start and finish points

p: Look at each example, then try it again without looking.

b: A boy walks 6 m east and then 3 m west. Total distance = 6 + 3 = 9 m. Displacement = 6 - 3 = 3 m east.
A girl walks 10 m north and then 10 m south. Distance = 10 + 10 = 20 m. Displacement = 0 m, because she is back at the start.
An athlete runs once round a circular track of radius 70 m. Distance = circumference = 2πr = 2 x 3.142 x 70 = 439.88 m. Displacement = 0 m, because the athlete finishes at the start.

p: In a 400 m race on a round track, the distance run is 400 m but the displacement after one full lap is zero.
A car's odometer shows distance travelled. A GPS shows displacement, because it shows where you are compared with where you started.
Pilots and ship captains must use displacement, because they need to know direction as well as distance.

units.activity: Draw a straight line on the floor or on a sheet of paper. Mark 0 in the middle, +5 m to the right and -5 m to the left. Walk (or move a small stone) from 0 to +5 and back to 0. Write the distance and the displacement at each stage.

units.title: Showing Movement on Graphs and Number Lines
units.summary: How to read position-time and distance-time graphs, how to use a number line, and how to find the size and direction of a displacement.

sections.h: Graphs of position, displacement and distance
p: A graph is a picture of movement. For a position-time graph, time is on the horizontal axis (x-axis) and position is on the vertical axis (y-axis). Read the shape of the line like a story:

A flat horizontal line means the object is not moving (it is stationary). A line sloping upwards means it is moving away from the origin. A line sloping downwards means it is moving towards the origin. The steeper the line, the faster the movement. The slope of the line tells you the velocity.
A displacement-time graph looks the same, but it shows displacement (change in position with direction). Its slope is the velocity.
A distance-time graph shows only the total ground covered, so it never goes downwards. Its slope is the speed.
The picture shows three position-time graphs: a stationary object (flat line), an object moving at uniform speed (straight sloping line) and an object whose speed is changing (a curve).

img.alt: Three graphs of distance against time: a horizontal line for a stationary object, a straight sloping line for uniform speed and a curve for non-uniform speed
img.cap: Stationary object, uniform speed and non-uniform speed.

p: Draw a straight line. Mark 0 as the origin. Put positive numbers to the right and negative numbers to the left. Now you can show position and displacement clearly.
A student walks from 0 to +5 m: distance = 5 m and displacement = +5 m. She then walks back to 0: total distance = 10 m and displacement = 0 m.
Remember that distance graphs do not show direction.

sections.h: When the movement is at a right angle
p: Sometimes a body moves in two directions that are at right angles, for example 100 km north and then 60 km east. The displacement is the straight line from start to finish. Use Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to find its size and direction.

b: A motorist travels 100 km due north and then 60 km due east.
Direction: tan θ = 60 / 100 = 0.6, so θ = 31 degrees. The motorist is 116.6 km from the start, 31 degrees east of north.
Total distance travelled = 100 + 60 = 160 km. Notice that distance (160 km) and displacement (116.6 km) are different.

p: Work through these and check your answer in the practice questions.

b: If a body moves from A to B and back to A in 20 s, covering 40 m in total, its displacement is 0 m and its average speed = total distance / total time = 40 / 20 = 2 m/s.

A student walks round a field 40 m long and 30 m wide. One full lap = 40 + 30 + 40 + 30 = 140 m. The displacement after a full lap is 0. From one corner to the opposite corner the displacement is √(40² + 30²) = √2500 = 50 m.

units.activity: Draw a position-time graph for this story: you stay at home for 2 minutes, walk away from home for 3 minutes, stand still for 2 minutes and then walk back home in 3 minutes. Label each part (stationary, moving away, stationary, moving back).

units.title: Scalar and Vector Quantities
units.summary: The difference between scalars and vectors, with examples, and how to draw a vector as an arrow.

p: A scalar quantity has size (magnitude) only. It has no direction. If I tell you the temperature is 30 degrees Celsius, you do not ask 'which direction?'. That is a scalar.
Common scalars: mass, time, temperature, distance, speed, energy, work, power, density and volume.
A vector quantity has both size and direction. If I tell you a force of 20 N, you still need to know which way it pushes. That is a vector.
Common vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum, electric field intensity and magnetic field strength.
Notice that pairs often go together: distance (scalar) and displacement (vector); speed (scalar) and velocity (vector).

A vector is drawn as an arrow. The length of the arrow shows the size. The direction the arrow points shows the direction. The start of the arrow is called the tail and the pointed end is the head. We choose a scale so the drawing fits on the page.
In the picture, the vector OA is a force of 4 N acting at 30 degrees to the horizontal. The scale is 1 cm = 1 N, so the arrow is drawn 4 cm long, with its tail at O and its head at A.

img.alt: A vector OA of 4 N drawn as a 4 cm arrow at 30 degrees to the x-axis, with tail at O and head at A
img.cap: Representation of a vector: scale 1 cm = 1 N.

ex.t: Worked example: draw a force of 6 N at 30° to the horizontal
b: Choose a scale, for example 1 cm = 1 N.
Draw a horizontal line from a point O.
Use a protractor to mark 30° above the line.
Draw an arrow 6 cm long along the 30° line and put the arrowhead at the end.
Label it '6 N at 30°'.

units.title: Adding Vectors
units.summary: How to add vectors that point in the same direction, in opposite directions, or at a right angle, with worked examples.

sections.h: Why vectors are added in a special way
p: Vectors cannot be added like ordinary numbers because direction matters. Two forces of 5 N can add up to 10 N, or to 0 N, or to something in between, depending on how they point. The single vector that has the same effect as the vectors together is called the resultant.
Case 1: two forces in the same direction along a straight line. They help each other, so the resultant R = F1 + F2.
Case 2: two forces in opposite directions along a straight line. They work against each other, so R = F1 - F2, and the resultant points in the direction of the bigger force.
Case 3: two forces at a right angle (90 degrees). Use Pythagoras' theorem: R² = F1² + F2². The angle θ of the resultant can be found from tan θ = F2 / F1.

Case 4: two forces at any other angle, between 0 and 180 degrees. Use the triangle law or the parallelogram law: draw the vectors tail to head, and the resultant goes from the first tail to the last head.

To add vectors A and B by the triangle law, draw A first. Then draw B starting from the head of A. The resultant R is the third side of the triangle, drawn from the start of A to the end of B, so R = A + B.
When the angle between A and B is θ, the size of the resultant is R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ). The largest possible resultant is A + B (when θ = 0°) and the smallest is A - B (when θ = 180°).

img.alt: Triangle law of vector addition: vector A, then vector B drawn from the head of A, and the resultant R from the tail of A to the head of B
img.cap: Triangle law: R = A + B.

sections.h: Worked example 1: the boat and the river
p: A boat travels due east at 40 m/s across a river that flows due south at 30 m/s. What is the resultant speed of the boat?

img.alt: A right-angled triangle with 40 m/s along the top, 30 m/s down the side and the resultant R as the slanting side
img.cap: The two velocities are at right angles.

b: The two velocities are at 90°, so R² = 40² + 30².

sections.h: Worked example 2: the aircraft in the wind
p: An aircraft tries to fly due north at 100 km/h, but the wind blows from east to west at 60 km/h. Find the resultant velocity.

b: The two velocities are at right angles, so RV² = 100² + 60² = 10 000 + 3 600 = 13 600.
RV = √13 600 = 116.7 km/h, which is about 117 km/h.
The angle west of north: tan θ = 60 / 100 = 0.6, so θ = 31°.
Answer: 117 km/h in the direction N 31° W.

sections.h: Worked example 3: the girl at school
p: A girl walks 40 m due east from the laboratory to the staff room and then 30 m due north to her classroom. How far is she from the laboratory in a straight line?

img.alt: A right-angled triangle with 40 m along the base and 30 m up the side
img.cap: 40 m east then 30 m north.

b: The distance walked is 70 m, but the displacement is only 50 m.

p: The opposite of adding is resolving. A slanting vector can be split into a horizontal part and a vertical part. If a force F acts at an angle θ above the horizontal, then the horizontal part is F cos θ and the vertical part is F sin θ.
Example: a boy pushes a box with a force of 15 N at 30° to the horizontal. Horizontal part = 15 cos 30° = 15 x 0.866 = 13.0 N. Vertical part = 15 sin 30° = 15 x 0.5 = 7.5 N.

units.title: Speed and Velocity
units.summary: Definitions, formulas and types of speed and velocity, and how they differ, with worked examples.

p: Speed is the distance travelled in one unit of time. It is a scalar quantity. The SI unit is metres per second (m/s).
Speed = distance / time.
If a cyclist covers 150 m in 30 s, speed = 150 / 30 = 5 m/s.

Uniform speed (constant speed): the body covers equal distances in equal times, no matter how small the time. A car on cruise control is an example. Its distance-time graph is a straight sloping line.
Variable (non-uniform) speed: the speed keeps changing. Its distance-time graph is a curve.
Average speed: total distance divided by total time. Average speed = total distance / total time.
Instantaneous speed: the speed at one particular moment, like the number on the speedometer at that moment.

img.alt: A distance-time graph with a straight line labelled uniform speed
img.cap: Uniform speed: a straight line on a distance-time graph.

p: When the speed changes, the line on a distance-time graph is curved. Compare this graph with the straight line above.

img.alt: A distance-time graph with a curved line labelled variable speed
img.cap: Variable speed: a curved line.

p: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement. It is the speed in a stated direction, so it is a vector quantity. The SI unit is m/s.
Velocity = displacement / time.
A body has uniform velocity when it is displaced by equal amounts in equal times, in the same direction.
Example: a runner moves 200 m east in 40 s. Velocity = 200 / 40 = 5 m/s east.
The two are not the same. A car going round a roundabout at a steady 50 km/h has a constant speed but its velocity keeps changing because its direction keeps changing.

b: A train travels 500 km in 5 hours. Average speed = 500 / 5 = 100 km/h.
To change to m/s: 100 km/h = 100 x 1000 / 3600 = 27.8 m/s.

units.activity: Walk 20 m in your compound or school corridor. Time yourself with a stopwatch and work out your average speed in m/s. Then walk the same 20 m again quickly and compare.

Which of these is a vector?

units.title: Acceleration
units.summary: What acceleration and deceleration mean, the formula a = (v - u) / t, and worked examples.

p: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. It tells how quickly the velocity is changing. It is a vector quantity and its SI unit is metres per second squared (m/s²).
Acceleration = change in velocity / time taken, or a = (v - u) / t.
Here u is the starting (initial) velocity, v is the final velocity and t is the time taken. The 'squared' in the unit comes from dividing a velocity (m/s) by a time (s).
Positive acceleration: the velocity increases (a car speeding up).
Negative acceleration, also called deceleration or retardation: the velocity decreases (a car braking). In calculations the value of a is negative.
Uniform acceleration: the velocity changes by equal amounts in equal times. A stone falling freely under gravity is an example (about 10 m/s² every second).
Take your time and follow the steps.

b: A car speeds up from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. Find its acceleration.

p: Example 2: a car slows from 25 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 s. a = (10 - 25) / 3 = -15 / 3 = -5 m/s². The negative sign shows deceleration. The car loses 5 m/s of velocity every second.
Example 3: a vehicle starts from rest and reaches 30 m/s in 6 s. Rest means u = 0. a = (30 - 0) / 6 = 5 m/s². This means its velocity grows by 5 m/s each second.

Can an object have zero velocity and still have acceleration? Yes. At the very top of its flight, a ball thrown upwards stops for an instant (v = 0) but gravity is still pulling it, so it still accelerates downwards at about 10 m/s².
Can a car travel at constant speed and still be accelerating? Yes, if it changes direction, because its velocity is changing.

units.activity: Think about a school bus leaving the bus stop. Write what happens to the velocity as it pulls away (positive acceleration), as it moves steadily (zero acceleration) and as it stops at the next stop (deceleration).

check.q: What is the SI unit of acceleration?
A car goes from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
What does a negative acceleration (deceleration) mean?
o: The car is going backwards forever

What does 'u' stand for in a = (v - u) / t?

units.title: Graphs of Motion
units.summary: How to read displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, and what the slope tells you.

p: A graph shows a whole journey at a glance. In Physics we meet two main motion graphs: the displacement-time graph and the velocity-time graph. In both, time is on the horizontal axis.

Here is a displacement-time graph of a journey from A to D. Read it like a story. From A to B the line slopes upwards: the object is moving away from the start with a steady velocity. From B to C the line is flat: the displacement is not changing, so the object has stopped. From C to D the line slopes steeply downwards: the object is travelling back to the start, and quickly, because the line is steep.
The slope (gradient) of a displacement-time graph is the velocity. The steeper the line, the greater the velocity.

img.alt: A displacement-time graph with points A, B, C and D: rising from A to B, flat from B to C, and falling from C to D
img.cap: Displacement-time graph: moving away, resting, then returning.

p: In a velocity-time graph the vertical axis shows velocity. A horizontal line means constant velocity (no acceleration). A line sloping upwards means the velocity is increasing: the object has positive acceleration. A line sloping downwards means the velocity is decreasing: the object has deceleration.
The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration. The area under the graph is the distance travelled (you will use this in the next unit).

img.alt: A velocity-time graph shaped like a trapezium: rising from the start, flat in the middle and falling to the time axis
img.cap: A journey that speeds up, runs at a steady velocity, and then slows to a stop.

sections.h: Summary of what the shapes mean
p: Learn these shapes. They are asked in every WAEC and NECO paper.

units.title: Using a Velocity-Time Graph
units.summary: Finding distance, acceleration and retardation from a velocity-time graph, with two fully worked examples.

p: From a velocity-time graph you can find: (1) the acceleration or retardation, which is the slope of the line, (2) the distance travelled, which is the area between the line and the time axis, and (3) the velocity at any moment, which you read from the vertical axis.
To find an area, split the shape into simple parts: a rectangle has area = length x width and a triangle has area = ½ x base x height.

A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly for 20 s to reach 25 m/s. It keeps this speed for 30 s and then slows uniformly to rest. The total time for the journey is 60 s. (a) Sketch the velocity-time graph. (b) Find the total distance travelled.

img.alt: Velocity-time graph: rising from 0 to 25 m/s in 20 s, constant at 25 m/s until 50 s, falling to 0 at 60 s, with three shaded areas
img.cap: The graph for Worked example 1. The three shaded parts are a triangle, a rectangle and another triangle.

b: (a) Velocity starts at 0 and rises in a straight line to 25 m/s at t = 20 s. It stays at 25 m/s from t = 20 s to t = 50 s. It then falls in a straight line to 0 at t = 60 s.
(b) Distance = area under the graph, split into three parts.
Acceleration part (triangle): ½ x 20 x 25 = 250 m.
Constant velocity part (rectangle): 30 x 25 = 750 m.
Slowing part (triangle): ½ x 10 x 25 = 125 m.
Total distance = 250 + 750 + 125 = 1125 m.

p: A body starts from rest and travels 120 m, 300 m and 180 m in three successive equal time intervals of 12 s each. During each interval it is uniformly accelerated. Sketch the velocity-time graph and find the velocity at the end of each interval.

img.alt: Velocity-time graph with points at 12 s (20 m/s), 24 s (30 m/s) and 36 s (0 m/s)
img.cap: The graph for Worked example 2.

b: For uniform acceleration, average velocity = (u + v) / 2, and distance = average velocity x time.
Interval 1 (0 to 12 s): average velocity = 120 / 12 = 10 m/s. Starting from 0: (0 + v) / 2 = 10, so v = 20 m/s.
Interval 2 (12 s to 24 s): average velocity = 300 / 12 = 25 m/s. (20 + v) / 2 = 25, so v = 30 m/s.
Interval 3 (24 s to 36 s): average velocity = 180 / 12 = 15 m/s. (30 + v) / 2 = 15, so v = 0 m/s.
Velocities at the end of the intervals: 20 m/s, 30 m/s and 0 m/s. The graph is a straight line up to 20 m/s at 12 s, then up to 30 m/s at 24 s, then down to 0 at 36 s.

sections.h: Finding acceleration and retardation from a graph
p: Acceleration = slope = change in velocity / change in time. In Worked example 1, the first part has acceleration = 25 / 20 = 1.25 m/s². The last part has retardation = 25 / 10 = 2.5 m/s² (the velocity falls by 25 m/s in 10 s).

units.title: Motion, Its Types, and Force
units.summary: Rest and motion, the five types of motion, and what a force is, with its effects and kinds.

p: Motion is a change in the position of a body with time, measured from a fixed reference point. A body is at rest if its position does not change with time. A body is in motion if its position changes with time.
Rest and motion are relative. A passenger sitting still in a moving bus is at rest compared with the seat but in motion compared with a tree by the roadside.
Translational motion: movement of the whole body from one place to another along a straight or curved path.
Linear motion: a kind of translational motion along a straight line (a car on a straight road, a falling stone).
Rotational motion: the body spins about an axis (a ceiling fan, the wheels of a bicycle).
Oscillatory (vibratory) motion: back-and-forth movement about a fixed point (a pendulum, a guitar string).
Circular motion: movement along a circle (the Moon going round the Earth).
Random motion: irregular, unpredictable movement (smoke particles, gas molecules).

img.alt: Five panels showing linear motion, curvilinear motion, circular motion, rotational motion and oscillatory motion
img.cap: Types of motion with examples.

p: A force is a push or a pull that can start, stop or change the motion of a body, or change its shape. Force is a vector quantity, so it has size and direction. The SI unit is the newton (N).
Force = mass x acceleration, or F = ma. A force of 1 N gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Example: what force gives a 4 kg trolley an acceleration of 3 m/s²? F = 4 x 3 = 12 N.
Start or stop a motion (kicking a stationary ball; a goalkeeper stopping it).
Change the direction of an object (a hockey stick turning the ball).
Change the speed of an object (pressing the accelerator).
Change the shape or size of an object (squeezing a sponge, stretching a spring).
Contact forces need the objects to touch: applied force, friction, tension in a rope, normal reaction from a surface, and air resistance.
Non-contact (field) forces act across a distance: gravitational force, magnetic force and electrostatic force.

units.title: Friction
units.summary: What friction is, its types, advantages, disadvantages, how to increase or reduce it, and a worked calculation.

p: Friction is a force that opposes the movement, or the tendency to move, of two surfaces in contact. It always acts in the direction opposite to the motion. Rub your two palms together quickly: the warmth you feel is caused by friction.
Static friction is the force that must be overcome to start a body moving. It acts on a body that is not moving yet.
Kinetic (dynamic) friction acts on a body that is already sliding. Static friction is greater than kinetic friction, which is why it is harder to get a heavy box moving than to keep it moving.

The size of the friction force depends on how rough the surfaces are and how hard they press together: F = μN, where μ (mu) is the coefficient of friction (it has no unit) and N is the normal reaction, the force with which the surface pushes up on the body. On a flat floor N = mg.
It lets us walk and drive without slipping.
It makes the brakes of vehicles work.
It lets us grip and hold tools.
It lets belts and pulleys work in machines.
It wears out machine parts and tyres.
It wastes energy as heat.
It lowers the efficiency of moving parts.
It makes moving heavy objects harder.
To reduce friction: use oil or grease (lubrication), polish the surfaces, use ball bearings or rollers, and give vehicles and aircraft a streamlined shape.
To increase friction: use rough surfaces, increase the weight pressing down, put treads on tyres, and wear rubber-soled shoes.

head: Where friction is used
How it helps
rows: Brake pads grip the wheel to slow it
The belt grips the rollers and the load
Rough soles stop you from slipping

p: A box of mass 5 kg is pulled along a horizontal floor with a force of 30 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the box and the floor is 0.2. Find the acceleration of the box. (g = 9.8 m/s²)

b: Normal reaction N = mg = 5 x 9.8 = 49 N.
Friction force = μN = 0.2 x 49 = 9.8 N.
Net force = 30 - 9.8 = 20.2 N.
Acceleration a = net force / mass = 20.2 / 5 = 4.04 m/s².

units.title: Equations of Motion
units.summary: The three equations for uniform acceleration, where they come from, and worked examples.

p: The equations of motion are three formulas that link five quantities: u (initial velocity), v (final velocity), a (acceleration), t (time) and s (displacement). They work only when the acceleration is uniform (constant) and the motion is in a straight line.
Start with the definition of acceleration: a = (v - u) / t. Rearranging gives the first equation: v = u + at.
For uniform acceleration, the average velocity is (u + v) / 2. Distance = average velocity x time, so s = ((u + v) / 2) x t. Replacing v with u + at gives the second equation: s = ut + ½at².
Finally, remove t between the first two equations to get the third: v² = u² + 2as.
Learn them by heart. Choose the one that has the quantity you want and the quantities you know.

units.title: Free Fall and Gravity
units.summary: Motion under gravity: objects thrown upwards, dropped, or thrown horizontally, with worked examples.

p: When an object is thrown upwards or released from a height and only gravity acts on it, it is in free fall. Near the surface of the Earth, gravity gives every falling object the same acceleration, g = 9.8 m/s² (about 10 m/s²), downwards. A heavy stone and a light stone dropped together reach the ground together if air resistance is small. In the equations of motion we simply replace a with g.

When an object moves upwards, gravity slows it down, so a = -g. The equations of motion become: v = u - gt, h = ut - ½gt² and v² = u² - 2gh. When an object falls downwards, gravity speeds it up, so a = +g and we use v = u + gt, h = ut + ½gt² and v² = u² + 2gh.
At the highest point of its flight, an object thrown upwards has v = 0 for an instant. The time to rise to the top is t = u / g and the greatest height is h = u² / 2g.

sections.h: Worked example 1: a ball thrown upwards
p: A ball is thrown upwards at 20 m/s. Find (a) the time it takes to reach its highest point and (b) the greatest height. Take g = 10 m/s².

b: u = 20 m/s, v = 0 at the top, g = 10 m/s².
(a) v = u - gt gives 0 = 20 - 10t, so t = 2 s.
(b) v² = u² - 2gh gives 0 = 400 - 20h, so h = 20 m.
The ball takes another 2 s to fall back, so the total time of flight is 4 s.

sections.h: Worked example 2: a stone dropped from a height
p: A stone is dropped from the top of a tower 45 m high. How long does it take to hit the ground, and how fast is it moving when it lands? (g = 10 m/s²)

b: h = ½gt² gives 45 = 5t², so t² = 9 and t = 3 s.

p: A particle is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from the top of a tower 20 m high. Find the horizontal distance travelled before it hits level ground. (g = 10 m/s²)

b: The vertical motion and the horizontal motion are independent. Downwards: initial vertical velocity = 0, h = 20 m.
h = ½gt² gives 20 = 5t², so t² = 4 and t = 2 s.
Horizontally the velocity stays 10 m/s (no force acts sideways).
Horizontal distance = 10 x 2 = 20 m.

units.title: Linear Momentum and Impulse
units.summary: The meaning of momentum, the formula p = mv, impulse as change in momentum, and worked examples.

p: Momentum is the quantity of motion a body has. A heavy lorry moving slowly and a small ball moving very fast can both be hard to stop. Momentum combines mass and velocity.
Linear momentum = mass x velocity, or p = mv. The SI unit is kilogram metre per second (kg m/s). Momentum is a vector quantity, and its direction is the direction of the velocity.
Example 1: a 5 kg object moves at 10 m/s. p = mv = 5 x 10 = 50 kg m/s.
When a force acts on a body, the momentum of the body changes. The force is the rate of change of momentum: F = (mv - mu) / t, where u is the initial velocity and v the final velocity.
Example 2: a 2 kg object speeds up from 5 m/s to 15 m/s in 4 s. Change in momentum = m(v - u) = 2 x (15 - 5) = 20 kg m/s. Force F = change in momentum / time = 20 / 4 = 5 N.
Impulse is the change in momentum caused by a force. Impulse = force x time = Ft = mv - mu. Its unit is the newton second (N s), which is the same as kg m/s.

A big force for a short time can give the same impulse as a small force for a long time. This is why you bend your knees when you land from a jump: you make the stopping time longer, so the force on your legs is smaller. It is also why a cricket fielder pulls their hands back when catching a fast ball.

sections.h: Worked example: impulse in a rope
p: A tractor of mass 5000 kg is used to tow a car of mass 2500 kg. The tractor moves at 3.0 m/s just before the towing rope becomes tight. Find the impulse in the rope when it jerks the car into motion.

b: When the rope becomes tight, the tractor and car move off together at a common velocity v. Momentum is conserved: 5000 x 3 = (5000 + 2500) x v.
Impulse on the car = change in its momentum = 2500 x 2 - 2500 x 0 = 5000 N s.
So the impulse in the rope is 5.0 x 10³ N s.

sections.h: Worked example: a very short force
p: A force of 100 N acts on a particle of mass 0.15 kg for 0.03 s. Find the change in the speed of the particle.

b: Ft = m Δv, so Δv = Ft / m.

units.title: Conservation of Momentum and Collisions
units.summary: The law of conservation of linear momentum, the types of collision, and worked examples.

sections.h: The law of conservation of linear momentum
p: The law states that when objects collide, the total momentum before the collision equals the total momentum after the collision, provided no external force acts on them. A system with no outside force is called an isolated system.

In symbols for two bodies: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2. Here m1 and m2 are the masses, u1 and u2 are the velocities before the collision and v1 and v2 are the velocities after. Remember that momentum is a vector, so give a velocity in the opposite direction a negative sign.
Elastic collision: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. The bodies bounce apart without any loss of energy. Collisions between gas molecules are very nearly elastic.
Inelastic collision: momentum is conserved but some kinetic energy is changed into heat, sound or deformation. Most real collisions are like this.
Perfectly inelastic collision: the bodies stick together after the collision and move with a common velocity. This loses the most kinetic energy.

sections.h: Worked example 1: bodies that stick together
p: A body of mass 5 kg moving at 10 m/s collides with a stationary body of mass 6 kg. They stick together. Find their common velocity.

b: Momentum before = 5 x 10 + 6 x 0 = 50 kg m/s.
Momentum after = (5 + 6) x v = 11v.
Conservation: 11v = 50, so v = 4.55 m/s in the original direction.

p: A trolley of mass 4 kg moves at 1.0 m/s on a smooth horizontal platform and collides with a stationary trolley of the same mass. They stick together. Find the total momentum just after the collision and the speed of the pair.

b: Momentum before = 4 x 1.0 + 4 x 0 = 4 kg m/s.
Momentum is conserved, so the total momentum after the collision is also 4 kg m/s.
Common velocity v = 4 / (4 + 4) = 0.5 m/s.

p: Rocket and jet engines: gas shoots backwards and the rocket moves forwards, so total momentum stays the same.
Guns: the bullet goes forward and the gun recoils backwards.
Road safety: crumple zones in cars lengthen the collision time to reduce the force on the passengers.
Sports: when a bat hits a ball, momentum is passed from the bat to the ball.

units.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
units.summary: Newton's three laws of motion, inertia, worked examples with forces, and real-life uses.

sections.h: Newton's first law (the law of inertia)
p: An object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless an outside (external) force acts on it.

Inertia is the reluctance of a body to change its state of rest or of uniform motion. The bigger the mass, the bigger the inertia. This is why passengers lean forward when a bus brakes suddenly: their bodies want to keep moving. It is the reason for seat belts.
The force applied on a body is directly proportional to the rate of change of its momentum and takes place in the direction of the force. For a body of constant mass, this gives F = ma.
The bigger the force, the bigger the acceleration. For the same force, the bigger the mass, the smaller the acceleration. This is why it is easier to push an empty wheelbarrow than a loaded one.
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with an equal force. The two forces act on different bodies.

Examples: when you walk, your foot pushes back on the ground and the ground pushes you forward. A rocket pushes gas downwards and the gas pushes the rocket upwards. A swimmer pushes the water backwards and the water pushes the swimmer forwards.

sections.h: Worked example 1: forces at an angle
p: Two forces, 100 N and 60 N, act on a block of mass 10 kg lying on a smooth horizontal floor as shown. The 100 N force acts at 45° above the horizontal and the 60 N force acts horizontally. Find the acceleration of the block. Neglect friction. (g = 9.8 m/s²)

img.alt: A 10 kg block on the floor with a 60 N force acting horizontally and a 100 N force at 45 degrees above the horizontal
img.cap: A 10 kg block pulled by two forces.

b: Split the 100 N force into two parts: horizontal part = 100 cos 45° = 70.71 N and vertical part = 100 sin 45° = 70.71 N (upwards).
Total horizontal force = 70.71 + 60 = 130.71 N.
The upward force (70.71 N) is smaller than the weight of the block (10 x 9.8 = 98 N), so the block stays on the floor and does not move up or down. The floor simply pushes up with a smaller reaction.
So the only unbalanced force is the horizontal one. a = F / m = 130.71 / 10 = 13.07 m/s².

sections.h: The picture of the split force
p: The picture shows how the 100 N force is split into a horizontal and a vertical part. Splitting a force this way is called resolving the force.

img.alt: The 100 N force at 45 degrees resolved into horizontal and vertical parts
img.cap: Resolving the 100 N force.

p: Example: a 1200 kg car moving at 25 m/s brakes to a stop in 5 s. Initial momentum = 1200 x 25 = 30 000 kg m/s. Average braking force = change in momentum / time = 30 000 / 5 = 6000 N.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds at 8 m/s. The contact lasts 0.2 s. Taking the direction towards the wall as positive, change in momentum = 0.5 x (-8) - 0.5 x 10 = -9 kg m/s. Average force = 9 / 0.2 = 45 N (size).
Real-life uses: seat belts (first law), braking systems (second law), rocket launch and walking (third law), and kicking a ball in sports.

units.title: Work
units.summary: What work means in Physics, the formula W = Fd cos θ, positive, negative and zero work, and worked examples.

p: In everyday speech, work means any effort. In Physics, work is done only when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force. Work = force x distance moved in the direction of the force.
If the force and the movement are in the same line, W = F x d. If the force makes an angle θ with the direction of movement, W = F d cos θ.
The SI unit of work is the joule (J). One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force.
A force must be applied.
The object must move (there must be a displacement).
The movement must have a part in the direction of the force.
If a boy pushes hard against a wall and the wall does not move, no work is done in the Physics sense, because the displacement is zero.
Positive work: the force and the movement are in the same direction (pushing a trolley forward).
Negative work: the force is opposite to the movement (friction slowing a sliding box, or a goalkeeper catching a ball).

Zero work: there is no movement, or the force is at 90 degrees to the movement. A person carrying a load along a level path does no work on the load, because the upward force is at right angles to the horizontal movement.
Try each one before looking at the working.

b: A force of 20 N moves an object through 5 m. W = F d = 20 x 5 = 100 J.
A force of 50 N pushes a cart through 20 m. W = 50 x 20 = 1000 J.
A boy pushes a wheelbarrow with 50 N for 10 m. W = 50 x 10 = 500 J.
A 10 N weight is lifted 8 m. W = 10 x 8 = 80 J.
A force of 100 N pulls a sledge 10 m along level ground with a rope at 60° to the ground. W = F d cos θ = 100 x 10 x cos 60° = 100 x 10 x 0.5 = 500 J.

units.title: Energy: Kinetic, Potential and Conservation
units.summary: Forms of energy, kinetic energy, potential energy, the principle of conservation of energy, and worked examples.

p: Energy is the ability (capacity) to do work. It is measured in joules (J), the same unit as work. When you do work on an object, you give it energy.

Mechanical energy (kinetic and potential), chemical energy (food, fuel, batteries), thermal or heat energy, electrical energy, sound energy, light energy and nuclear energy. Energy can change from one form to another. In a torch, chemical energy in the battery becomes electrical energy and then light and heat.
Kinetic energy (K.E.) is the energy a body has because it is moving. K.E. = ½mv², where m is the mass in kg and v is the speed in m/s.
Notice that speed is squared: if you double the speed of a car, its kinetic energy becomes four times bigger. This is why high speed is so dangerous on the road.

b: Find the K.E. of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s. K.E. = ½ x 2 x 3² = ½ x 2 x 9 = 9 J.
A ball of mass 0.5 kg is kicked at 10 m/s. K.E. = ½ x 0.5 x 10² = 0.25 x 100 = 25 J.
A car of mass 1000 kg moves at 10 m/s. K.E. = ½ x 1000 x 100 = 50 000 J.

p: Potential energy (P.E.) is the energy a body has because of its position or state. The gravitational potential energy of a body of mass m raised through a height h is P.E. = mgh. A stretched spring or a bent bow also stores potential energy.

b: A body of mass 4 kg is lifted to a height of 5 m. P.E. = mgh = 4 x 10 x 5 = 200 J (g = 10 m/s²).
A 4 kg object is raised 10 m. P.E. = 4 x 10 x 10 = 400 J.

p: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be changed from one form to another. The total energy of an isolated system stays the same.

Example: a ball thrown upwards. At the start it has only kinetic energy. As it rises, kinetic energy changes to potential energy. At the top, all the energy is potential. When it falls back, potential energy changes back to kinetic energy. At every point, K.E. + P.E. stays the same (if we ignore air resistance).

units.title: Power
units.summary: What power is, its formula and units, and worked examples from past WAEC and NECO questions.

p: Power is the rate at which work is done, or the rate at which energy is transferred. Two people can do the same work, but the one who does it faster has more power.
Power = work done / time taken, or P = W / t. (Be careful: power is work divided by time, not multiplied.) The SI unit of power is the watt (W). 1 W = 1 J/s.
Other units: 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W, and 1 horsepower (hp) = 746 W.
Check each answer carefully.

b: A machine does 3000 J of work in 60 s. P = W / t = 3000 / 60 = 50 W.
A machine does 1500 J of work in 25 s. P = 1500 / 25 = 60 W.
A man of mass 70 kg runs up stairs 5 m high in 7 s. Work = mgh = 70 x 10 x 5 = 3500 J. Power = 3500 / 7 = 500 W.
A pump transfers 6000 J of energy to water in 30 s. P = 6000 / 30 = 200 W.

p: The units of power are the same ones you see on electrical appliances. A 60 W bulb uses 60 J of electrical energy every second. A 2 kW electric iron uses 2000 J every second. Your electricity bill is based on the energy used, which is power x time (for example, a 2 kW heater used for 3 hours uses 6 kilowatt-hours).

WAEC style: (a) Define work and state its SI unit. Answer: Work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force; the unit is the joule. (b) A force of 50 N pushes a cart 20 m. W = 1000 J. (c) Work is done only when there is displacement in the direction of the force. (d) A boy pushes a wall that does not move: no work is done, because the displacement is zero.

NECO style: define kinetic energy (energy of a body due to its motion) and potential energy (energy of a body due to its position or state). A ball of 0.5 kg kicked at 10 m/s has K.E. = 25 J. A 4 kg body lifted 5 m has P.E. = 200 J.
No machine turns all the energy it receives into useful work. Some is wasted as heat or sound. Efficiency = (useful work output / total work input) x 100%.
Example: a machine uses 500 J to do 400 J of useful work. Efficiency = 400 / 500 x 100% = 80%.

units.title: Simple Machines and Their Types
units.summary: What a machine is, what machines do for us, and the six simple machines: lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, screw and wedge.

p: A machine is a device that makes work easier. It does not give us free energy. It helps in one or more of these ways: it multiplies the force we apply (a small effort lifts a large load), it changes the direction of the force (pulling down to lift something up), or it increases the speed or distance moved.
Basic jobs of a machine: to multiply force, to change the direction of a force, to multiply speed or distance (for example the gears on a bicycle), and to transfer a force from one point to another.

A lever is a stiff bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum. We apply an effort at one place to move a load at another place. There are three classes of lever, depending on where the fulcrum, load and effort are.
First class lever: the fulcrum is between the effort and the load (a see-saw, scissors, a crowbar).
Second class lever: the load is between the fulcrum and the effort (a wheelbarrow, a nutcracker, a bottle opener).
Third class lever: the effort is between the fulcrum and the load (tongs, a fishing rod, a broom).

A pulley is a wheel on an axle with a rope or belt running over it. A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force (as at the top of a flagpole). A movable pulley moves with the load and halves the effort needed. A pulley system (block and tackle) combines fixed and movable pulleys. Its velocity ratio equals the number of rope sections supporting the load, which is the same as the number of pulleys for the systems in your syllabus. Cranes and the hoists used on building sites use pulleys.

img.alt: A block and tackle pulley system with four pulleys lifting a 1200 N load, with the effort E on the free end of the rope
img.cap: A block and tackle pulley system lifting a 1200 N load.

p: An inclined plane is a flat surface set at a slope. It is easier to push a heavy drum up a ramp than to lift it straight up, but you must push it a longer distance. The velocity ratio of an inclined plane is VR = 1 / sin θ, which is the same as the length of the slope divided by its height. Ramps, staircases and mountain roads are inclined planes.

img.alt: An inclined plane with the sloping side XY, the vertical height YZ and the horizontal base XZ
img.cap: An inclined plane: slope XY, vertical height YZ.

sections.h: Wheel and axle, screw, and wedge
p: Wheel and axle: a large wheel fixed to a small axle so that they turn together. Examples: a steering wheel, a door knob, a screwdriver handle, a water-well winch. VR = R / r (radius of the wheel divided by the radius of the axle).

Screw: an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder. Examples: a screw jack, a bottle cap, a drill bit. For a screw jack, VR = 2πR / p, where R is the length of the effort arm and p is the distance between two threads (the pitch).
Wedge: two inclined planes joined back to back, used to split, cut or lift. Examples: an axe, a knife, a chisel.

units.title: Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency
units.summary: The meaning and formulae of effort, load, mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency, and how they are related.

p: Effort (E) is the force we apply to operate the machine. Load (L) is the resistance, or weight, that we want to move.
Mechanical advantage (MA) is the ratio of the load to the effort: MA = load / effort. It has no unit. A MA of 4 means that 1 N of effort lifts a load of 4 N.
Velocity ratio (VR) is the ratio of the distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load: VR = distance moved by effort / distance moved by load. It also has no unit.
Efficiency (η) is the ratio of the useful work output to the total work input, written as a percentage.
Work output = load x distance moved by the load. Work input = effort x distance moved by the effort.
Efficiency = (work output / work input) x 100%, which can be written as Efficiency = (MA / VR) x 100%.
No real machine is 100% efficient, because some energy is always wasted overcoming friction between moving parts and in heating or making sound.
Pulley system: VR = number of pulleys (rope sections supporting the load).
Inclined plane: VR = 1 / sin θ = length of slope / height.
Wheel and axle: VR = R / r.
Screw jack: VR = 2πR / p.

MA = L / E. VR = distance moved by effort / distance moved by load. Efficiency = MA / VR x 100%. Rearranged: MA = efficiency x VR, and L = MA x E. Learn these four lines; every machine problem uses them.

units.title: Machine Problems and Machines in Daily Life
units.summary: Worked problems on MA, VR and efficiency, taken from the pulley, inclined plane and past-question types, plus everyday uses.

p: A block and tackle system has six pulleys. A force of 50 N applied to it lifts a load W. If its efficiency is 40%, calculate W.

b: VR = number of pulleys = 6. Effort E = 50 N. Efficiency = 40% = 0.4.
Efficiency = (MA / VR), so MA = 0.4 x 6 = 2.4.
MA = load / effort, so W = 2.4 x 50 = 120 N.

p: The picture shows a block and tackle with 6 pulleys supporting a load of 100 N. If its efficiency is 75%, calculate the effort N.

img.alt: A block and tackle pulley system with an effort N on the free end of the rope
img.cap: Block and tackle with effort N.

b: VR = 6. Efficiency = 0.75.
MA = efficiency x VR = 0.75 x 6 = 4.5.
MA = load / effort, so effort = load / MA = 100 / 4.5 = 22.2 N.

p: A simple machine of 75% efficiency lifts a load of 5000 N when an effort of 500 N is applied. Calculate its velocity ratio.

b: MA = load / effort = 5000 / 500 = 10.
Efficiency = MA / VR, so 0.75 = 10 / VR.

p: A machine of efficiency 75% lifts a load of 600 N through a vertical height of 2 m. Find (i) the work done on the load and (ii) the work input to the machine.

b: (i) Work output = load x height = 600 x 2 = 1200 J.
(ii) Efficiency = work output / work input, so work input = 1200 / 0.75 = 1600 J.

p: An inclined plane 5 m long raises a load of 1000 N through a vertical height of 1.25 m. A force of 300 N pushes the load up the slope. Find the VR, MA and efficiency.

b: VR = length / height = 5 / 1.25 = 4.
MA = load / effort = 1000 / 300 = 3.33.

sections.h: Problem 6: a quick one, and a short reason
p: The velocity ratio of a machine is 5 and its efficiency is 80%. Find MA: MA = 0.8 x 5 = 4.
Two reasons why no machine is 100% efficient: energy is lost to friction between moving parts, and some energy is turned into heat or sound instead of useful work.

Lever: crowbar, scissors, pliers. Pulley: lifting cranes, flag hoist. Inclined plane: ramp for loading goods. Wheel and axle: cars, rolling chairs, door knobs. Wedge: axe, chisel, knife. Screw: jack, bottle cap, car wheel nut.
A simple machine does only one basic job. A compound machine combines several simple machines, for example a bicycle (wheel and axle, levers and gears) or a pair of scissors with its screw.

units.title: Heat and Temperature
units.summary: The meaning of heat energy and temperature, how they differ, and what thermometric properties are.

p: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a place of higher temperature to a place of lower temperature. It stops flowing when both are at the same temperature. Heat is measured in joules (J). It moves by conduction, convection and radiation.

Temperature is a measure of how hot or cold a body is. It tells us the direction in which heat will flow: from the body at the higher temperature to the one at the lower temperature. It is measured in degrees Celsius (°C), degrees Fahrenheit (°F) or kelvin (K). The SI unit is the kelvin.
A bath tub of lukewarm water holds much more heat than a cup of hot tea, even though the tea has a higher temperature. Temperature does not depend on how much material there is; heat does.

units.title: Thermometers
units.summary: The main types of thermometer, how each works and where each is used, and how to calibrate a mercury thermometer.

p: Mercury expands evenly when heated, so the thread of mercury in a narrow glass tube rises as the temperature rises. It is accurate, used in laboratories and has a range from about -10 °C to 110 °C. It cannot be used in very cold places because mercury freezes at -39 °C. Mercury is liked because it does not wet glass, conducts heat well, is easy to see and expands regularly.

How it is calibrated: stand the thermometer upright with the bulb in melting pure ice. Wait until the mercury thread stops moving and mark this as the lower fixed point (0 °C). Then hold the bulb in the steam above boiling pure water. When the thread stops rising, mark the upper fixed point (100 °C). Divide the space between the two marks into 100 equal parts.

Alcohol (usually coloured red) expands more than mercury and freezes only at about -115 °C, so it can be used in very cold regions, from about -80 °C to 78 °C. It is also less poisonous than mercury, but it is less accurate and it wets the glass.

A clinical thermometer measures the body temperature of a person. It has a short range from 35 °C to 42 °C so it can be read accurately. It has a narrow bend, called a constriction, near the bulb, which stops the mercury from flowing back so that you can read it after removing it from the patient. You shake it to bring the mercury back to the bulb.
Digital thermometer: reads quickly and shows the value as numbers on a screen. Used in hospitals and homes.
Thermocouple: uses the voltage made where two different metals meet. It can measure very high temperatures (up to about 1800 °C) and is used in industry.
Bimetallic strip: two metals bonded together that expand by different amounts, so the strip bends when heated. It is used in thermostats for irons and fridges.
Gas thermometer: uses the pressure of a gas at constant volume. It is very accurate.
Resistance thermometer: uses the change of electrical resistance of a platinum wire.

sections.h: Desirable properties of a thermometer liquid
p: It should expand regularly, expand a lot for a small change in temperature, respond quickly (good conductor of heat), be easy to see, not stick to the glass, and have a wide range between its freezing and boiling points.

units.title: Temperature Scales and Conversions
units.summary: Fixed points, the Celsius, Kelvin and Fahrenheit scales, conversion formulae, and worked examples including uncalibrated thermometers.

sections.h: Fixed points and the fundamental interval
p: The lower fixed point is the temperature of pure melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure (760 mm of mercury). The upper fixed point is the temperature of steam from pure boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure. The fundamental interval is the difference between the upper and lower fixed points.
Celsius (centigrade) scale: ice point = 0 °C, steam point = 100 °C, so the fundamental interval is divided into 100 equal parts.
Kelvin scale: an absolute scale. Ice point = 273 K, steam point = 373 K. It also has 100 equal parts, so a change of 1 °C is the same as a change of 1 K. 0 K is the coldest possible temperature.
Fahrenheit scale: ice point = 32 °F, steam point = 212 °F, so the interval has 180 parts.
Celsius to Kelvin: K = °C + 273. Kelvin to Celsius: °C = K - 273.
Celsius to Fahrenheit: °F = (9/5) x °C + 32, or °F = 1.8 x °C + 32.
Fahrenheit to Celsius: °C = (5/9) x (°F - 32).

b: Convert 25 °C to kelvin: K = 25 + 273 = 298 K.
Convert 0 °C to °F: °F = 1.8 x 0 + 32 = 32 °F.
Convert 273 K to °C: °C = 273 - 273 = 0 °C.
A thermometer reads 77 °F. °C = (5/9) x (77 - 32) = (5/9) x 45 = 25 °C. In kelvin = 25 + 273 = 298 K.

p: A change in temperature is the same size in °C and in K. Example: an object is heated from 30 °C to 57 °C. The rise is 57 - 30 = 27 °C, which is also a rise of 27 K. (Do not add 273 to a change; add 273 only when converting a temperature reading. 27 °C itself is 300 K.)

Sometimes a thermometer has the wrong fixed points. Because the scale is evenly spaced, we can still find the true Celsius temperature using proportions: (reading - lower point) / (upper point - lower point) = (true temperature - 0) / (100 - 0).

units.title: Heat Measurement and Specific Heat Capacity
units.summary: How heat moves, units of heat, specific heat capacity, the formula Q = mcΔθ and worked examples.

p: Heat is energy that flows from a hot place to a cold place. It travels by conduction (through solids), convection (in liquids and gases) and radiation (as waves, like the heat from the Sun). The SI unit of heat is the joule (J). An older unit is the calorie: 1 calorie = 4.186 J. Heat is a scalar quantity.
Different materials need different amounts of heat to warm up. A pot of water takes much longer to heat than an equal mass of iron.
Specific heat capacity (c) is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K). Its unit is joule per kilogram per kelvin (J/kg K).
The heat Q needed (or given out) is Q = m c Δθ, where m = mass in kg, c = specific heat capacity and Δθ = change of temperature (final minus initial).

Water has a very high specific heat capacity. It takes a lot of heat to warm up and gives out a lot when it cools. That is why the sea stays cooler than the land during the day, why hot water bottles keep us warm, and why water is used to cool car engines.
The heat capacity (C) of a whole body is the heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 K. Heat capacity = mass x specific heat capacity, so C = mc. Its unit is J/K. So Q = C Δθ.
Take your time with the numbers.

b: Heat needed to raise 1.5 kg of water from 25 °C to 100 °C: Q = mcΔθ = 1.5 x 4200 x (100 - 25) = 6300 x 75 = 472 500 J.
A 2 kg metal needs 7200 J to rise from 20 °C to 80 °C. c = Q / (mΔθ) = 7200 / (2 x 60) = 60 J/kg K.
How much heat is given out when 3 kg of iron cools from 150 °C to 50 °C? Q = 3 x 460 x 100 = 138 000 J.

units.title: Latent Heat
units.summary: What latent heat is, latent heat of fusion and vaporisation, the formula Q = mL, and worked examples.

sections.h: Heat that does not change the temperature
p: When you heat ice, its temperature rises to 0 °C. Then it starts melting, and while it melts the temperature stays at 0 °C, even though you keep supplying heat. The same thing happens when water boils: it stays at 100 °C. The heat is not raising the temperature; it is breaking the forces that hold the particles together.
Latent heat is the heat energy absorbed or released when a substance changes state without any change of temperature.
Specific latent heat of fusion (Lf): the heat needed to change 1 kg of a solid to a liquid at its melting point, without a change of temperature.
Specific latent heat of vaporisation (Lv): the heat needed to change 1 kg of a liquid to a gas at its boiling point, without a change of temperature.
Formula: Q = mL, where m is the mass (kg) and L is the specific latent heat (J/kg).
The same amounts of heat are given out in the reverse changes (freezing and condensing).

sections.h: Why steam burns more than boiling water
p: Steam at 100 °C carries 2.26 million joules of extra heat per kilogram compared with water at 100 °C. When steam touches your skin and turns back to water, it gives out all that latent heat, so it burns much more than boiling water. Sweating cools you for the same reason: sweat takes latent heat from your skin when it evaporates.
Check the calculation each time.

b: A 0.5 kg substance absorbs 167 000 J to vaporise. L = Q / m = 167 000 / 0.5 = 334 000 J/kg.
A 0.3 kg substance melts at 0 °C using 100 000 J. Lf = 100 000 / 0.3 = 3.33 x 10⁵ J/kg.
Heat needed to melt 2 kg of ice at 0 °C: Q = mL = 2 x 3.34 x 10⁵ = 6.68 x 10⁵ J.

A box of volume 0.28 m³ is 70% filled with iron filings at 25 °C. Find the energy to melt 10% of the filings. (Density of iron 8000 kg/m³, latent heat of fusion 1.38 x 10⁵ J/kg, specific heat capacity 460 J/kg K, melting point 1500 °C.) Mass of filings = 0.28 x 0.70 x 8000 = 1568 kg. 10% of this = 156.8 kg. Heat to warm it from 25 °C to 1500 °C: mcΔθ = 156.8 x 460 x 1475 = 1.064 x 10⁸ J. Heat to melt it: mL = 156.8 x 1.38 x 10⁵ = 2.16 x 10⁷ J. Total = 1.064 x 10⁸ + 0.216 x 10⁸ = 1.28 x 10⁸ J.

units.title: Calorimetry and the Method of Mixtures
units.summary: How heat exchange is measured, the rule heat lost = heat gained, and worked examples with mixtures and electric heaters.

p: Calorimetry is the measurement of the heat exchanged in a physical or chemical process. The container used is called a calorimeter. It is usually a thin metal can (copper or aluminium) with a lid, surrounded by an insulator, so that very little heat is lost to the air.

When a hot substance is mixed with a cold one and no heat escapes to the surroundings, the heat lost by the hot substance equals the heat gained by the cold substance (and the calorimeter): heat lost = heat gained.
Using Q = mcΔθ on both sides gives a simple equation. The final temperature is the same for everything in the mixture.
Method of mixtures: mix hot and cold substances and measure the final temperature.
Electrical method: a heater of known power (P = VI) supplies heat for a measured time, so the energy supplied is E = VIt = Pt.
Using a temperature change: apply Q = mcΔθ to a substance whose specific heat capacity is known.
200 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with 300 g of water at 20 °C. Find the final temperature. (Ignore heat losses.)

b: Let the final temperature be θ. Heat lost by hot water = 0.2 x 4200 x (80 - θ). Heat gained by cold water = 0.3 x 4200 x (θ - 20).

p: A nursing mother prepared baby's milk at 85 °C. To cool 300 g of the milk to 40 °C, she placed the bottle in an aluminium bowl of heat capacity 90 J/K containing 500 g of water at 26 °C. Find the specific heat capacity of the milk. (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg K; neglect heat losses and the heat capacity of the bottle.)

b: Heat lost by the milk = heat gained by the water + heat gained by the bowl.

p: A 40 V electric heater supplies a current of 12 A to a body of mass 1.5 kg that is already at its melting point. The body melts completely, then its temperature rises by 60 °C in a further 72 s. Find its specific heat capacity.

b: Energy supplied in the 72 s = VIt = 40 x 12 x 72 = 34 560 J.
This energy raised the temperature by 60 °C: 34 560 = 1.5 x c x 60 = 90c.

units.title: The Particulate Nature of Matter
units.summary: What matter is, the idea that all matter is made of particles, and how particles are arranged in solids, liquids and gases.

p: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space (volume). A stone, water and air are all matter. Light and sound are not matter, because they have no mass.

sections.h: Matter is made of tiny particles
p: The particulate nature of matter means that all matter is made of very small separate pieces called particles. Depending on the substance, the particles are atoms, molecules or ions. An atom is the smallest particle of an element. A molecule is a group of two or more atoms joined together (water molecules are made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom). An ion is an atom, or group of atoms, that carries an electric charge.

The particles are extremely small and cannot be seen with the naked eye. They are always moving. They attract each other with forces called intermolecular forces. There are spaces between the particles, and these spaces are large in gases.
The picture shows the three states of matter, solid, liquid and gas, and how the particles are arranged in each. Read the table below as well.

p: When a solid is heated, its particles gain energy and vibrate harder until they break out of their fixed positions: the solid melts into a liquid. With more heat the particles move faster and escape from the liquid: the liquid boils (or evaporates) into a gas. When a gas is cooled, the particles slow down and come together again (condensation), and when a liquid is cooled, it freezes. All these changes show that matter is made of particles whose motion depends on the amount of energy they have.

units.title: Diffusion, Brownian Motion and the Kinetic Theory
units.summary: Evidence that particles move: diffusion and Brownian motion, the kinetic theory of matter, and its everyday applications.

p: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a region where there are many of them (high concentration) to a region where there are fewer (low concentration), until they are evenly spread. It happens fastest in gases, slower in liquids and very slowly in solids.

Examples: perfume spreads through a room; a drop of ink spreads through a glass of water; crystals of potassium permanganate placed in water colour all of the water without stirring; the smell of cooking gas or fried plantain spreads from the kitchen to the house.
Explanation: the particles are always moving and bumping into each other, so over time they spread out evenly.

Brownian motion is the random, zig-zag movement of tiny visible particles, such as pollen grains in water or smoke particles in air, caused by collisions with the much smaller, invisible molecules of the fluid around them. It was first seen by Robert Brown with pollen grains.

You can see it by looking at smoke in a small glass cell with a microscope. The smoke specks dance about randomly. This is strong evidence that the molecules of air are always moving and that matter is made of particles.

The kinetic theory explains the behaviour of matter by the motion of its particles. Its main ideas are: matter is made of very small particles; the particles are always in constant random motion; there are spaces between the particles; collisions between particles and with the walls of the container are perfectly elastic (no energy is lost); temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles; and the forces between particles are strong in solids, weaker in liquids and almost zero in gases.
Perfume spreading in air is diffusion in gases.
Sugar dissolving in water is particles mixing and spreading.
A car tyre becomes harder in the afternoon because the air molecules gain kinetic energy and hit the tyre wall harder.
A refrigerator works using latent heat and the motion of molecules.
Boiling water produces steam because the molecules move so fast that they escape from the liquid.

units.title: Fluids at Rest: Pressure in a Liquid
units.summary: What a fluid is, how pressure acts in a liquid at rest, the formula P = ρgh, what affects it and worked examples.

p: A fluid is any substance that can flow and take the shape of its container. Liquids and gases are fluids. Fluids have no fixed shape, they push in all directions, they can flow easily and gases can also be compressed.
This topic has two parts: fluids at rest (fluid statics) and fluids in motion (fluid dynamics). The picture shows how the topic is divided.

img.alt: A diagram with Fluids at Rest and Motion in the centre, linked to pressure, density, buoyancy, Pascal's principle, flow rate, viscosity, continuity equation and Bernoulli's principle
img.cap: The ideas in this topic: fluids at rest and fluids in motion.

p: Pressure is the force acting on each unit of area. Pressure = force / area, or P = F / A. The SI unit is the pascal (Pa), which is one newton per square metre (N/m²).

A liquid has weight, so the liquid above a point presses down on that point. The deeper you go, the more liquid is above you and the greater the pressure. This is why a diver feels more pressure in his ears deeper down, and why the walls of a dam are built thicker at the bottom.

Formula: P = ρgh, where P is the pressure (Pa), ρ (rho) is the density of the liquid (kg/m³), g is the acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/s² or about 10 m/s²) and h is the depth below the surface (m).

Facts about pressure in a liquid at rest: it increases with depth; at the same depth it is the same in all directions; and it does not depend on the shape of the container or the amount of liquid, only on the depth and the density.

sections.h: What affects the pressure at a point
p: Only two things: the depth of the point below the surface, and the density of the liquid. Deeper means more pressure. A denser liquid (like mercury) gives more pressure at the same depth than a less dense liquid (like water).

Look at the picture of a cylinder in a liquid. The pressure P1 on the bottom face is bigger than the pressure P2 on the top face because the bottom is deeper. This difference pushes the cylinder upwards. That upward push is called upthrust, which you will meet again in Unit 4.

img.alt: A cylinder submerged in a liquid with arrows showing a smaller pressure P2 on the top face and a larger pressure P1 on the bottom face
img.cap: The bottom of the cylinder is deeper, so P1 is greater than P2.

p: Try them yourself first.

b: Pressure at a depth of 5 m in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²): P = ρgh = 1000 x 9.8 x 5 = 49 000 Pa.
Pressure at a depth of 10 m in sea water of density 1030 kg/m³ (g = 10 m/s²): P = 1030 x 10 x 10 = 103 000 Pa.

A liquid of volume 2.00 m³ and density 1000 kg/m³ is mixed with 3.00 m³ of another liquid of density 8000 kg/m³. Density of the mixture = total mass / total volume = (2 x 1000 + 3 x 8000) / (2 + 3) = 26 000 / 5 = 5200 kg/m³.

units.title: Pascal's Principle and Its Uses
units.summary: Pascal's principle, the formula F1/A1 = F2/A2, and how hydraulic machines such as lifts and car brakes work.

p: Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to a confined (enclosed) fluid is transmitted equally and without loss in all directions through the fluid.

If we push on one piston with force F1 and area A1, the pressure is F1 / A1. This same pressure acts on a second piston of area A2 and gives a force F2. So F1 / A1 = F2 / A2. A small force on a small piston gives a big force on a big piston.

A hydraulic machine has two cylinders of different widths joined together and filled with oil. Oil is used because it cannot be compressed easily and it does not rust the metal. When you push down the small piston, the oil pushes the big piston up with a much bigger force. The big piston moves a shorter distance than the small piston, so work is not created from nothing.
Hydraulic lifts and jacks that raise cars in a workshop.
Car brakes: when you press the brake pedal, the pressure is passed through the brake fluid to all four wheels at once.
Hydraulic presses that squeeze metal sheets or oil seeds.
Dentists' and barbers' chairs.
The arms of excavators and bulldozers.
A hydraulic press has a small piston of area 0.01 m² and a large piston of area 0.5 m². A force of 200 N is applied to the small piston. Find the force on the large piston.

b: F1 / A1 = F2 / A2, so F2 = F1 x A2 / A1.
The force is multiplied by 50, because the area of the big piston is 50 times that of the small one.

p: A small piston of area 5 cm² is pushed with a force of 40 N. What load can the large piston of area 400 cm² lift? Pressure = 40 / 5 = 8 N/cm². Force on the big piston = 8 x 400 = 3200 N.
