units.title: Archimedes' Principle, Relative Density and Floating
units.summary: Upthrust, Archimedes' principle, apparent weight, finding relative density of a stone, and the law of floatation.

p: When you put an object in water, the water pushes up on it. This upward force is called upthrust. That is why you feel lighter in a swimming pool.
Archimedes' principle states that when a body is wholly or partly immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced = ρ x g x V, where ρ is the density of the fluid, g is gravity and V is the volume of fluid displaced.
Apparent weight = true weight (weight in air) - upthrust.
Look at each one carefully.

b: A body weighing 14 N in air is partly immersed in water and displaces 200 g (0.2 kg) of water. Upthrust = weight of water displaced = 0.2 x 10 = 2 N.

A metal cube of volume 0.002 m³ is immersed in a liquid of density 1200 kg/m³ (g = 10 m/s²). Upthrust = ρgV = 1200 x 10 x 0.002 = 24 N. If its weight in air is 25 N, its apparent weight in the liquid = 25 - 24 = 1 N.

sections.h: Finding the relative density of a stone
p: Relative density = density of a substance / density of water. It has no unit.

Method: weigh the stone in air (W1). Weigh the stone when it is fully immersed in water (W2). The upthrust = W1 - W2. Because the upthrust equals the weight of an equal volume of water, relative density = weight in air / upthrust = W1 / (W1 - W2).
Example: a stone weighs 4.0 N in air and 3.0 N in water. Upthrust = 1.0 N. Relative density = 4.0 / 1.0 = 4. So the stone is 4 times denser than water.
The law of floatation states that a floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats. That means a body floats when its weight is equal to the upthrust on it.

An object floats if its density is less than the density of the fluid. It sinks if its density is greater. Steel sinks but a steel ship floats because the ship is hollow: its average density (including the air inside) is smaller than the density of water, so it can displace a lot of water.
Ships and submarines (a submarine fills tanks with water to sink and with air to rise).
Hydrometers, which measure the density of liquids such as battery acid and milk.
Ice floats on water because its density is slightly less.
Life jackets and floating logs.
Icebergs, where about nine-tenths of the ice is below the water.

units.title: Fluids in Motion: Streamline Flow, Continuity and Bernoulli
units.summary: Streamline and turbulent flow, the equation of continuity, Bernoulli's principle and where they are used.

p: Streamline (laminar) flow is smooth flow in parallel layers that do not mix, such as oil moving slowly in a narrow pipe. It happens with low velocity, smooth surfaces and small pipes.
Turbulent flow is irregular, swirling flow, such as a waterfall or a fast river. It happens at high speed or around obstacles.

For a steady flow of a fluid that cannot be compressed, the amount of fluid passing each point every second is the same. So the cross-sectional area A times the velocity v is the same everywhere: A1v1 = A2v2.

This means a fluid flows faster in a narrow pipe and slower in a wide pipe. Your thumb over the end of a garden hose makes the water shoot out faster. Blood speeds up where an artery narrows. Irrigation pipes and water mains are designed with this rule.

b: A pipe has cross-sectional areas 0.04 m² and 0.01 m² at its two ends. Water enters at 3 m/s. Find the exit velocity.

p: Bernoulli's principle states that in the streamline flow of a fluid, the sum of the pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume is constant: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant.
P is the pressure, ρ the density, v the velocity and h the height. The most important idea is this: where a fluid moves faster, its pressure is lower.
Aeroplane wings: the wing is curved on top, so air flows faster over the top than below. The pressure above is lower than below, which gives an upward force (lift).
Atomisers and sprayers (perfume, insecticide): fast air across a tube lowers the pressure and pulls liquid up.
Chimneys and carburettors.
Sailing and the swerving of a spinning ball.

units.title: Surface Tension
units.summary: What surface tension is, its effects, what affects it, and how it can be reduced.

p: The surface of a liquid behaves like a stretched elastic skin. The force acting along the surface of a liquid that causes this is called surface tension. It is caused by the attraction between the molecules of the liquid (cohesion). A molecule inside a liquid is pulled equally in all directions, but a molecule at the surface is pulled only inwards and sideways, so the surface tries to become as small as possible.
A pond skater (a small insect) walks on the surface of water without sinking.
A needle or a razor blade, placed carefully, floats on water.
Mercury forms round beads and raindrops are round.
Water forms small round drops on a waxed or oily surface.
Soap bubbles are round, and a small amount of liquid hangs from a tap before dropping.
The type of liquid: mercury has a very large surface tension; water is medium; alcohol is small.
Temperature: surface tension decreases when the temperature rises, so hot water is better at cleaning.
Impurities: most dissolved impurities, such as soap or detergent, reduce the surface tension.
Raise the temperature of the liquid.
Add soap or detergent. This is why soapy water spreads and cleans well.
Add alcohol or camphor to the water.
Remember that a high surface tension is what lets small insects and a needle stay on top of water. When the surface tension is reduced (for example by soap), they sink.

units.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Boyle's Law
units.summary: What a gas is, the assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases, and Boyle's law with graphs, an experiment and worked examples.

p: A gas is a state of matter with no fixed shape or volume. It takes the shape and volume of its container. The particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

sections.h: Assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases
p: A gas is made up of a very large number of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) in constant random motion.
The volume of the particles is tiny compared with the volume of the container.
There are no forces of attraction or repulsion between the particles, except when they collide.
Collisions between the particles and the walls of the container are perfectly elastic (no energy is lost).
The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the absolute temperature (in kelvin): K.E. average = (3/2) k T, where k = 1.38 x 10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant.
Gas pressure is caused by the particles hitting the walls of the container again and again.
Boyle's law states that at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure. When the pressure rises, the volume falls, and the other way round.
In symbols: P ∝ 1/V, so PV = constant, or P1V1 = P2V2 for two different conditions of the same gas.
Think of a bicycle pump: when you push the plunger and the air is squeezed into a smaller space, the pressure goes up.
A graph of pressure against volume is a curve called a hyperbola: when V is small P is big, and when V is big P is small. A graph of pressure against 1/volume is a straight line through the origin.

img.alt: Two graphs: pressure against volume showing a falling curve, and pressure against one over volume showing a straight line through the origin
img.cap: Left: P against V (hyperbola). Right: P against 1/V (straight line).

p: Dry air is trapped in a glass tube of uniform width (tube C) that is joined by rubber tubing to an open tube (B) containing mercury. By raising or lowering tube B, the length of the air column in C changes. The length l measures the volume, because the tube has the same width all along. The difference h between the mercury levels in B and C is read each time. The atmospheric pressure H is read from a barometer.

If the mercury in B is higher than in C, the trapped air pressure is P = H + h (in cmHg). If the mercury in B is lower than in C, then P = H - h. Plot P against 1/l. A straight line shows that P is inversely proportional to V.

img.alt: Apparatus with a closed tube C holding trapped air of length l and an open tube B whose mercury level is higher by h
img.cap: Tube B raised: the mercury in B is higher than in C, so P = H + h.

sections.h: The other position of tube B
p: In this picture the open tube B has been lowered, so the mercury level in B is below the level in C. The pressure of the trapped air is then smaller than the atmospheric pressure: P = H - h.

img.alt: Apparatus with a closed tube C holding trapped air of length l and an open tube B whose mercury level is lower by h
img.cap: Tube B lowered: the mercury in B is lower than in C, so P = H - h.

The tube has the same width all along, so volume is proportional to length. Boyle's law: H x 5.0 = (H + 11 560) x 4.5.

units.title: Charles's Law and the Pressure Law
units.summary: How the volume of a gas depends on temperature (Charles's law) and how pressure depends on temperature (pressure law), with worked examples.

p: In all gas laws, temperatures must be in kelvin. K = °C + 273. If you use °C, your answer will be wrong. This is the most common mistake in gas-law questions.
Charles's law states that at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (in kelvin).

In symbols: V ∝ T, so V / T = constant, or V1 / T1 = V2 / T2. A balloon left in a hot sun grows bigger because the air inside expands. A hot-air balloon rises because the heated air expands and becomes less dense.

b: A gas has a volume of 100 cm³ at 27 °C. It is heated at constant pressure until its volume is 120 cm³. Find the new temperature.
In degrees Celsius: 360 - 273 = 87 °C.

p: The pressure law states that at constant volume, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.

In symbols: P ∝ T, so P / T = constant, or P1 / T1 = P2 / T2. A sealed can of air that is heated may burst because the pressure rises. A pressure cooker uses this law to reach a temperature above 100 °C. A car tyre pressure rises on a long hot journey.

b: A fixed mass of gas at 27 °C is heated at constant volume until its pressure doubles. Find the final temperature.

p: Boyle's law: constant temperature; P and V change in opposite ways. Charles's law: constant pressure; V and T change together. Pressure law: constant volume; P and T change together.

units.title: The General Gas Law, the Ideal Gas and Molar Volume
units.summary: Combining the gas laws, the equation PV = nRT, Avogadro's law, molar volume, real versus ideal gases and applications.

p: Boyle's law, Charles's law and the pressure law can be joined into one equation that works when pressure, volume and temperature all change together: P1V1 / T1 = P2V2 / T2, or PV / T = constant. Remember to change °C to kelvin and use the same units for both sides.

b: The volume and pressure of a given mass of gas at 27 °C are 76 cm³ and 80 cmHg. Find its volume at s.t.p. (273 K and 76 cmHg).

p: A gas of volume 3 L at 300 K and 2 atm is heated to 600 K and its pressure is raised to 4 atm. Find its new volume. V2 = P1V1T2 / (T1P2) = (2 x 3 x 600) / (300 x 4) = 3600 / 1200 = 3 L.

For a gas that contains n moles, the law becomes PV = nRT. P is the pressure (Pa), V is the volume (m³), n is the number of moles, R is the universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol K, often taken as 8.3) and T is the temperature in kelvin. A mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.02 x 10²³ particles.
Number of moles n = mass / molar mass.

b: Find the pressure of one mole of an ideal gas of volume 10⁻² m³ at 27 °C. (R = 8.3 J/mol K)

p: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain the same number of molecules.
At s.t.p. (standard temperature 273 K and standard pressure 1 atm), one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm³ (22.4 litres). This is called the molar volume.
Example: a gas at s.t.p. has a volume of 44.8 L. Number of moles = 44.8 / 22.4 = 2 mol. Example: 5.6 g of helium (He = 4 g/mol) is 5.6 / 4 = 1.4 mol.

An ideal gas follows the assumptions of the kinetic theory exactly: no forces between particles, perfectly elastic collisions and particles with negligible volume. Real gases do not, so they behave nearly ideally only at low pressure and high temperature. At high pressure and low temperature, the particles are close together and the forces between them matter, so real gases deviate from the ideal gas law (this is explained by the Van der Waals equation, which you will study in later classes).

sections.h: Where the gas laws are used
p: Car air bags (Boyle's law), hot-air balloons (Charles's law), pressure cookers (pressure law), weather balloons that expand as they rise, and breathing (your lungs increase their volume, the pressure falls and air flows in).

units.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
units.summary: The meaning and conditions of SHM, its terms (amplitude, period, frequency, angular velocity) and its equations.

p: Many things move to and fro again and again: a swing, a pendulum, a guitar string, the piston of a car engine. When this repeated motion follows a special rule, we call it simple harmonic motion (SHM).

Simple harmonic motion is a periodic motion in which the acceleration of a body is directly proportional to its displacement from a fixed point (the equilibrium position) and is always directed towards that point. In symbols a = -ω²x. The minus sign shows that the acceleration points towards the centre, which is the job of the restoring force.
There is a restoring force that always acts towards the equilibrium position.
The size of this force is proportional to the displacement.
The motion repeats itself in a regular pattern (it is oscillatory).

Examples: a simple pendulum swinging through a small angle, a mass on a spring (horizontal or vertical), a vibrating tuning fork and a swing. A footballer's ball being passed to and fro is not SHM, because the force from the players does not follow the displacement rule.
Learn these terms and their meanings.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The maximum displacement from the mean position
The time taken for one complete oscillation (unit: second)
The number of oscillations in one second (unit: hertz, Hz)
The position of the particle in its cycle at a given instant

p: Displacement: x = A sin ωt (or x = A cos ωt, depending on where the timing starts).
Velocity: v = ω√(A² - x²). The maximum velocity (at the centre) is v = ωA.
Acceleration: a = -ω²x. The maximum acceleration (at the ends) is a = ω²A.
Period and frequency: T = 2π / ω = 1 / f. For a mass m on a spring of spring constant k, T = 2π√(m/k).

At the ends of the motion the displacement is greatest, the speed is zero for an instant and the acceleration is greatest. At the centre (equilibrium) the displacement is zero, the speed is greatest and the acceleration is zero.

A body going round a circle of radius r with speed v has an angular velocity ω = v / r. Example: an object whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 2.0 m at 8 m/s has ω = 8 / 2.0 = 4.0 rad/s. The force needed to keep it moving in the circle is the centripetal force F = mv²/r.

units.title: Energy in SHM and the Simple Pendulum
units.summary: The energy changes in SHM, the period of a simple pendulum T = 2π√(l/g), worked examples and applications.

p: A body in SHM keeps swapping its energy between kinetic and potential energy. At the ends, the body stops for an instant and has only potential energy (maximum). At the centre it moves fastest and has only kinetic energy (maximum). The total energy stays constant, if there is no friction.
K.E. = ½mv² = ½mω²(A² - x²). The total energy = ½mω²A².

img.alt: A pendulum swinging between positions R and Q with the lowest point C. At R and Q potential energy is maximum and kinetic energy is zero; at C potential energy is zero and kinetic energy is maximum
img.cap: Energy in a swinging pendulum: P.E. is greatest at R and Q, K.E. is greatest at C.

p: A simple pendulum is a small heavy bob hung on a light thread from a fixed support. For small angles (less than about 10 degrees) its motion is simple harmonic. Its period is T = 2π√(l/g), where l is the length of the thread in metres and g is the acceleration due to gravity.

The period depends on the length of the pendulum (longer pendulum, longer period) and on g. It does not depend on the mass of the bob, nor on the amplitude (for small swings). This is why pendulum clocks keep good time.
The period of a simple pendulum of length 80.0 cm doubles when the length is increased by x. Find x.

b: T is proportional to √l. If T doubles, then √l2 = 2√l1, so l2 = 4 l1.

p: The ear drum resonates with amplitude 0.8 x 10⁻⁷ m when an external body vibrates at 2400 Hz. Find the acceleration. (π = 3.142)

b: a = ω²r = (2πf)² r.

p: A sonometer wire vibrates in SHM with maximum amplitude 1.0 cm. The maximum acceleration is 988 m/s². Find the frequency of vibration. (π = 22/7)

b: a = ω²A, with A = 0.01 m. So 988 = ω² x 0.01, giving ω² = 98 800 and ω = 314.3 rad/s.

p: The period of a pendulum of length 1.5 m (g = 9.8 m/s²): T = 2π√(1.5/9.8) = 2π x 0.391 = 2.46 s.
A body of mass 0.5 kg oscillates at 4 Hz with amplitude 6 cm. ω = 2πf = 25.1 rad/s; maximum speed = ωA = 25.1 x 0.06 = 1.51 m/s; maximum acceleration = ω²A = 631 x 0.06 = 37.9 m/s².
Why does a pendulum clock gain time in a valley and lose time on a mountain top? g is a little bigger in the valley, so T is a little smaller and the clock ticks faster.
Uses of SHM: pendulum and quartz clocks, car suspension and shock absorbers, seismographs for earthquakes, and the strings and tuning forks of musical instruments.

units.activity: Make a simple pendulum with a stone and a 1 m string. Time 20 swings and divide by 20 to find the period. Then shorten the string to 25 cm and repeat. Compare the two periods and check that the shorter one is about half the first.

units.title: Projectile Motion
units.summary: What a projectile is, its path, the two independent motions, and the formulae for range, maximum height and time of flight.

p: A projectile is any object that, once thrown or launched, keeps moving because of its own inertia and is acted on only by gravity (and a little air resistance). Examples: a stone thrown upwards, a football kicked into the air, a javelin, an athlete doing the high jump, a stone shot from a catapult and a bullet fired from a gun.
The path of a projectile is called its trajectory. Without air resistance, the trajectory is a curve called a parabola.
Projectile motion can happen in three ways: (a) an object thrown straight upwards, (b) an object thrown horizontally from a height, and (c) an object thrown at an angle to the horizontal.
The secret of solving projectile problems is to treat the horizontal motion and vertical motion separately. They happen at the same time but do not affect each other.
Horizontal (along the x-axis): there is no force sideways, so the velocity stays constant and equal to u cos θ.
Vertical (along the y-axis): gravity pulls down, so the motion has uniform acceleration g downwards. The starting vertical speed is u sin θ.

The picture shows a projectile launched with speed u at angle θ. At each point you can see the horizontal part ux = u cos θ, which never changes, and the vertical part uy = u sin θ, which decreases to zero at the highest point A and then becomes negative as the object comes down.

img.alt: Parabolic path of a projectile from O to B showing the launch angle, horizontal and vertical velocity components at three points, the maximum height H at A and the range R
img.cap: The trajectory of a projectile with its velocity components, maximum height H and range R.

p: Range (R): the horizontal distance from the point of launch to the point where the object lands at the same level.
Maximum height (H): the greatest vertical height reached.
Time of flight (T): the time the projectile spends in the air from launch to landing.

sections.h: The formulae (launch and landing at the same level)
p: Learn this table. Here u is the launch speed, θ is the launch angle and g is the acceleration due to gravity.

head: Quantity
Formula
rows: x = u cos θ x t
y = u sin θ x t - ½gt²

p: Higher launch speed increases both range and height. The launch angle changes the shape; 45° gives the greatest range. A stronger gravity (g) shortens both range and height. A higher launch point gives a longer flight time and a longer range. Air resistance reduces height and range and changes the shape. Spin and shape matter too, as in a curved free kick in football.

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Greater g shortens range and height
Higher launch gives longer flight and range

units.title: Projectile Calculations
units.summary: Worked examples on range, maximum height and time of flight, including a projectile launched from a height.

p: The ratio of the maximum range to the maximum height of a projectile is 4. Find the angle of projection.

b: Range R = u² sin 2θ / g. Maximum height H = u² sin²θ / 2g.
R / H = (u² sin 2θ / g) x (2g / u² sin²θ) = 2 sin 2θ / sin²θ.
Using sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ: R / H = 4 sin θ cos θ / sin²θ = 4 cos θ / sin θ = 4 / tan θ.
So 4 / tan θ = 4, tan θ = 1, and θ = 45°.

p: An object is projected at 80 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Find the maximum height reached. (g = 10 m/s²)

An object is projected from a height of 80 m above the ground with a velocity of 40 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Find (a) the maximum height above the ground, and (b) the time of flight. (g = 10 m/s²)

img.alt: A projectile launched at 40 m/s from the top of an 80 m platform, rising 20 m above the launch point to point A, 100 m above the ground, and then landing on the ground
img.cap: A projectile launched from the top of an 80 m platform.

b: Starting vertical speed = 40 sin 30° = 20 m/s upwards.
(a) Extra height above the launch point = (20)² / (2 x 10) = 400 / 20 = 20 m. So the greatest height above the ground = 80 + 20 = 100 m (this is what the picture shows).
(b) The time to rise to the top = 20 / 10 = 2 s. The time to come down from 100 m: 100 = ½ x 10 x t², so t² = 20 and t = 4.47 s.
Total time of flight = 2 + 4.47 = 6.47 s.

Note: the formula T = 2u sin θ / g = 2 x 40 x 0.5 / 10 = 4 s is the time to come back to the launch level only. When the landing is lower than the launch point (80 m lower here), the object stays in the air for longer, as we just found.

p: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 60° to the horizontal. Find the time of flight, the maximum height and the range. (g = 10 m/s², sin 60° = 0.866)

b: Time of flight T = 2u sin θ / g = 2 x 20 x 0.866 / 10 = 3.46 s.

p: A stone is projected from the ground at 60° and lands 100 m away. R = u² sin 2θ / g gives 100 = u² x 0.866 / 10, so u² = 1155 and u = 34 m/s. Time of flight = 2 x 34 x 0.866 / 10 = 5.9 s.
A football is kicked at 15 m/s at 40° (g = 9.8 m/s²). Time to reach the maximum height = u sin θ / g = 15 x 0.643 / 9.8 = 0.98 s. Range = u² sin 80° / g = 225 x 0.985 / 9.8 = 22.6 m.
A particle is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from the top of a tower 20 m high (g = 10 m/s²). The fall time comes from 20 = ½ x 10 x t², so t = 2 s. The horizontal distance = 10 x 2 = 20 m.

units.activity: A cricket ball is thrown at 30 m/s at 45°. Work out its maximum height, time of flight and range with g = 10 m/s². (answers: H = 22.5 m; T = 4.24 s; R = 90 m)

units.title: Waves and Their Parts
units.summary: What a wave is, the parts of a wave, and the quantities used to describe it: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period and speed.

p: A wave is a disturbance that moves through a medium (or through space) and carries energy from one place to another without carrying matter along with it. If you tie a rope to a post and shake it up and down, a wave runs along the rope, but the rope itself stays where it is. Waves start from vibrations. Light, sound and water waves are all around us.

Look at the wave picture. Rest position: the middle line, where the particles are when no wave is passing. Displacement: how far a particle has moved from its rest position. Amplitude: the maximum displacement from the rest position, measured to the top of a crest or the bottom of a trough. Crest (peak): the highest point. Trough: the lowest point. Period: the time for one complete wave to pass a point.
In the picture below, the period is shown as the time for one complete wave (here, 4 seconds), and the amplitude is the height of the crest above the rest line.

img.alt: A wave graph of displacement in metres against time in seconds showing the period between two crests, a crest, a trough and the amplitude
img.cap: A displacement-time graph of a wave: period, crest, trough and amplitude.

p: Wavelength (λ) is the distance covered by one complete wave, for example from one crest to the next crest. It is measured in metres.
Frequency (f) is the number of complete waves passing a point each second. The unit is the hertz (Hz).
Period (T) is the time for one complete wave. T = 1 / f. The unit is the second.
Wave speed (v) is how fast the wave travels. v = f x λ. The unit is m/s.

Phase describes the position of a point in the wave cycle. Two points are in phase if they have the same displacement and move in the same direction at the same time (for example two crests). They are out of phase if they do not.

sections.h: Classification of waves by the need for a medium
p: Mechanical waves need a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel. Examples: sound waves, water waves, waves on a rope and seismic waves. Electromagnetic waves do not need a medium and can travel through a vacuum. Examples: light, radio waves, X-rays and gamma rays. That is why sunlight can reach us from space, but sound cannot.

head: Type of wave
Needs a medium?

rows: Light, radio waves, X-rays, gamma rays

units.title: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
units.summary: The two kinds of wave by direction of vibration: how they move, their features and examples, and how to tell them apart.

p: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction in which the wave travels. A wave on a rope (shake the end up and down and the wave moves along) is a good example.
Features: it is made of crests and troughs. It can travel through solids and on the surface of liquids.
Examples: light waves, all electromagnetic waves, water ripples and waves on strings.
In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth along the same direction in which the wave travels. A slinky spring pushed and pulled along its length shows this.
Features: it is made of compressions (places where the particles are squeezed together) and rarefactions (places where the particles are spread out). It can travel through solids, liquids and gases.
Examples: sound waves and waves along a slinky spring.

sections.h: The two kinds in one picture
p: The picture shows both waves. In the longitudinal wave, the lines show how close the particles are: where they are close together is a compression, and where they are far apart is a rarefaction. One wavelength is the distance from one compression to the next. In the transverse wave, you can see the crests and troughs, the amplitude and the wavelength.

img.alt: A longitudinal wave drawn as vertical lines with compressions and expansions and a transverse wave drawn as a sine curve with crests, troughs, amplitude and wavelength
img.cap: A longitudinal wave (top) and a transverse wave (bottom).

units.title: Properties of Waves
units.summary: Reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference, stationary waves and polarisation, with worked examples on refraction.

p: Reflection is the bouncing back of a wave when it hits a surface. Light bouncing off a mirror and an echo (sound bouncing off a wall) are examples. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

Refraction is the bending of a wave as it passes from one medium into another. It happens because the wave changes speed. A stick in a glass of water looks bent for this reason. The ratio sin i / sin r is a constant for the two media. It is called the refractive index n, and n = speed in the first medium / speed in the second medium (when going from air or vacuum into the other).

img.alt: A ray of light going from air into glass, bending towards the normal; the incident ray, reflected ray, refracted ray, normal and the angles i and r are marked
img.cap: Reflection and refraction of a ray at an air-glass boundary.

p: Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or round an obstacle. It is biggest when the gap is about the same size as the wavelength. It is why you can hear someone speaking around a corner.

Interference happens when two or more waves overlap. If crest meets crest, the waves add and produce a bigger wave (constructive interference). If crest meets trough, they cancel (destructive interference).
A stationary (standing) wave is formed when two waves of equal amplitude and frequency travel in opposite directions and combine. Guitar strings and the air in organ pipes make stationary waves.
Polarisation means restricting the vibration to one plane only. Only transverse waves can be polarised, so it is proof that light is a transverse wave.

img.alt: Ordinary light passing through a crystal which lets only one plane of vibration through, producing polarised light which cannot pass through a second crystal turned at right angles
img.cap: Polarisation: only vibrations in one plane get through the crystal.

sections.h: Worked example 1: speed in shallow water
p: Surface waves travelling in deep water at 15 m/s meet a shallow-water boundary. The angles of incidence and refraction are 45° and 30°. Find the speed in the shallow water.

b: sin i / sin r = speed in first medium / speed in second medium.

sections.h: Worked example 2: radio waves entering water
p: Radio waves travel in air at 3.0 x 10⁸ m/s. Water has a refractive index 4/3. Find the speed of radio waves in water.
Refractive index = speed in air / speed in water, so speed in water = 3.0 x 10⁸ / (4/3) = 3.0 x 10⁸ x 3/4 = 2.25 x 10⁸ m/s.
A ray of light is incident on a glass block of refractive index 1.5 at an angle of incidence of 60°. Find the angle of refraction.
n = sin i / sin r, so 1.5 = sin 60° / sin r, so sin r = 0.866 / 1.5 = 0.5774. r = 35°.

units.title: Wave Calculations and Graphs
units.summary: How to show waves as graphs of distance or time, the wave equation v = fλ, and worked calculations.

p: We can draw a wave as a graph in two ways: displacement against distance (a snapshot of the wave at one instant) and displacement against time (the movement of one point as time passes). In the distance graph you can measure the wavelength, the crest and the trough. In the time graph you can measure the period.

The picture below is a displacement-distance graph. The wavelength can be measured between two crests, or between any two matching points, such as two troughs. The amplitude is the distance from the rest line to a crest or to a trough.

img.alt: A wave graph of displacement against distance showing peaks, troughs, the amplitude and the wavelength measured between two peaks or two troughs
img.cap: A displacement-distance graph: peaks, troughs, amplitude and wavelength.

p: Wave speed = frequency x wavelength, or v = fλ, where v is in m/s, f is in Hz and λ is in m. Since f = 1 / T, we also have v = λ / T. For a given medium the speed is fixed, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
Try each one yourself first.

b: A wave has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 2 m: v = 5 x 2 = 10 m/s.
A wave travels at 340 m/s with frequency 170 Hz: λ = v / f = 340 / 170 = 2 m.
A wave has a period of 0.02 s: f = 1 / T = 1 / 0.02 = 50 Hz.
What is the frequency of a radio wave of wavelength 150 m if its speed in free space is 3 x 10⁸ m/s? f = v / λ = 3 x 10⁸ / 150 = 2.0 x 10⁶ Hz.

p: Radio and TV signals (communication), microwaves (cooking and mobile phone networks), infrared (remote controls, heat), visible light (seeing), ultraviolet (sterilising), X-rays (medical pictures) and gamma rays (treating cancer). All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum, 3.0 x 10⁸ m/s.

Diffraction of sound helps us hear people around corners and inside a building because the waves spread through doors and windows. Interference of waves explains the loud and quiet spots in a hall, noise-cancelling headphones and the colours of oil on water.

units.title: Welcome and Table of Contents
units.summary: What SS1 English Studies First Term covers, how the lessons are organised, how to use them, and a map of every unit.

p: English is the language of school, of examinations, of business and of much of the world. Good English helps you in every subject, because you must read the questions, understand them and write clear answers. In this course you will practise all the parts of English that WAEC, NECO and JAMB test: speaking and sounds, vocabulary, reading, listening, writing and grammar.

This is the First Term course. It follows the Nigerian scheme of work for SS1, week by week. Each week has several short lessons, such as Spoken English, Vocabulary Development, Reading Comprehension, Listening Comprehension, Continuous Writing and Grammar.

Every unit has simple notes, tables, examples and, where it helps, a picture. At the end there is an activity to try at home, and a few practice questions to check yourself. The practice questions do not count towards any mark. They help you to see if you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.
Because English is about using the language, do the activities. Speak aloud, write in your notebook, listen to the radio, and read a newspaper a little every day.

units.title: Spoken English: Telling a Story Aloud (Oral Narrative)
units.summary: What oral composition and a narrative are, the parts of a good story, the language used in stories, and how to tell one aloud.

p: Oral composition means speaking to share your thoughts, feelings and experiences in an organised and fluent way. You build sentences and paragraphs in speech, in a clear order, so that the listener understands you easily. Oral composition is not only for competitions. Whenever you tell your parents what happened at school, you are doing oral composition.

A narrative is a story or an account of events, real or imagined. It tells what happened, how it happened, when it happened and to whom. A narrative can be a personal experience, a folk tale, a legend or a made-up story.
A good story has five parts. Learn them in this order.

head: Part
What it does
Example
rows: Shows the main idea of the story
The Day I Got Lost; My First Day in Boarding School
Gives the setting (where and when) and the main characters
One sunny afternoon, my mother sent me to the market.
Tells the events in clear order
I met my friend Bassey and we played football.
The most exciting or important part
My mother was waiting angrily at the door.
Ends the story and shows what was learned
That day I learned that obedience is better than fun.

p: Use past tense verbs: went, saw, heard, felt, ran.
Use connectors to show the order of events: first, then, later, afterwards, suddenly, finally.
Use descriptive words to paint a picture: beautiful, noisy, frightened, bright, terrible.
Use direct speech to make the story lively: “Stop!” my mother shouted.
Topic: A Day I Will Never Forget.

One sunny afternoon, I was sent by my mother to buy some bread from the market. On my way, I met my best friend, Bassey. We decided to play football before going home. When I returned, my mother was very angry because the bread was already cold and she had waited for me for more than one hour. That day, I learned that obedience is better than fun.
Notice the connectors (on my way, when I returned), the past tense (was sent, met, decided) and the lesson at the end.

Look at a picture (for example children playing football) and describe what you see in complete sentences. Arrange your ideas in order: beginning, middle, end. Tell your story to a partner, then to the class. Speak slowly and clearly, look at your listeners and do not rush.

p: Vocabulary is the set of words you know and use in a language or about a topic. A wide vocabulary helps you express ideas clearly and understand other people. In this unit we learn the words for things found in and around a home.
The kitchen is where food is cooked.

Used to strain or separate particles

units.title: Grammar: Nouns and Their Number
units.summary: What a noun is, singular and plural, and the rules for forming plural nouns, with examples.

p: A noun is the name of a person, animal, place, thing or idea. Examples: girl, book, Lagos, dog, honesty.
Number tells us whether we are talking about one thing or more than one. A singular noun refers to one item (boy, table, apple). A plural noun refers to more than one item (boys, tables, apples).
Most nouns become plural by adding -s, but many follow other rules. Study the table and learn at least two new examples for each rule.

head: Rule
Singular to plural
rows: book to books; car to cars
2. Add -es to nouns ending in s, x, z, ch, sh
box to boxes; bush to bushes
3. Change y to ies when a consonant comes before it
baby to babies; lady to ladies
4. Add -s if a vowel comes before y
toy to toys; day to days
5. Change f or fe to ves
leaf to leaves; knife to knives
man to men; child to children; tooth to teeth
7. Same form in singular and plural
sheep to sheep; species to species
8. Compound nouns: add -s to the main word
mother-in-law to mothers-in-law; passer-by to passers-by

p: I saw two men carrying boxes.
The children are playing with toys.
The wives cooked delicious food.
There are many deer in the forest.
The ladies wore beautiful dresses.

Some words end in f but only take -s, such as roof to roofs and chief to chiefs. Some words that end in o take -es (tomato to tomatoes, potato to potatoes) while others take -s (photo to photos, piano to pianos). When you are not sure, check a dictionary.

sections.h: A game to practise: Change It!
p: The teacher says a singular noun and the class says the plural. Teacher: foot. Students: feet. Teacher: knife. Students: knives. Teacher: table. Students: tables. Play it with a friend at home using words around you.

units.activity: Write ten singular nouns from things around you and change each to its plural form. Write down which rule you used for each one.

units.title: Reading: Finding Word Meanings from Context
units.summary: The five kinds of context clue (definition, synonym, antonym, example and inference) and how to use them to work out new words.

p: Context means all the words, sentences and paragraphs around an unfamiliar word. Think of it as the neighbourhood the word lives in. Instead of stopping to use a dictionary for every new word, you can use clues from the text to make an intelligent guess, called an inference. This helps you read faster and builds your confidence and vocabulary.
Learn the clue type and its signal words, then practise spotting them.

head: Clue type
How it helps
Signal words
Example
rows: is, means, is called, that is, commas, dashes, brackets
The anthology, which is a collection of poems, was beautifully bound.
A similar word or phrase is nearby
or, that is, in other words
The boy was elated, or very happy, after winning the prize.
Unlike his gloomy sister, John is always cheerful.
such as, for example, including, like
He enjoys aquatic sports like swimming and water polo.
After walking for hours in the sun, she was exhausted.

p: Definition: Semantics, the study of word meanings, is a fascinating branch of linguistics.
Synonym: He was known for his timorous nature; he was scared of almost everything.
Antonym: Some students were diligent in their studies, but others were simply lazy. (Diligent must mean the opposite of lazy: hardworking.)
Example: Nigerian delicacies such as jollof rice, moi-moi and pounded yam are delicious. (Delicacies are special, tasty foods.)
Inference: The classroom was in disarray; books were on the floor, chairs were overturned and a broken window let in the rain. (Disarray means untidiness or chaos.)
Read the passage, then see how each bold word can be worked out.

The annual village festival was a boisterous event. Unlike the quiet, sombre mood of the previous month following the drought, this celebration was full of life. The air was filled with the aroma of roasting yams and simmering stew. Children ran everywhere, their shouts and laughter adding to the happy clamour. The elders, remembering past celebrations, prayed that the prolific harvest would continue for many years to come.

Clue
Meaning

A pleasant smell, especially from food
Inference: the elders prayed the harvest would continue

units.title: Vocabulary: Family Life
units.summary: Words used to talk about family relationships and family customs, with meanings and examples, and how a family tree shows them.

p: Family life means the relationships, roles, activities and responsibilities in a family. This vocabulary helps us describe our own lives, understand society and read literature. A nuclear family is parents and their children. An extended family also includes grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins, often living together or nearby.
Study the words and make a sentence of your own with each one.

p: A family tree is a diagram that shows how family members are connected. At the top are the grandparents. They have children: your father and your uncle. Your father married your mother, and your uncle married your aunt. Your parents had you and your siblings. Your uncle and aunt had children, who are your cousins.

p: My father's brother is my uncle. My sister's daughter is my niece. A man whose wife has died is a widower. My aunt's children are my cousins. A family with only parents and children is a nuclear family. Having only one husband or wife at a time is monogamy. A woman engaged to be married is a fiancee. My mother's mother is my grandmother.

units.title: Listening Comprehension: National Values in a Story
units.summary: What listening comprehension is, how to listen for the main idea and details, and a story, 'The Honest Farmer', about national values.

p: Listening comprehension is an active skill. It is not only hearing sounds. It is the ability to understand, explain, judge and remember what is said. It includes finding the main idea, finding specific details, noticing the speaker's tone and understanding hidden messages or morals.
National values are the shared beliefs and principles that are important for the good of a nation. Examples are honesty, integrity, discipline, unity, patriotism and respect for elders.
Grievance: a complaint or injustice. Unanimously: all together, with everyone agreeing. Integrity: being honest and having strong moral principles. Bounty: a reward.
Ask someone to read this story to you twice while you listen. Or read it aloud yourself, slowly.

In the old village of Kpatakpa, there was a great famine. The King, wanting to test his people, announced a competition. 'I will give one bag of seed corn to every farmer,' he declared. 'Go and plant it. In six months, whoever brings me the most impressive harvest will receive a great bounty and be declared Farmer of the Year.'

Adewale, a young farmer known for his integrity, received his seeds. He planted them, watered them, and tended the soil, but nothing grew. His pot remained empty. He watched in despair as his neighbours boasted of their tall, green stalks of corn.
When the day came, farmers lined up with huge pots of corn. Adewale felt ashamed but knew he must be honest. He brought his empty pot before the King. The crowd laughed.

'Silence!' the King boomed. He pointed to Adewale. 'This,' he announced, 'is your Farmer of the Year!' The crowd gasped. The King explained, 'The seeds I gave you were all boiled. They could not grow. When you all saw your seeds failing, you brought corn from your own barns to deceive me. Only this man had the honesty and courage to bring me the truth. He is the only one worthy of trust.' Adewale was rewarded not just with a bounty, but with the leadership of the village granary.

Main idea: the King wanted to find out who was honest. Detail: the seeds were boiled, so they could never grow. Detail: Adewale brought an empty pot because nothing grew and he chose to tell the truth. Value shown by Adewale: honesty and integrity (and courage). Bad quality shown by the other farmers: dishonesty and deceit. Moral: honesty is better than a false reward; truthful people can be trusted with responsibility.

sections.h: How to become a better listener
p: Pay attention and look at the speaker. Avoid distractions such as phones. Do not interrupt. Take short notes of main points. Ask questions when you do not understand, and try to repeat the main idea in your own words.

units.activity: Listen to the national anthem and the national pledge. Write down two national values you can find in the words (for example unity, loyalty, peace). Then listen to your school principal's assembly speech or a radio news item and write a 3 to 5 sentence summary.

check.q: Why did the King hold the competition?

check.q: Which of these helps you to listen well?

units.title: Continuous Writing: A Narrative Composition
units.summary: The steps for writing a good narrative essay: introduction, body, climax and conclusion, using 'My First Day at College' as the model.

p: A narrative composition is a piece of writing that tells a story. The story can be a real experience or an imagined one. Its purpose is to entertain, to share an experience or to teach a lesson. A good narrative is interesting and well organised, and makes the reader feel part of the story.

sections.h: The four parts of a narrative
p: Introduction (the beginning): hook the reader and introduce the setting and the main characters. Ways to begin: with action (The alarm blared, jolting me from a dream), with dialogue ('Wake up! You will be late for your first day!' my mother shouted), with description (The new, stiff cotton of my college uniform scratched my neck) or with feeling (My stomach was a knot of excitement and terror).

Body (the middle): develop the story. Tell events in chronological order (first, next, then, later, finally). Use sensory details, which means sight, sound, smell, taste and touch. Use vivid verbs and adjectives: do not say walk, say trudged, raced or strolled. Add a conflict, such as getting lost, meeting a bully or feeling homesick.
Climax: the peak of the story, the most exciting moment or turning point, where the main problem is faced.
Conclusion (the end): wrap up the story. You can reflect on what you learned, end with your final feeling, or link back to the introduction.

sections.h: Sample outline: My First Day at College
p: Introduction: the dread and excitement on the morning; the new uniform and heavy bag; the noisy bus ride; the huge, scary school gate.

Body: getting lost on the big campus among identical buildings and many new faces; the assembly ground with the booming voice of the principal and the scary looks of the seniors; going to the first class and meeting the first friends.

Climax: at break, I could not find the toilets. I walked straight into the tallest, meanest-looking student I had ever seen and stammered for directions. Instead of being mean, he laughed, pointed me the right way and said, 'Don't worry, JJC, you will get used to it.'
Conclusion: it was not as scary as I thought; relief; the scary senior was actually kind; hope for the rest of the term.
Weak: It was a Monday and I went to school.
Better: My heart was thumping like a drum as the school bus rattled towards the gate I had feared for weeks.
Notice that the better sentence uses a strong comparison, a vivid verb and a feeling.

units.activity: Write a full narrative of about 250 to 300 words on 'My Most Embarrassing Moment'. Use the four parts, past tense, sensory details and vivid verbs. Swap with a classmate: give one compliment and one suggestion for improvement.

units.title: Grammar: Nouns and Gender
units.summary: The four genders in English (masculine, feminine, common and neuter), the conversion table, and practice activities.

p: In English grammar, gender is a way of classifying nouns as masculine (male), feminine (female), common (either male or female) or neuter (no gender). Gender in English is natural: it depends on the real sex of the person or animal, not on the word. In some other languages, such as French, even tables and chairs are masculine or feminine. In English they are not.
Masculine: male beings. Examples: man, boy, uncle, king, father, bull, actor, prince, husband, widower, stallion, wizard, fox, groom.
Feminine: female beings. Examples: woman, girl, aunt, queen, mother, cow, actress, princess, wife, widow, mare, witch, vixen, bride.
Common: beings that can be male or female. Examples: teacher, child, doctor, student, cousin, friend, parent, baby, person, singer, artist, driver.
Neuter: non-living things and ideas. Examples: table, pen, book, car, stone, chair, school, computer. Abstract nouns such as love, honesty, fear and happiness are also neuter.
Many masculine nouns have their own feminine form.
To change the gender of a sentence, change the noun and any other words that depend on it. Example: The king spoke to his subjects. Answer: The queen spoke to her subjects.
Why is 'doctor' common gender? Because a doctor can be a man or a woman. If we want to show the sex we add a word: a male doctor, a female doctor.

units.activity: Walk around your home. List ten neuter nouns (things) and five common gender nouns (for example student, teacher). Then write five sentences, each using one common gender noun.

units.title: Spoken English: The Fricative Sounds /θ/, /ð/, /ʃ/, /ʒ/ and /z/
units.summary: How to say five difficult consonant sounds correctly: voiceless and voiced pairs, spellings, example words, minimal pairs and sentence drills.

p: A fricative is a consonant sound made by forcing air through a narrow gap so that a hissing or rubbing sound is produced. These five sounds are often hard for Nigerian speakers of English because many of our local languages do not use the same tongue and teeth positions. Common mistakes: saying /t/ for /θ/ (tink instead of think), /d/ for /ð/ (dis instead of this) and /s/ for /ʃ/ (see instead of she).
Voiced means your vocal cords vibrate. Put your fingers on your throat (Adam's apple). If you feel a buzz, the sound is voiced. If you feel nothing, it is voiceless.

How to make it: put the tip of your tongue lightly between your upper and lower front teeth. Breathe out so the air slips between tongue and teeth. Do not vibrate your vocal cords. It is a soft hiss. Spelling: th.
Examples. Beginning: think, thin, theme, three, thief, thunder. Middle: author, bathroom, method, nothing. End: bath, mouth, path, cloth, breath, fourth.
This is the sister sound of /θ/. Put your tongue in exactly the same place, but this time hum, so the throat vibrates. Spelling: th.
Examples. Beginning: this, that, the, them, then, though. Middle: mother, father, brother, weather, other. End (rare): breathe, bathe, clothe, soothe.
Key contrast: breath /breθ/ (noun, no voice) and breathe /briːð/ (verb, voiced). bath /bɑːθ/ (noun) and bathe /beɪð/ (verb).

This is the 'be quiet' sound. Round your lips slightly. Raise the front of your tongue towards the roof of your mouth, just behind the bump behind your top teeth, and push air out over the tongue. No vibration. Spellings: sh, ti, si, ci, ch (in some words).
Examples. Beginning: she, ship, shop, shout, sure, sugar. Middle: nation, station, motion, ancient, machine. End: fish, wash, push, cash, dish.
This is the sister sound of /ʃ/. Use the same mouth position but vibrate the vocal cords. It is less common. Spellings: s, si, ge.
Examples. Beginning (very rare): genre. Middle: measure, pleasure, treasure, vision, television, usual. End: beige, garage, mirage.
This is the buzzing sound of a bee or a zip. It is the voiced sister of /s/. Place your tongue as for /s/ and vibrate your vocal cords. Spellings: z and s.
Examples. Beginning: zoo, zebra, zip, zero. Middle: lazy, easy, music, busy. End: is, was, has, breeze, please, noise.
Minimal pairs are two words that are the same except for one sound. Say them aloud to train your ear and tongue.
Their father thinks that this thing is better than that thing.
My brother took a bath and then went to bathe the dog.
They thanked the author for the thoroughly good book.
She usually measures the treasure on television.
The explosion caused confusion in the garage.
It was a pleasure to wash Sheila's special beige shirt.
Zainab's lazy cousins refused to pick the beans.

units.title: Reading Comprehension: Word Meanings in a Passage on Farming
units.summary: A practice passage on modern and traditional farming, with comprehension questions and word-in-context practice.

p: Remember: a definition clue gives the meaning (A silo, which is a tower for storing grain, stood nearby). An example clue gives examples (He grows staple crops such as yam, cassava and maize). An antonym or contrast clue gives an opposite (The old farmer preferred manual methods, but his son used mechanised tools like tractors). An inference clue needs you to think (The soil was barren; nothing would grow on it).
Read slowly. The words in bold in your textbook are subsistence, rudimentary, mechanised, erosion and bountiful.

Modern agriculture is very different from the farming of our ancestors. In the past, most farming was subsistence farming, where farmers grew just enough food to feed their own families. They used rudimentary tools like hoes and cutlasses and relied on manure (animal waste) to improve soil fertility.

Today, many farms are large-scale, commercial operations. This mechanised farming uses complex machinery like tractors for ploughing and harvesters for gathering crops. Instead of just manure, farmers now use chemical fertilisers to enrich the soil and pesticides to protect crops from insects. While this is more efficient, it can be expensive.

A major challenge for all farmers is erosion, the process where wind or water wears away the rich topsoil. Another is drought. To combat a lack of rain, some farms have built complex irrigation systems, using pipes and sprinklers to water the fields. The goal is to ensure a bountiful harvest, one that is plentiful and feeds the nation.
1. Main topic: how farming has changed from old methods to modern methods, and the problems farmers face.
2. Subsistence farming is growing just enough food for the family. Commercial farming is large-scale farming for sale.
3. Two rudimentary tools: hoes and cutlasses.
4. Two modern methods: chemical fertilisers (to enrich soil) and pesticides (to protect crops).
5. Irrigation solves the problem of too little rain (drought).
Subsistence: the passage says farmers grew 'just enough food to feed their own families', so subsistence means at the level needed just to live.
Rudimentary: hoes and cutlasses are given as examples of simple tools, and they are contrasted with 'complex machinery', so rudimentary means basic or simple.
Mechanised: it is contrasted with rudimentary tools and tractors are given as an example, so mechanised means done with machines.
Erosion: a definition clue follows it: the process where wind or water wears away the rich topsoil.
Bountiful: the synonym 'plentiful' follows it, so a bountiful harvest is a large, plentiful harvest.

units.title: Grammar: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
units.summary: The difference between countable and uncountable nouns, quantifiers (many, much, few, little), partitives, and special cases such as news and trousers.

p: Countable nouns name things that we can count one by one. They have a singular and a plural form: a book, two books; one chair, six chairs; an idea, many ideas. Some plurals are irregular: man to men, woman to women, child to children, foot to feet, tooth to teeth, person to people, mouse to mice.

Rules for using them: a singular countable noun needs a determiner before it (a, an, the, my, this). Wrong: I saw bird fly. Right: I saw a bird fly. They go with quantifiers that show number: many, few, a few, several, a number of, these, those. Example: Many students attended the lecture.

Uncountable (mass) nouns name things that cannot be counted one by one: substances, materials, ideas or masses. They have no plural form: we do not say informations, advices or furnitures. They take a singular verb: The water is cold. This information is vital.

Common groups: liquids and gases (water, milk, oil, petrol, air); materials (wood, glass, paper, gold, rice, sugar, flour, cement); abstract ideas (information, advice, news, knowledge, happiness, love, courage); general groups (furniture, luggage, money, traffic); subjects and activities (mathematics, physics, football, swimming).

We cannot say 'an advice'. To count them, we use partitives (units of measure): a piece of advice, a bottle of water, a grain of rice, a loaf of bread, a cup of tea, an item of news, a piece of furniture. They go with quantifiers that show amount: much, little, a little, a lot of, plenty of, some, any. Example: There isn't much information on that topic. I need a little sugar for my tea.

Uncountable
rows: much, little, a little, a lot of

p: Plural in form, singular in meaning: news, mathematics, physics, economics, politics, athletics. They take a singular verb. The news is on at 6 pm. Mathematics is an important subject.

Always plural: trousers, scissors, spectacles, shorts, jeans, pliers, congratulations, thanks, premises. They take a plural verb. My trousers are new. The scissors are on the table. To make them singular, use 'a pair of': I bought a pair of trousers.
She gave me many advices. Correct: She gave me a lot of advice (or many pieces of advice).
The furnitures are in the lorry. Correct: The furniture is in the lorry.
I need an information about the school. Correct: I need some information about the school.
Politics are a dirty game. Correct: Politics is a dirty game.
My jean is torn. Correct: My jeans are torn.

Which sentence is correct?
Which quantifier goes with an uncountable noun?

units.title: Listening Comprehension: A Poem, 'The Rainy Morning'
units.summary: Listening for the main idea, details, mood and rhyme in a short poem, with new words and discussion questions.

sections.h: Before you listen: three new words
p: Dawn: the very beginning of the morning, when light first appears. Lawn: an area of short grass in a garden or park. Bloom (verb): to open up, as when a flower opens.
Ask someone to read it twice, or read it aloud yourself and listen carefully.
The rain began at dawn,
Falling softly on the lawn.
Children stayed inside the room,
Watching flowers start to bloom.
The farmer smiled beneath the sky,
For crops will grow when fields are dry.
1. The poem is mainly about a rainy morning and how people feel about it.
2. The rain began at dawn.
3. The children were inside the room, watching the flowers start to bloom.
4. The farmer smiled because the rain would help his crops to grow.
5. 'When fields are dry' means that the rain is welcome because the fields were dry before the rain.
6. Rhyming words: dawn and lawn, room and bloom, sky and dry.

The mood is the feeling of a poem. Here the mood is calm, happy and hopeful. Rhyme is when the end sounds of lines are the same: dawn and lawn, room and bloom, sky and dry. Poets use rhyme to make poems musical and easy to remember. This poem is written in rhyming pairs, called couplets.

Good listening helps you learn in class, keeps you safe from danger when you hear warnings, and helps you understand other people. To be a good listener: pay attention, avoid distractions and do not interrupt.

Why did the farmer smile?
o: The rain would help his crops grow

The word 'dawn' means

units.title: Reading Comprehension: A Cultural Day Celebration
units.summary: A passage about a school cultural day, with comprehension questions and vocabulary-in-context practice.

p: Cultural day is when a school celebrates the traditions of its people, such as clothing, food, music and dance. Read the passage twice. First read for the general idea; second time, read for details.

Last Saturday, our school organised a cultural day celebration. It was a day set aside to appreciate the rich and diverse traditions of our country. Students came in different traditional attires, representing various tribes in Nigeria. There were Igbos in their isi-agu outfits, Yorubas in flowing agbada, and Hausas in their babanriga and elegant veils.

The event was a feast for the senses. There were displays of energetic local dances, mouth-watering traditional dishes, and short drama sketches showing historical events. Parents and teachers were visibly impressed by the students' creativity and talent. In his closing speech, the principal praised everyone for showcasing the beauty of our culture, reminding us that 'our diversity is our strength.'
1. The purpose was to appreciate the rich and diverse traditions of the country.
2. Students wore traditional attires from different tribes (isi-agu, agbada, babanriga).
3. Two activities: local dances, traditional dishes, or drama sketches.
4. Parents and teachers were impressed.
5. The principal's message: 'our diversity is our strength'.
6. Main idea: a school cultural day celebrated Nigeria's different cultures and showed that diversity is a strength.
Attires: clothes. The passage talks about students wearing different traditional outfits.
Displays: shows or presentations, such as dances, food and drama.
Creativity: the ability to use new ideas and to be original.
To showcase: to show something in a way that displays its best qualities.
Agbada: from the context (flowing, worn by Yorubas) it is a type of clothing, a wide flowing robe.

A summary gives the main points in your own words and is much shorter than the original. Example in three sentences: A school celebrated a cultural day in which students wore traditional dress of different tribes. There were dances, food and drama, and parents and teachers were impressed. The principal said that diversity is our strength.

units.activity: In a short paragraph, explain why you think a cultural day is important in a school. Then write a three-sentence summary of the passage in your own words.

check.q: What was the purpose of the cultural day?
o: To appreciate the traditions of the country

check.q: What does 'attires' mean?
What was the principal's main message?
To 'showcase' something means to
What is the main idea of the passage?
o: A school held a football match

units.title: Continuous Writing: 'A Day I Will Never Forget'
units.summary: Features of a good narrative (tense, order, point of view, characters, setting and plot) and a full outline for writing about a memorable day.

p: Tense: mostly past tense (I saw, he ran, we were shouting, it had happened). Structure: events in chronological order. Point of view: usually first person (I, me, we, our). Key elements: characters (the people in the story), setting (where and when it happens) and plot (the sequence of events with an introduction, rising action, climax and resolution). Language: sensory details, vivid verbs (dashed instead of ran, whispered instead of said) and transition words (first, next, later, suddenly, finally).
Picture the plot as a hill: the story climbs through the rising action to the climax, then comes down through the falling action to the resolution.

img.alt: A rising and falling curve showing the five parts of a story: introduction, rising action, climax at the top, falling action and resolution
img.cap: The shape of a story's plot.

sections.h: Sample outline: A Day I Will Never Forget
p: Introduction (paragraph 1). Hook: start with a sentence that grabs the reader's attention. Example: My hands were trembling and my heart was beating like a drum. Set the scene: introduce the day, the place and the general feeling. Example: It was the day of the state mathematics competition and I was the one chosen to represent my school.

Body, rising action (paragraphs 2 and 3). Describe the events leading to the main moment and build up suspense. Example: the journey to the city, the huge hall, the stern look of the quizmaster. Describe the challenge. Example: the first few questions were impossible and our score was falling behind.

Climax (paragraph 4). The main event, the most exciting part. Example: the final tie-breaker question came and no one else on my team knew it. All eyes were on me. I took a deep breath and remembered a formula my teacher had shown me the day before.

Conclusion (paragraph 5). Resolution: what happened in the end. Reflection: why you will never forget the day and what you learned. Example: when they announced our school as the winner, the hall erupted. I learned that preparation and courage are the keys to success.

Plan before you write: one line for each paragraph. Keep to one main story. Use new paragraphs for new events. Check that your verbs are all in the past tense. Read your work aloud to find mistakes. Underline five vivid verbs you used and ask if they could be stronger.

units.activity: Write a composition of about 250 words on 'A Day I Will Never Forget' (a happy, sad, scary or embarrassing day). Follow the structure, and then underline five vivid verbs you used.

check.q: What is the climax of a story?
In which tense is a narrative usually written?
Which point of view does a personal narrative usually use?
Which is a transition word?
The setting of a story tells
o: Where and when the story takes place

units.title: Grammar: Types of Nouns
units.summary: Proper, common, concrete, abstract and collective nouns, and how one noun can belong to several types.

p: Nouns can be sorted in several ways. This table summarises the five main types.

head: Type
Definition
Examples
rows: The name of a specific person, place, organisation or thing; it starts with a capital letter
Nigeria, Mary, Lagos, Coca-Cola, Mr Ade
A general name for people, places, things or ideas
Something you can see, touch, hear, smell or taste
book, chair, tree, ball, music, perfume
An idea, feeling, quality or concept you cannot touch
love, wisdom, happiness, anger, courage, time
The name of a group treated as one unit
team, class, herd, flock, crowd, family, army

p: A noun can be classified in more than one way. Love is a common, abstract and uncountable noun. Book is a common, concrete and countable noun. Nigeria is a proper, concrete and countable noun (one country).
Classify the nouns in the sentence: The class showed kindness to the old man in Abuja.
class: collective, common, concrete, countable. kindness: abstract, common, uncountable. man: common, concrete, countable. Abuja: proper, concrete.
Proper or common? If it is the name of one particular person, place or thing, it is proper and takes a capital letter (Lagos). If it is a general name, it is common (city).
Concrete or abstract? Ask: can I see, hear, touch, smell or taste it? If yes, it is concrete. If it is a feeling or idea, it is abstract (beauty).

units.activity: Identify and classify all the nouns in this paragraph: 'Nigeria is a country with great beauty and diversity. The people show courage and unity during festivals.' Then write five sentences, each containing at least two different types of noun.

check.q: Which of these is a proper noun?
Which noun is abstract?
'Flock' (of birds) is a
Which noun is concrete?
The main difference between a proper noun and a common noun is
o: A proper noun names a specific person, place or thing
A common noun starts with a capital letter
A proper noun is never a person

units.title: Spoken English: Consonant Clusters with /w/
units.summary: The /w/ glide and the clusters /tw/, /dw/, /sw/, /kw/ and /gw/: how to say them smoothly, with word lists, minimal pairs and sentence drills.

p: The /w/ sound (as in wet) is a semi-vowel, also called a glide. Air flows smoothly with no friction, so it is not a full consonant, but it cannot form a syllable alone, so it is not a vowel.
To make /w/: round your lips tightly and push them forward as if to say 'oo'. Keep your tongue high at the back. Then glide into the next vowel by letting your lips relax.

When /w/ follows another consonant (/t/, /s/, /k/, /g/, /d/) it makes a consonant cluster. The two sounds must blend: round your lips for /w/ while you are still forming the first consonant. A common mistake is to say the sounds separately ('tu-win' for twin) or to leave out the /w/.
Learn how each is made and practise the example words.

head: Cluster
How to make it
Examples
rows: Tongue tip on the ridge behind the top teeth for /t/; round your lips before releasing, release together
twin, twelve, twenty, twist, twig, twilight, between
Same as /tw/ but voiced; use your vocal cords
Start the hissing /s/ and round your lips for /w/ while hissing
sweet, swim, sweep, switch, swear, swing, swan
Back of tongue to the soft palate for /k/ (spelled qu); round lips before release
queen, quick, quiet, quake, question, equal, request
language, anguish, linguist, Gwen, guava, penguin

p: Minimal pairs: tick and quick; tip and twin; sit and sweet; get and Gwen; dell and dwell.

Sentences to read aloud, blending the clusters smoothly: The twins swept twenty-two rooms quickly. The queen spoke quietly about the dwarf. Gwen swam with the swan, swirling in the water. I have a question about the twist in the plot. The dwindling light of twilight made the dwelling look eerie.

Which word contains the /kw/ cluster?
A common mistake with 'twin' is
How do you make /w/?
o: Press your tongue on your teeth
Round your lips and push them forward

units.title: Vocabulary: Agricultural Implements (Farm Tools and Machines)
units.summary: Simple (manual) tools and mechanised machines used in farming, what each does, and practice in using the words.

p: Agricultural implements are the tools, devices and machines used in farming to make work easier, faster and more efficient. Without them, modern farming and food production would be very difficult. We group them in two classes: simple (manual) implements, which are hand tools powered by human effort and common on small subsistence farms, and mechanised implements, which are machines powered by an engine or electricity and used in large commercial farming.
Learn what each tool looks like and what it is used for.

head: Implement
Description and use
rows: A tool with a flat blade on a long handle, used for digging, removing weeds and making ridges
A long, heavy, single-edged blade used for clearing thick grass, bushes and small trees
A tool with a row of teeth (tines), used for gathering leaves, smoothing soil or removing rubbish
A tool with a flat, sharp-edged blade for digging, lifting and turning soil, especially for making holes
A tool with a broad, curved blade for scooping and moving loose materials such as sand, manure or grain
A small cart with one wheel, used for carrying loads such as crops, manure and tools by hand
A tool with a short, curved blade, used for harvesting grasses or grain crops such as rice
A container with a spout, used for watering plants by hand

p: These machines save time and energy on large farms.

head: Implement
Description and use
rows: The main vehicle of a farm. It gives the power to pull or run most other machines
A large, heavy implement pulled by a tractor that cuts deep into the soil and turns it over, burying weeds and preparing the land for planting
Used after ploughing. It breaks up large clumps of soil and makes a finer, smoother seedbed
An implement that forms long raised hills of soil (ridges) for crops such as yam, cassava and potatoes
A machine that sows seeds automatically at an even depth and spacing
A large, complex machine that cuts, threshes (separates) and collects mature grain crops such as maize, rice or wheat
A machine that applies liquid pesticides, herbicides or fertilisers to crops

p: Complete the passage with words from the lists.

To prepare his large farm for planting maize, the farmer first used a (1) pulled by his tractor to turn over the soil. The ground was still lumpy, so he pulled a (2) over it to smooth it out. For the smaller vegetable garden, his son used a (3) to dig up the weeds and a (4) to carry manure to the plots. To plant the yams, they needed a (5) to make raised beds of soil.
Answers: 1 plough, 2 harrow, 3 hoe, 4 wheelbarrow, 5 ridger.

sections.h: Why mechanised farming is more efficient
p: Machines work much faster than people, cover a larger area, need fewer workers and can do heavy work without getting tired. This is why large commercial farms use them. However, they cost a lot to buy and run, so many small farmers still use manual tools.

units.activity: Draw and label five farm implements (at least two manual and two mechanised). Ask a parent or guardian about two farm tools they know and write what they are used for. Then write about 100 words on 'The Importance of Farm Mechanisation in Nigeria'.

check.q: Which implement is used after ploughing to make the soil finer?
A sickle is used for
Which is a mechanised implement?
A small cart with one wheel is a
A ridger is used to
o: Form raised hills of soil for planting

units.title: Listening Comprehension: 'The Hardworking Farmer'
units.summary: Listening for who, what, where, when and why, with factual and inferential questions on a short passage about a farmer.

p: Produce (noun): farm products such as fruits and vegetables that have been grown. Dedication: being committed and working very hard for something. Community: a group of people living in the same place.
Ask someone to read this twice, or read it aloud yourself. Listen for who, what, where, when and why.

Mr Bassey is a hardworking farmer in Ikot Ekpene. Every morning, he wakes up early to feed his animals and check the crops. He uses a tractor to plough the land and a harvester during the harvest season. His children help him to carry produce home using wheelbarrows. Because of his dedication, Mr Bassey's farm produces enough food for the whole family and others in the community.
1. The main character is Mr Bassey.
2. He lives in Ikot Ekpene.
3. Every morning he wakes up early, feeds his animals and checks the crops.
4. He uses a tractor and a harvester.
5. His children use wheelbarrows.
6. His farm is so successful because of his dedication (hard work).
Moral lesson: hard work and dedication bring success and can benefit others too.

Subsistence or commercial? The passage says the farm produces food for 'others in the community', so he grows more than his family needs. That shows commercial farming (or at least farming beyond subsistence).
Why listening skills matter in school: you understand lessons and instructions, you remember more, you answer questions correctly and you avoid mistakes.
