units.title: Quadratic Expressions: Factorisation
units.summary: What a quadratic equation is, and how to factorise: the difference of two squares, trinomials with a = 1, trinomials with a not equal to 1 (the AC method), and common factors.

p: A linear equation such as 2x + 3 = 11 has one solution (x = 4) and its graph is a straight line. A quadratic equation such as x² − 4x + 3 = 0 has the highest power of x equal to 2. It can have up to two solutions (here x = 1 or x = 3) and its graph is a curve called a parabola.

The standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0 where a, b and c are numbers and a is not 0. For x² − 5x + 6 = 0: a = 1, b = −5, c = 6. For 2x² + 3x − 4 = 0: a = 2, b = 3, c = −4. For 4x² − 9 = 0: a = 4, b = 0, c = −9.

Quadratics describe situations where change speeds up or slows down: a ball thrown in the air (h = −5t² + 20t), the profit of a business, the area of a rectangle (A = x(x + 3)) and the arch of a bridge.

Factorisation means breaking an expression into simpler parts (factors) that multiply to give the original. 30 = 2 × 3 × 5. In the same way x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4). Factorising helps us to simplify expressions, solve equations and see patterns.

sections.h: Case 1: the difference of two squares
p: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b). Look for two perfect squares with a minus between them. Examples: x² − 49 = x² − 7² = (x − 7)(x + 7). 4y² − 25 = (2y)² − 5² = (2y − 5)(2y + 5). 9 − 16z² = (3 − 4z)(3 + 4z). x² − 121 = (x − 11)(x + 11).

Find two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b. Example: x² + 7x + 12. Pairs that multiply to 12: (1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4). Which pair adds to 7? 3 + 4 = 7. So x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4).
Example: x² − 5x − 14. The numbers multiply to −14 and add to −5: 2 and −7. So (x + 2)(x − 7).
Memory aid: the SUM tells you what to add, the PRODUCT tells you what to multiply.

sections.h: Case 3: ax² + bx + c where a is not 1 (the AC method)
p: Step 1: multiply a × c. Step 2: find two numbers that multiply to a × c and add to b. Step 3: split the middle term using these numbers. Step 4: group in pairs and take out common factors.

Example: 3x² + 10x − 8. a × c = 3 × (−8) = −24. Two numbers with product −24 and sum 10: −2 and 12. Split: 3x² − 2x + 12x − 8. Group: (3x² − 2x) + (12x − 8) = x(3x − 2) + 4(3x − 2) = (x + 4)(3x − 2). Check by expanding: 3x² − 2x + 12x − 8 = 3x² + 10x − 8. Correct.
Another: 5x² − 13x − 6. a × c = −30. Numbers with product −30 and sum −13: −15 and 2. 5x² − 15x + 2x − 6 = 5x(x − 3) + 2(x − 3) = (5x + 2)(x − 3).

sections.h: Always take out the common factor first
p: 3x² − 12x has the common factor 3x. So 3x² − 12x = 3x(x − 4). Looking for a common factor first makes the problem easier.

units.title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorisation
units.summary: The zero product rule, step-by-step solving, worked examples, common mistakes, and word problems.

p: If M × N = 0, then M = 0 or N = 0 (or both). The only way a product can be zero is for at least one factor to be zero. This turns one quadratic equation into two simple linear equations.
Step 1: write the equation in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0. Step 2: factorise the left side. Step 3: set each factor equal to zero. Step 4: solve each simple equation.
Example 1: solve x² − 8x + 15 = 0. Numbers that multiply to 15 and add to −8: −3 and −5. (x − 3)(x − 5) = 0. So x = 3 or x = 5. The graph of y = x² − 8x + 15 crosses the x-axis at 3 and 5.

Example 2: solve 6x² − 5x = 4. Standard form: 6x² − 5x − 4 = 0. a × c = −24. Numbers with product −24 and sum −5: 3 and −8. 6x² + 3x − 8x − 4 = 0, so 3x(2x + 1) − 4(2x + 1) = 0, which gives (3x − 4)(2x + 1) = 0. So x = 4/3 or x = −1/2. Check x = 4/3: 6 × 16/9 − 5 × 4/3 = 32/3 − 20/3 = 4. Correct.
Example 3: solve 4x² − 25 = 0. This is a difference of squares: (2x − 5)(2x + 5) = 0, so x = 5/2 or x = −5/2.
Example 4: solve 3x² − 12x = 0. Take out the common factor: 3x(x − 4) = 0. So x = 0 or x = 4.
Example 5: solve x² − 9x = 0: x(x − 9) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 9. Example 6: solve x² − 11x + 28 = 0: (x − 4)(x − 7) = 0, so x = 4 or x = 7.
Example 7: solve x(x + 3) = 10. Expand: x² + 3x − 10 = 0. (x + 5)(x − 2) = 0, so x = 2 or x = −5. Example 8: solve 3x² + 19x = 14. 3x² + 19x − 14 = 0 gives (3x − 2)(x + 7) = 0, so x = 2/3 or x = −7.

Problem: the product of two consecutive positive integers is 56. Find them. Let the integers be n and n + 1. n(n + 1) = 56, so n² + n − 56 = 0. Two numbers that multiply to −56 and add to 1: −7 and 8. (n − 7)(n + 8) = 0, so n = 7 or n = −8. We need positive integers, so n = 7. The integers are 7 and 8 (check: 7 × 8 = 56).

Problem: the product of two consecutive odd integers is 63. Let them be n and n + 2. n(n + 2) = 63, so n² + 2n − 63 = 0, (n + 9)(n − 7) = 0. So n = 7 (the integers 7 and 9) or n = −9 (the integers −9 and −7).

Always put the equation in standard form before factorising. Check the signs: the numbers must add to b and multiply to a × c. Check your answers by substituting. Always take out the common factor first. Remember that not all quadratics factorise nicely: for example x² + 9 = 0 has no real solutions because no real number squared gives −9.

units.title: Forming a Quadratic Equation from Its Roots
units.summary: The roots-to-equation method, the sum and product formula x² − (sum)x + (product) = 0, and worked examples with whole, fraction and surd roots.

sections.h: Roots, equation and graph go together
p: The roots (solutions) of a quadratic equation, its equation and its graph are three ways of showing the same thing. This week we go from the roots back to the equation.
If the roots are α and β (alpha and beta), the factors are (x − α) and (x − β). So (x − α)(x − β) = 0. Expand: x² − βx − αx + αβ = 0, which is x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.
Golden formula: x² − (sum of roots)x + (product of roots) = 0. The sum of the roots gives the coefficient of x (with a minus sign) and the product gives the constant term.
Find the equation whose roots are 4 and −3. Sum = 4 + (−3) = 1. Product = 4 × (−3) = −12. So x² − 1x − 12 = 0, that is x² − x − 12 = 0. Check: (x − 4)(x + 3) = x² − x − 12.

Find the equation whose roots are 1/2 and 3/2. Sum = 1/2 + 3/2 = 2. Product = (1/2)(3/2) = 3/4. So x² − 2x + 3/4 = 0. Multiply by 4 to clear the fraction: 4x² − 8x + 3 = 0. Check: (2x − 1)(2x − 3) = 4x² − 8x + 3.

sections.h: Example 3: roots with a square root
p: Find the equation whose roots are 2 + √3 and 2 − √3. Sum = (2 + √3) + (2 − √3) = 4. Product = (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1. So x² − 4x + 1 = 0. When the roots are a pair like a ± b√c, the sum and product are always whole numbers or fractions.

Roots 5 and 2: x² − 7x + 10 = 0. Roots 0 and −7: sum −7, product 0, so x² + 7x = 0. Roots 2/3 and −1/2: sum 1/6, product −1/3, so x² − x/6 − 1/3 = 0, or 6x² − x − 2 = 0. Sum of roots 5 and product −14: x² − 5x − 14 = 0.
In reverse: for 2x² − 6x + 5 = 0, divide by 2 to get x² − 3x + 2.5 = 0. So the sum of the roots is 3 and the product is 2.5.

units.title: Drawing the Graph of a Quadratic
units.summary: The parabola, its features (vertex, axis of symmetry, roots, y-intercept), and the five steps to draw an accurate graph with a worked example.

p: The graph of a quadratic is a smooth curve called a parabola. If a is positive (a > 0), it is U-shaped and has a lowest point (a minimum). If a is negative (a < 0), it is n-shaped and has a highest point (a maximum).

Key features: the vertex is the turning point; the axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex (the curve is a mirror image on both sides); the roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis (y = 0); the y-intercept is where it crosses the y-axis (x = 0).

sections.h: Five steps to draw a quadratic graph
p: Step 1: make a table of values with x-values around the expected vertex. Step 2: work out each y-value by substituting. Step 3: choose scales so the graph fits the page. Step 4: plot the points carefully. Step 5: draw a smooth curve through the points (never straight lines between them).

sections.h: Worked example: y = x² − 2x − 3 for −2 ≤ x ≤ 4

img.alt: Graph of y = x squared minus 2x minus 3: a U-shaped curve through the points (−2, 5), (−1, 0), (0, −3), (1, −4), (2, −3), (3, 0) and (4, 5)
img.cap: The graph of y = x² − 2x − 3 with its vertex at (1, −4), roots at −1 and 3, and axis of symmetry x = 1.

p: Roots: x = −1 and x = 3 (where the curve crosses the x-axis). Vertex: (1, −4), a minimum point. Axis of symmetry: x = 1. y-intercept: (0, −3). The minimum value of y is −4.
A quick way to find the axis of symmetry is x = −b/(2a). Here a = 1 and b = −2 so x = 2/2 = 1.
This has a = −1, so it is n-shaped with a maximum. The vertex is at (−1, 9). The roots of 8 − 2x − x² = 0 are x = −4 and x = 2. The maximum value of y is 9.

units.title: Using Quadratic Graphs and Applications
units.summary: Three things you can find from a graph, how to solve related equations, the number of roots, and real-life problems about a garden and a thrown ball.

p: 1. Finding the roots: the roots of x² − 2x − 3 = 0 are where y = 0: x = −1 and x = 3.
2. Finding a maximum or minimum: for y = x² − 2x − 3 the vertex (1, −4) gives the minimum value −4.

3. Solving a related equation: to solve x² − 2x − 1 = 0, rewrite it as x² − 2x − 3 = 2. So draw the line y = 2 on the same graph and read the x-values where it cuts the curve: x ≈ −0.4 and x ≈ 2.4. In the same way, for y = 8 − 2x − x² the equation 8 − 2x − x² = 5 is solved by drawing y = 5. This gives x ≈ −3 and x ≈ 1.

A parabola can cross the x-axis at two points (two different roots), touch it at one point (one repeated root) or miss it completely (no real roots). In later work you will meet the discriminant b² − 4ac: if it is positive there are two roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

A rectangular garden is 4 m longer than it is wide, and its area is 45 m². Find its size. Let the width be w, so the length is w + 4. Area: w(w + 4) = 45, so w² + 4w − 45 = 0. Factorise: numbers that multiply to −45 and add to 4 are 9 and −5. (w + 9)(w − 5) = 0, so w = −9 or w = 5. A width cannot be negative, so w = 5. The length is 9. Check: 5 × 9 = 45 m². The garden is 5 m by 9 m.

A ball is thrown upward. Its height in metres after t seconds is h = −5t² + 20t. Find the greatest height and when it lands. Since a = −5 is negative, the graph is n-shaped, so the vertex is the maximum. The vertex is at t = −b/(2a) = −20/(2 × −5) = 2 seconds. The maximum height is −5(2)² + 20(2) = −20 + 40 = 20 m. The ball is on the ground when h = 0: −5t² + 20t = 0, so −5t(t − 4) = 0 and t = 0 (the start) or t = 4. It lands after 4 seconds.
Another: h = −4t² + 16t. The vertex is at t = 2, with a maximum height of −16 + 32 = 16 m. The height is 12 m when −4t² + 16t − 12 = 0, which is t² − 4t + 3 = 0, so t = 1 or t = 3 seconds.

Check roots by substituting. Choose x-values around the vertex when you draw a graph. Clear fractions by multiplying through. Reject answers that do not make sense (a negative length). Do not forget units. Do not join plotted points with straight lines.

units.title: Logical Reasoning: Simple Statements and Truth Values
units.summary: What a statement (proposition) is, what is not a statement, truth values, and how to tell the difference.

p: Mathematics is about careful thinking and proof. Logic decides whether an argument is valid. It is also the base of computer programming (if-else rules), law, science (testing a hypothesis) and everyday decisions such as 'if it rains, I will take an umbrella'.

A simple statement (or proposition) is a sentence that declares a fact and can be clearly called either true (T) or false (F), but not both and not neither. We use small letters p, q, r and s to stand for statements.
A false statement is still a statement, because it has a definite truth value (false).

head: Letter
Statement
Truth value
Reason
rows: Lagos is a city in Nigeria.
A fact that can be checked
The human head is made of wood.

p: A question (What is your name?) asks and does not declare. A command (Pass the salt.) tells someone to act. An opinion (This food is delicious.) is a personal feeling and cannot be checked. An exclamation (Wow, amazing!) expresses emotion. An open sentence (x + 3 = 8 or x > 10) has a letter in it, so it is true or false only when we know x.

Which are simple statements? (a) The year 2024 is a leap year. Yes, true (2024 ÷ 4 = 506 with no remainder). (b) Solve the equation. No, a command. (c) Red is a beautiful colour. No, an opinion. (d) 5 − 1 = 3. Yes, false (5 − 1 = 4). (e) x > 10. No, an open sentence.

More: The square root of 16 is 4 (true statement). Water boils at 100 °C at sea level (true statement). Please solve this problem (command). That movie was boring (opinion). 'This sentence is false' is a paradox: if it is true then it is false, and if it is false then it is true, so it has no consistent truth value and is not a simple statement.
True: Nigeria gained independence in 1960. The sum of the angles in a triangle is 180°. Water freezes at 0 °C at standard pressure. Paris is in France. 7 × 8 = 56.
False: There are 8 days in a week. Humans can breathe underwater. 5 × 6 = 31. Rome is in Asia. 9 − 4 = 6.

units.title: Logical Reasoning: Negation
units.summary: The negation of a statement, the symbol ~, how to form correct negations, the truth table of negation, and common mistakes (such as 'all' and 'some').

p: The negation of a statement says the opposite: it denies the original. The symbol is ~ and ~p is read 'not p'. Example: p: It is raining. ~p: It is not raining. p: 2 + 2 = 4. ~p: 2 + 2 ≠ 4.
Method 1: say 'It is not the case that...'. p: Monday is the first day of the week. ~p: It is not the case that Monday is the first day of the week.
Method 2: put 'not' in the right place. p: Monday is the first day of the week. ~p: Monday is not the first day of the week.
Method 3: reverse the maths symbol. > becomes ≤. < becomes ≥. = becomes ≠. For example, p: x > 5 gives ~p: x ≤ 5. And r: 10 ≥ 7 gives ~r: 10 < 7.
If the statement already has 'not', take it away: q: A triangle does not have 4 sides. ~q: A triangle has 4 sides.
Negation always flips the truth value: if p is true then ~p is false, and if p is false then ~p is true.

head: p
~p
Example
rows: p: It is raining (true). ~p: It is not raining (false).

sections.h: A tricky one: all and some
p: The negation of 'All cats are black' is NOT 'No cats are black'. It is 'Not all cats are black', or 'Some cats are not black'. If 'All cats are black' is false, it does not mean that no cat is black; it only means at least one cat is not black.
Example: let p: A square has four equal sides (true), and q: 2 is an odd number (false). Then ~p: A square does not have four equal sides (false), and ~q: 2 is not an odd number (true).

sections.h: Common mistakes and fallacies in thinking
p: Do not confuse an opinion with a statement: ask 'can it be checked as true or false?'. Make sure the negation completely reverses the meaning. Do not treat an open sentence as a statement.

Some wrong arguments (fallacies) in everyday life: attacking the person instead of the idea (Your idea is wrong because you are young); assuming one thing caused another (I wore red and won, so red is lucky); jumping to a conclusion from too little evidence (I met one rude person from that city, so everyone there is rude); using feelings instead of reasons.

units.title: Compound Statements: AND and OR
units.summary: Joining simple statements, the symbols for AND (conjunction) and OR (disjunction), their truth tables and examples, and how to translate sentences into symbols.

p: A compound statement joins two or more simple statements with a connective such as AND, OR or IF-THEN. Compound statements let us describe real situations: 'If it is raining, then I will take an umbrella'. The symbols are ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (if...then), ↔ (if and only if) and ~ (not).
p ∧ q is read 'p and q'. It is true only when both p and q are true. Think of it as a demanding teacher: both must be correct.

b: p: You have a ticket (true). q: The show is today (true).
p ∧ q: You have a ticket and the show is today. This is true.
If either one is false, the whole statement is false.

p: p ∨ q is read 'p or q'. It is false only when both p and q are false. This is the inclusive OR: one, or the other, or both.

b: p: I will have tea. q: I will have coffee.
p ∨ q: I will have tea or coffee. It is true if I have either, or both. It is false only if I have neither.

p: Let p: The food is hot. Let q: The drink is cold.
The food is hot and the drink is cold: p ∧ q.
The food is not hot or the drink is cold: ~p ∨ q.
If the food is hot, then the drink is not cold: p → ~q.
Let p: It is sunny. Let q: It is hot. 'It is not sunny and it is hot' is ~p ∧ q.

units.title: Compound Statements: IF-THEN, IF AND ONLY IF and Truth Tables
units.summary: The conditional and biconditional, how to build truth tables, tautologies and contradictions, and uses in computing.

sections.h: The conditional: IF p THEN q (p → q)
p: p is the antecedent (the condition) and q is the consequent (the result). p → q is false only when p is true and q is false (a broken promise). In all other cases it is true.

Example: p: It is raining. q: The ground is wet. p → q: If it is raining, then the ground is wet. It is false only when it is raining and the ground is dry. If it is not raining, the promise is not tested, so the statement counts as true by convention.

sections.h: The biconditional: p IF AND ONLY IF q (p ↔ q)
p: p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value, and false when they are different. It means (p → q) and (q → p) both hold.
Example: A figure is a square if and only if it has four equal sides and four right angles. Both parts describe exactly the same thing.
AND: true only with T, T. OR: false only with F, F. IF-THEN: false only with T then F. IF AND ONLY IF: true only when the values match.

sections.h: How to build a truth table
p: List all the combinations of T and F for the letters. Work out the inner parts first and then work outwards. Example: p ∧ ~q. Columns: p, q, ~q, p ∧ ~q. Rows: TT gives F, F, so p ∧ ~q is F. TF gives T, so T. FT gives F. FF gives F. So p ∧ ~q is true only when p is true and q is false.
Example: p ∨ ~q. TT: ~q = F, so T. TF: ~q = T, so T. FT: ~q = F, so F. FF: ~q = T, so T.
Example: (p ∨ q) → p. TT gives T. TF gives T. FT: p ∨ q = T, p = F, so F. FF: p ∨ q = F, so T.
A tautology is always true whatever the truth values: p ∨ ~p (it is raining or it is not raining). A contradiction is always false: p ∧ ~p (it is raining and it is not raining).
Evaluating: if p is T and q is T, then p → ~q is T → F, which is F. If p is F and q is F, then p ↔ q is T. If p: Lagos is in Ghana (F) and q: 2 × 3 = 6 (T), then p → q is F → T = T.

Computer programs use these ideas all the time. IF (age >= 18) AND (has_id = True) THEN grant access, ELSE refuse. A contract might say IF (contract signed) AND (payment made) THEN the obligation is met. In science, IF the hypothesis is true THEN we expect a result; if the result does not happen, the hypothesis is false.

units.title: Revision of First Term Mathematics
units.summary: A topic-by-topic revision guide for First Term: key formulas, a three-level revision method, a self-check for each topic, and exam tips.

p: Week 1 number bases, Week 2 modular arithmetic, Week 3 indices, Week 4 logarithms, Week 6 calculations with logarithms, Week 8 changing the subject and variation, Week 9 quadratic equations by factorising, Week 10 quadratic roots and graphs, Weeks 11 and 12 logical reasoning. Mathematics builds step by step, and each topic supports the next.

Level 1, understanding the why: definitions, meanings and why a formula works. Level 2, doing the how: methods and steps. Level 3, knowing the when: which method to use for which kind of question. Spend time on all three levels. Do many past WAEC and NECO questions.
Number bases: to base 10, expand with place values. From base 10, repeated division (whole part) and repeated multiplication (fraction). Carry and borrow the base.
Modular arithmetic: a ≡ b (mod m) if m divides a − b. Reduce first, then calculate. Add m to a negative result.
Indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ, a⁰ = 1, a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, a^(1/n) = the nth root. Equal bases, equal indices.
Logarithms: y = aˣ means x = logₐ y. log(MN) = log M + log N, log(M/N) = log M − log N, log Mᵖ = p log M. Keep the mantissa positive.
Formulas and variation: do the same to both sides; unwrap using reverse BODMAS. y = kx, y = k/x, y = kxz.
Quadratics: factorise, then use the zero product rule. Roots give x² − (sum)x + (product) = 0. A graph shows roots, vertex and axis of symmetry.
Logic: statements are true or false. ~p flips the truth value. p ∧ q needs both true. p ∨ q needs one. p → q fails only on T then F. p ↔ q needs matching values.

sections.h: A quick self-check (try each without notes)
p: Convert 1101₂ to base 10 (13). Evaluate −20 (mod 6) (4). Write 0.00032 in standard form (3.2 × 10⁻⁴). Solve 4^(x+1) = 8 (x = 1/2). Write 2⁵ = 32 in log form (log₂ 32 = 5). Make C the subject of F = (9/5)C + 32 (C = 5(F − 32)/9). If y ∝ 1/x and y = 5 when x = 4, find y when x = 10 (2). Factorise x² + 2x − 15 ((x + 5)(x − 3)). Find the equation with roots 5 and 2 (x² − 7x + 10 = 0). Write the negation of 'x < 5' (x ≥ 5).

Read each question twice. Show every step, because marks are given for method. Write units where needed. Check your answers by substituting back. Manage your time: do the easy questions first. Stay calm; you have prepared well.

p: Welcome back. In First Term you worked with numbers, algebra and logic. In Second Term the main subject is geometry and trigonometry. You will draw exact shapes with a ruler and compasses, study the paths of moving points (loci), prove important theorems about triangles and parallel lines, and meet trigonometry, which links angles and lengths and is used by engineers, pilots and surveyors.
Geometry needs a sharp pencil, a ruler, compasses, a protractor (for checking) and a clean page. Many questions in WAEC and NECO ask you to draw, so practise often.

units.title: Constructions: Bisecting Angles and Making 60°, 90°, 30° and 45°
units.summary: The two tools of pure construction, how to bisect an angle, and how to construct 60°, 90°, 30° and 45° angles with a ruler and compasses only.

p: Geometric construction means drawing exact shapes using only two tools: an unmarked straightedge (a ruler used only to draw straight lines) and a pair of compasses (for drawing arcs and circles). A protractor may be used only to check your work at the end. This idea goes back to ancient Greece and Euclid. It shows how exact reasoning can create exact shapes.
Tips: use a sharp pencil, keep the compass radius firm, make your arcs light but clear, and never rub out your construction arcs because they show your method.

To bisect means to cut into two equal halves. To bisect an angle ABC: (1) Put the compass point on the vertex B and draw an arc that cuts both arms, at P and Q. (2) Put the compass point on P and draw an arc inside the angle. (3) Without changing the radius, put the point on Q and draw another arc that crosses the first at R. (4) Draw a straight line from B through R. This line BR bisects the angle, so angle ABR = angle RBC.

img.alt: Construction of an angle bisector: arc from B cutting both arms at P and Q, equal arcs from P and Q meeting at R, and the line BR
img.cap: Bisecting angle ABC: the arcs from P and Q meet at R, and BR is the bisector.

p: Draw a straight line and mark a point P on it. With the compass point on P, draw a wide arc that cuts the line at Q. Without changing the radius, put the compass point on Q and draw another arc that cuts the first arc at R. Join P to R. Angle RPQ is exactly 60°.
Why it works: PQ, PR and QR are all the same length (the compass radius), so triangle PQR is equilateral, and every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.

img.alt: Construction of a 60 degree angle: arc from P cutting the line at Q, arc from Q cutting it at R, and the line PR
img.cap: Constructing 60° with an equilateral triangle PQR.

p: Draw a straight line and mark a point P in the middle of it. With the compass point on P, draw an arc that cuts the line on both sides, at X and Y. Increase the compass radius. Put the point on X and draw a large arc above the line. Without changing the radius, put the point on Y and draw another arc to cross the first at Z. Draw a line from P through Z. Angle ZPY is 90°. (If you draw arcs below too you get a second point W, and ZW is the perpendicular bisector of XY.)

img.alt: Construction of a perpendicular: small arc from P cutting the line at X and Y, larger arcs from X and Y meeting at Z above and W below
img.cap: Constructing 90° at P.

p: 30°: construct 60°, then bisect it. You get two angles of 30°. 45°: construct 90°, then bisect it. You get two angles of 45°. In the same way, bisect 30° to get 15°, and bisect 45° to get 22.5°.

units.title: Constructing Angles Like 135° and Constructing Triangles
units.summary: Building bigger angles from basic angles, the conditions that fix a triangle (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) and worked constructions.

p: 135° is not a basic angle, but 135° = 90° + 45°. Steps: draw a straight line AB and mark a point P on it. Construct a 90° angle at P, giving a line PQ. Angle QPB is 90° and angle QPA is also 90°. Now bisect the angle QPA. This makes a 45° angle. The bisector PR makes angle RPB = 90° + 45° = 135°.

sections.h: What do you need to draw a triangle?
p: A triangle is rigid, so three pieces of information can fix it: SSS (all three sides), SAS (two sides and the angle between them), ASA (two angles and the side between them) and RHS (a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side).

General steps: (1) Draw the longest or most convenient side first as the base. (2) Use the next piece of information: construct an angle or measure another side. (3) Find the third corner where the remaining lines or arcs meet.

Construct triangle ABC with AB = 7 cm, BC = 8 cm and AC = 6 cm. Draw AB = 7 cm. With the compass set to 6 cm, draw an arc from A. Set the compass to 8 cm and draw an arc from B so that it cuts the first arc at C. Join AC and BC.

sections.h: Example 2: ASA with a constructed angle
p: Construct triangle ABC where AB = 6 cm, angle CAB = 60° and angle CBA = 45°. Draw AB = 6 cm. At A construct 60° and draw a long line. At B construct 90° lightly, bisect it to get 45°, and draw a long line. The two lines cross at C. Triangle ABC is the required triangle.

Construct triangle ABC with AB = 8 cm, angle CAB = 30° and angle CBA = 60°. Draw AB = 8 cm. At A construct 30°; at B construct 60°. Where the lines cross is C. Measure BC: it should be 4 cm, half of AB. Angle ACB = 180° − 30° − 60° = 90°, so the triangle is right-angled.

units.title: Copying an Angle and Constructing Quadrilaterals
units.summary: How to copy an angle exactly, how to construct a parallelogram and a rhombus by splitting them into triangles, and their properties.

p: Sometimes you are given any angle and must copy it. To copy angle ABC to a new point P: (1) Draw a line PQ for one arm of the new angle. (2) With the compass point on B, draw an arc that cuts both arms of angle ABC at M and N. (3) Without changing the radius, put the point on P and draw the same arc, cutting PQ at X. (4) Set the compass to the distance MN. (5) Put the point on X and draw an arc that cuts the arc from step 3 at Y. (6) Draw a line from P through Y. Angle YPQ is an exact copy of angle ABC.
A quadrilateral is not rigid, so you usually need five pieces of information. The trick is to split the shape into two triangles and construct each in turn.

Example: construct parallelogram ABCD with AB = 6 cm, BC = 4 cm and angle ABC = 60°. (1) Draw AB = 6 cm. (2) At B construct a 60° angle. (3) Measure 4 cm along the new line and mark C. (4) To find D: set the compass to 4 cm and draw an arc from A; set it to 6 cm and draw an arc from C; they meet at D. (5) Join A to D and C to D.
Another method for D: copy the angle at B to A, using the rule for parallel lines, and draw a line from A parallel to BC.

sections.h: Properties of a parallelogram (to check your drawing)
p: Opposite sides are equal and parallel. Opposite angles are equal. Adjacent angles add up to 180°. The diagonals bisect each other.

A rhombus has four equal sides. Construct a rhombus ABCD with side 5 cm and angle ABC = 60°. Draw AB = 5 cm. At B construct 60° and mark C so that BC = 5 cm. With the compass set to 5 cm, draw arcs from A and from C; they meet at D. Join AD and CD. The diagonals of a rhombus cross at 90° and bisect the angles.

units.title: Locus: The Path of a Moving Point
units.summary: What a locus is, the four basic loci (circle, perpendicular bisector, parallel lines and angle bisector) and real-life examples.

p: A locus (plural loci) is the set of all points that obey a given rule. You can think of it as the path a point traces when it moves according to a rule. The idea comes from ancient Greece, and it is used today in GPS tracking, robotics and computer graphics.
Learn these four. They appear in every WAEC and NECO paper.

img.alt: Four panels: a circle around a point, the perpendicular bisector of two points, two parallel lines either side of a line, and the angle bisectors of two intersecting lines

p: Locus 1: all points 3 cm from a point X form a circle of radius 3 cm. Locus 2: every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A as from B. Locus 3: points 2 cm from a line AB form a pair of parallel lines, 2 cm above and 2 cm below it (with a half-circle at each end if AB is a segment). Locus 4: for two lines that meet, points equidistant from both lie on the angle bisector; there are two bisectors (inside and outside the angle).
Other loci: the tip of the minute hand of a clock traces a circle. The locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines 6 cm apart is a line parallel to both, 3 cm from each.

units.title: Proofs in Geometry: The Angle Sum of a Triangle
units.summary: Axioms and theorems, how a proof is written (given, to prove, construction, proof, conclusion), and the proof that the angles of a triangle add up to 180°.

p: An axiom (or postulate) is a statement that we accept as true without proof, such as 'the shortest distance between two points is a straight line'. A theorem is a statement that is not obvious, but that we can prove using logic and axioms. This week we learn to write a proper proof.

sections.h: How to set out a proof
p: Step 1, Given: the information you start with. Step 2, To prove: what you want to show. Step 3, Construction: any line you add to the diagram (if needed). Step 4, Proof: a step-by-step argument with a reason for every statement. Step 5, Conclusion: finish with a closing statement, often Q.E.D. (from Latin, 'which was to be shown').

sections.h: Theorem 1: the angles of a triangle add up to 180°
p: Given: a triangle ABC. To prove: angle A + angle B + angle C = 180°. Construction: through A draw a line XY parallel to BC.
The picture shows the line XY drawn through A. The angle at X side equals angle B, and the angle at Y side equals angle C. Together with angle A they make a straight line.

head: Statement
Reason
rows: Angle XAB = angle ABC (call it b)
Alternate angles are equal (XY is parallel to BC)
Angle YAC = angle ACB (call it c)
Alternate angles are equal (XY is parallel to BC)
Angle XAB + angle BAC + angle YAC = 180°
Angles on a straight line add up to 180°
So angle A + angle B + angle C = 180°

img.alt: Triangle ABC with a line XY drawn through A parallel to BC, showing the alternate angles equal to B and C
img.cap: The line XY through A is parallel to BC.

p: Example 1: a triangle has angles 2x, 3x and 40°. Find x. The sum is 180°: 2x + 3x + 40 = 180, so 5x = 140 and x = 28°. The angles are 56°, 84° and 40°; check: 56 + 84 + 40 = 180.
Example 2: one angle of a triangle is 90°. The other two are x and 2x. Then x + 2x = 90, so x = 30°. The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°.
Example 3: the angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. The sum of the ratio parts is 9, so one part is 180° ÷ 9 = 20°. The angles are 40°, 60° and 80°.
Example 4: can a triangle have angles 50°, 60° and 80°? Add them: 50 + 60 + 80 = 190, which is not 180. So no.

units.title: The Exterior Angle of a Triangle
units.summary: What an exterior angle is, the exterior angle theorem and its proof, and worked examples.

p: If you extend one side of a triangle, you form an angle outside the triangle. This is the exterior angle. In the picture, side BC is extended to D, and the exterior angle is angle ACD.

img.alt: Triangle ABC with BC extended to D, showing the exterior angle ACD equal to angle A plus angle B
img.cap: The exterior angle ACD equals angle A plus angle B.

p: The exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles. Given: triangle ABC with BC extended to D. To prove: angle ACD = angle A + angle B.

Statement 1: angle A + angle B + angle ACB = 180°. Reason: the angles of a triangle add up to 180° (Theorem 1). Statement 2: angle ACD + angle ACB = 180°. Reason: angles on a straight line BCD add up to 180°. Statement 3: so angle A + angle B + angle ACB = angle ACD + angle ACB. Reason: both equal 180°. Statement 4: subtract angle ACB from both sides: angle A + angle B = angle ACD. Q.E.D.

Example 1: in a triangle, two angles are 50° and 70°. The exterior angle at the third corner is y. By the theorem, y = 50° + 70° = 120°. Another way: the third angle is 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°, and y = 180° − 60° = 120°.

Example 2: in triangle PQR, angle P = 2x, angle Q = 3x, and the exterior angle at R is 140°. By the theorem, 140° = 2x + 3x, so x = 28°. Then angle P = 56°, angle Q = 84°, and angle R inside = 180° − 140° = 40°. Check: 56 + 84 + 40 = 180.
Example 3: the exterior angle of a triangle is 110° and one of the interior opposite angles is 40°. The other is 110° − 40° = 70°.

units.title: Riders: The Angle Toolbox
units.summary: The angle facts you need to solve riders: straight lines, points, vertically opposite angles, parallel lines (Z, F, C patterns), and triangle facts.

p: A rider is a geometry problem that needs a chain of reasoning from theorems you know, to find an angle or to prove something. Think of yourself as a detective. Every step must have a reason.

sections.h: Angle facts to learn by heart
p: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles at a point add up to 360°. Vertically opposite angles (formed when two lines cross) are equal.

When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, three pairs of angles are related. Alternate angles are equal (the Z pattern). Corresponding angles are equal (the F pattern). Co-interior (allied) angles add up to 180° (the C pattern).

img.alt: Three diagrams of parallel lines cut by a transversal showing the Z pattern with equal alternate angles, the F pattern with equal corresponding angles and the C pattern with co-interior angles adding up to 180 degrees
img.cap: The Z, F and C patterns for parallel lines.

p: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides (the base angles) are equal. In an equilateral triangle all three angles are 60°. The angles in a right-angled triangle other than the right angle add up to 90°.

Write the reason for every step. Mark every angle you find on the diagram. Look for parallel lines, straight lines, isosceles triangles and vertically opposite angles. If you are stuck, find any angle you can and then use it.

units.title: Congruent Triangles, Polygons, Parallelograms and the Intercept Theorem
units.summary: The four conditions for congruent triangles, angles in polygons, properties of parallelograms and the intercept theorem.

p: Two triangles are congruent if they are exactly the same shape and size. You can prove it if one of these four conditions is true: SSS (three sides equal), SAS (two sides and the angle between them equal), ASA (two angles and the side between them equal), RHS (a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side equal). In SAS the angle must be between the two sides, and in ASA the side must be between the two angles.

Opposite sides are equal and parallel. Opposite angles are equal. Adjacent angles add up to 180°, so if angle A = 100° then angle B = 80°. The diagonals bisect each other. A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal.

The sum of the interior angles of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°. The sum of the exterior angles of any polygon is always 360°. In a regular polygon all sides and angles are equal, so one exterior angle = 360° ÷ n and one interior angle = 180° minus the exterior angle.
Example: a regular nonagon (n = 9). The sum of interior angles = 7 × 180° = 1260°. One interior angle = 1260° ÷ 9 = 140°. One exterior angle = 360° ÷ 9 = 40°. Check: 140° + 40° = 180°.

More: a regular pentagon has interior angle (3 × 180°) ÷ 5 = 108°. A polygon with an interior angle sum of 900° has n − 2 = 5, so n = 7 sides. A regular polygon with exterior angle 30° has 360 ÷ 30 = 12 sides.

If three or more parallel lines cut two transversals, they divide the transversals in the same ratio. In the simplest case, if the parallel lines cut off equal pieces on one transversal, they cut off equal pieces on the other. For example, equally spaced parallel lines divide any line crossing them into equal parts.

units.title: Solving Riders: Worked Examples
units.summary: Three worked riders using parallel lines, polygons and a proof that a parallelogram with a bisected angle is a rhombus.

sections.h: Rider 1: parallel lines and a triangle
p: Two parallel lines AB and CD are cut by a straight line EF. EF meets AB at G and CD at H, with E above G and F below H. Angle EGB = 65°. Find angle GHD, angle BGH and angle AGH.
Angle GHD = 65°. Reason: it corresponds to angle EGB (corresponding angles, AB parallel to CD).
Angle BGH = 180° − 65° = 115°. Reason: angles on the straight line EGH add up to 180°.
Angle AGH = 65°. Reason: it is vertically opposite to angle EGB.
Check habit: opposite angles at a crossing are equal; angles along a line add to 180°.

A regular polygon has 9 sides. (a) Sum of interior angles = (9 − 2) × 180° = 1260°. (b) One interior angle = 1260° ÷ 9 = 140°. (c) One exterior angle = 360° ÷ 9 = 40°. Check: 140° + 40° = 180°. And 9 × 40° = 360°.

sections.h: Rider 3: prove that the parallelogram is a rhombus
p: Given: parallelogram ABCD in which the diagonal AC bisects angle DAB. To prove: ABCD is a rhombus (all four sides equal).

Proof. Angle DAC = angle CAB (call each x), because AC bisects angle DAB (given). AB is parallel to DC, so angle DCA = angle CAB = x (alternate angles). So angle DCA = angle DAC = x. In triangle ADC the angles at A and C are equal, so the triangle is isosceles and DA = DC (sides opposite equal angles are equal). But in a parallelogram AB = DC and AD = BC (opposite sides are equal). So AB = BC = CD = DA. So ABCD is a rhombus. Q.E.D.

Given: triangle ABC with AB = AC, and D is the midpoint of BC. Prove that triangles ABD and ACD are congruent. AB = AC (given). BD = DC (D is the midpoint). AD is common to both triangles. So the triangles are congruent by SSS. It follows that angle B = angle C and angle ADB = angle ADC = 90°.

units.title: Trigonometric Ratios: Sine, Cosine and Tangent
units.summary: The sides of a right-angled triangle, the ratios sine, cosine and tangent, SOH CAH TOA, and worked examples.

p: The word comes from the Greek trigonon (triangle) and metron (measure). Trigonometry studies the connection between the sides and the angles of triangles. It was developed by Greek, Indian and Arab mathematicians for astronomy, navigation and building. Today it is used in engineering, physics, computer graphics and GPS.

sections.h: The sides of a right-angled triangle
p: A right-angled triangle has one angle of 90°. Choose one of the other angles and call it θ (theta). The hypotenuse (HYP) is the longest side, always opposite the 90° angle. The opposite (OPP) is the side opposite θ. The adjacent (ADJ) is the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse. If you change to the other acute angle, the opposite and adjacent sides swap over.

img.alt: A right-angled triangle with the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides labelled for the angle theta, and the memory aid SOH CAH TOA
img.cap: The three sides, and SOH CAH TOA.

sections.h: The three ratios: SOH CAH TOA
p: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse (SOH). cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse (CAH). tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent (TOA). These ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle.
In triangle PQR, angle Q = 90°, PQ = 5 cm and QR = 12 cm. Find PR, sin P, cos P and tan R.
PR² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169, so PR = 13 cm (Pythagoras).
For angle P: opposite = QR = 12, adjacent = PQ = 5, hypotenuse = 13. So sin P = 12/13 and cos P = 5/13.
For angle R: opposite = PQ = 5, adjacent = QR = 12. So tan R = 5/12.

A right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse of 15 cm and an angle of 35°. Find the side x next to the 35° angle. Relative to 35°, x is the adjacent side and 15 is the hypotenuse. We have A and H, so use CAH: cos 35° = x/15. So x = 15 × cos 35° = 15 × 0.8192 = 12.29 cm.
To find an angle you need two sides. Label the sides for the angle. Choose the ratio that uses them. Write the equation. Then use the inverse button on your calculator (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹).
Which ratio? Have H and O: sin. Have H and A: cos. Have O and A: tan. To find a side: angle and H, want O: sin. Angle and H, want A: cos. Angle and O, want A: tan. Angle and A, want O: tan.

units.activity: A right-angled triangle has opposite = 3 cm and hypotenuse = 5 cm. Find the angle. (Use sin θ = 3/5 = 0.6, so θ = sin⁻¹ 0.6 = 36.9°.)

units.title: Using Trigonometry to Find Sides and Angles
units.summary: A clear step-by-step method for finding missing sides and angles in right-angled triangles, with worked examples and real-life problems.

sections.h: Method for finding a missing side
p: You need one angle and one side. Step 1: label the sides OPP, ADJ and HYP for the given angle. Step 2: choose SOH, CAH or TOA, whichever uses the side you know and the side you want. Step 3: write the equation, put in the numbers, and solve. Make sure your calculator is in degree mode.

sections.h: Method for finding a missing angle
p: You need two sides. Step 1: label the sides for the unknown angle θ. Step 2: choose the ratio that uses your two sides. Step 3: write the equation. Step 4: use the inverse function on the calculator (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹) to get θ.

sections.h: Example 1: a missing side using cosine
p: The hypotenuse is 15 cm and the angle is 35°. Find x, the side next to the angle. x is adjacent and 15 is the hypotenuse, so use CAH. cos 35° = x/15. x = 15 × cos 35° = 15 × 0.8192 = 12.29 cm.

sections.h: Example 2: a missing angle using tangent
p: The opposite side is 10 cm and the adjacent side is 8 cm. Find θ. Use TOA: tan θ = 10/8 = 1.25. θ = tan⁻¹ 1.25 = 51.3°.

A 12 m ladder leans against a wall and makes an angle of 70° with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? The ladder is the hypotenuse. The height is opposite the 70° angle. Use SOH: sin 70° = h/12. h = 12 × sin 70° = 12 × 0.9397 = 11.28 m.
A rectangle is 15 cm long and 8 cm wide. What angle does its diagonal make with the 15 cm side? Opposite = 8 and adjacent = 15. tan θ = 8/15 = 0.5333, so θ = tan⁻¹ 0.5333 = 28.1°.

sections.h: Example 5: using Pythagoras and ratios together
p: If cos θ = 4/5, draw a right-angled triangle with adjacent = 4 and hypotenuse = 5. The opposite side is √(25 − 16) = 3. So sin θ = 3/5 and tan θ = 3/4. Also (cos θ)² + (sin θ)² = 16/25 + 9/25 = 1.

units.activity: A ladder 6 m long leans against a wall with its foot 2 m from the wall. Find the angle between the ladder and the ground. (Use cos θ = 2/6, so θ = 70.5°.)

units.title: Trigonometric Ratios of 30°, 45° and 60°
units.summary: Deriving the exact values of sin, cos and tan for 30°, 45° and 60° from two special triangles, a summary table, and exact-value problems.

p: Calculators can find the ratio of any angle, but 30°, 45° and 60° appear so often that you must know them without a calculator. Their ratios are exact values that use surds such as √2 and √3. They appear in regular polygons, engineering, physics and computer graphics.

Draw a right-angled isosceles triangle with the two equal sides each 1 unit. By Pythagoras the hypotenuse is √(1² + 1²) = √2. The angles are 45°, 45° and 90°. So sin 45° = 1/√2 = √2/2, cos 45° = 1/√2 = √2/2 and tan 45° = 1/1 = 1.

Draw an equilateral triangle with each side 2 units. All the angles are 60°. Cut it down the middle (bisect it) to get two right-angled triangles. Each has hypotenuse 2, base 1, and height h where 2² = 1² + h², so h² = 3 and h = √3. The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°.
For 60°: opposite = √3, adjacent = 1, hypotenuse = 2. So sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2 and tan 60° = √3.
For 30°: opposite = 1, adjacent = √3, hypotenuse = 2. So sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2 and tan 30° = 1/√3 = √3/3.

img.alt: A 45-45-90 triangle with sides 1, 1 and root 2, and a 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, root 3 and 2
img.cap: The two special triangles.

p: Notice that sin 30° = cos 60° and sin 60° = cos 30°. The sines increase from 1/2 to √2/2 to √3/2, and the cosines decrease in the same way.
Example 2: find the acute angle x if 2 sin x = √3. Then sin x = √3/2. From the table, x = 60°.

Example 3: an equilateral triangle of side 10 cm. Find its exact height. The height splits it into a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 10, opposite to 60° is h. sin 60° = h/10, so √3/2 = h/10 and h = 5√3 cm (about 8.66 cm).
Example 4: a square has diagonal 10 cm. Find its side. The diagonal makes two 45° triangles. Side = 10 × sin 45° = 10 × √2/2 = 5√2 cm.
Example 5: solve 4 cos² x = 3 for acute x. cos² x = 3/4, cos x = √3/2, so x = 30°.
Example 6: evaluate 2 sin 30° cos 30°. = 2 × (1/2) × (√3/2) = √3/2.

units.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
units.summary: What the angles of elevation and depression are, why they are equal, and how to solve height and distance problems.

p: The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight when you look up at something. The angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight when you look down at something. Both are measured from the horizontal line, not from the vertical.

From the top of a tower, the angle of depression to a car on the ground is θ. From the car, the angle of elevation to the top of the tower is also θ. This is because the two horizontal lines are parallel and the line of sight is a transversal, so the two angles are alternate angles.

img.alt: A tower with a horizontal line at the top and a line of sight down to a car, showing the angle of depression equal to the angle of elevation at the car
img.cap: Angle of depression = angle of elevation (alternate angles).

p: A man stands 100 m from the base of a building. The angle of elevation of the top is 60°. Find the height. The height is opposite the 60° angle and the ground distance is adjacent. Use TOA: tan 60° = h/100, so h = 100 × √3 = 173.2 m.

From the top of a cliff 80 m high, the angle of depression of a boat is 30°. How far is the boat from the foot of the cliff? The angle of elevation from the boat to the cliff top is also 30°. Use TOA: tan 30° = 80/d. So 1/√3 = 80/d and d = 80√3 = 138.6 m.
A vertical pole is 10 m high. From a point on the ground 10 m away, tan θ = 10/10 = 1, so the angle of elevation is 45°.
From a window the angle of depression of an object 20 m from the house is 45°. Height of the window = 20 × tan 45° = 20 m.
The shadow of a mast is 30 m long and the sun's angle of elevation is 30°. The mast's height = 30 × tan 30° = 10√3 = 17.3 m.

From the top of a lighthouse 120 m high, two boats A and B in a line are seen at angles of depression 30° and 60°. Boat A (30°): distance = 120 ÷ tan 30° = 120√3 = 207.8 m. Boat B (60°): distance = 120 ÷ tan 60° = 40√3 = 69.3 m. The boats are 80√3 = 138.6 m apart.

units.title: Trigonometric Ratios of Angles from 0° to 360°
units.summary: The four quadrants, which ratios are positive in each (ASTC), reference angles, and exact values for angles such as 120°, 150°, 225° and 300°.

p: Angles can be drawn on an x-y graph, starting from the positive x-axis and turning anticlockwise. Quadrant I is 0° to 90° (x and y positive). Quadrant II is 90° to 180° (x negative, y positive). Quadrant III is 180° to 270° (x and y negative). Quadrant IV is 270° to 360° (x positive, y negative).
Remember the memory aid All Students Take Cash, starting from Quadrant I and going anticlockwise: A, S, T, C.

img.alt: The four quadrants of a graph with ASTC marked: All in the first, Sin in the second, Tan in the third and Cos in the fourth
img.cap: The ASTC rule: All, Sin, Tan, Cos.

p: To find the ratio of any angle, relate it to the acute angle it makes with the horizontal x-axis. This is the reference angle. In Quadrant II: reference = 180° − angle. In Quadrant III: reference = angle − 180°. In Quadrant IV: reference = 360° − angle. Then find the ratio of the reference angle and give it the sign from ASTC.
sin 120°: Quadrant II so sine is positive. Reference = 180° − 120° = 60°. sin 120° = sin 60° = √3/2.
cos 240°: Quadrant III so cosine is negative. Reference = 240° − 180° = 60°. cos 240° = −cos 60° = −1/2.
tan 315°: Quadrant IV so tangent is negative. Reference = 360° − 315° = 45°. tan 315° = −tan 45° = −1.
sin 210°: Quadrant III so sine is negative. Reference = 30°. sin 210° = −1/2. cos 135°: Quadrant II, cosine negative, reference 45°. cos 135° = −√2/2.
If sin θ = 3/5 and θ is in Quadrant II, draw the triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5, so adjacent = 4. In Quadrant II cosine and tangent are negative: cos θ = −4/5 and tan θ = −3/4.

Is cos 100° positive or negative? 100° is in Quadrant II, so cosine is negative. Is tan 200° positive? 200° is in Quadrant III, so tangent is positive. The reference angle of 130° is 50°. The reference angle of 315° is 45°.

units.title: The Unit Circle and the Graphs of Sine, Cosine and Tangent
units.summary: The unit circle, key values at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270°, and the graphs of y = sin x, y = cos x and y = tan x, with their period and amplitude.

p: The unit circle has its centre at the origin (0, 0) and radius 1. Let P(x, y) be a point on the circle, with the line OP making an angle θ with the positive x-axis. In the right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is 1, so cos θ = x/1 = x and sin θ = y/1 = y. So cosine is the x-coordinate of P and sine is the y-coordinate of P. Also tan θ = y/x.

img.alt: A unit circle with the point P at angle theta, its x-coordinate being cos theta and its y-coordinate sin theta, with key angles marked
img.cap: On the unit circle, P = (cos θ, sin θ).

sections.h: Key values on the unit circle
p: At 0° the point is (1, 0): cos 0° = 1, sin 0° = 0, tan 0° = 0. At 90° the point is (0, 1): cos 90° = 0, sin 90° = 1, and tan 90° is undefined (division by zero). At 180° the point is (−1, 0): cos 180° = −1, sin 180° = 0, tan 180° = 0. At 270° the point is (0, −1): cos 270° = 0, sin 270° = −1, and tan 270° is undefined.
Points for the special angles: 30° is (√3/2, 1/2), 45° is (√2/2, √2/2) and 60° is (1/2, √3/2).

sections.h: The graphs of sine and cosine
p: The sine graph shows the height (y-value) of P as it goes round the circle. Table: sin 0° = 0, sin 90° = 1, sin 180° = 0, sin 270° = −1, sin 360° = 0. It is a smooth wave. The period is 360° (it repeats every 360°). The amplitude is 1 (the biggest height from the middle line). The values are between −1 and 1.

The cosine graph shows the x-value of P. cos 0° = 1, cos 90° = 0, cos 180° = −1, cos 270° = 0, cos 360° = 1. It has the same wave shape as sine but starts at its peak. It is the sine graph shifted by 90°. The period is 360° and the amplitude is 1.

img.alt: The graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x from 0 to 360 degrees on the same axes
img.cap: y = sin x (blue) and y = cos x (orange).

p: tan x = sin x ÷ cos x. At 0°, tan = 0. As the angle gets close to 90°, sin goes to 1 and cos goes to 0, so tan becomes very large. At 90° it is undefined, so the graph has a vertical line it never touches, called an asymptote. The same happens at 270°. The graph repeats in the same pattern every 180°, so the period of tan is 180° (not 360°). Its range is all real numbers.

img.alt: The graph of y = tan x with vertical asymptotes at 90 and 270 degrees
img.cap: y = tan x has asymptotes at 90° and 270°.

p: Example 1: find x between 0° and 360° for which sin x = 0.5. Draw the line y = 0.5 on the sine graph. It cuts the curve at two points. The first is at 30° (special angle). The second is in Quadrant II: 180° − 30° = 150°. So x = 30° or 150°.

Example 2: find x for which cos x = −0.5. The line y = −0.5 cuts the cosine curve in Quadrants II and III. The reference angle is 60° (cos 60° = 0.5). Quadrant II: 180° − 60° = 120°. Quadrant III: 180° + 60° = 240°. So x = 120° or 240°.

units.title: Revision of Second Term Mathematics
units.summary: A summary of constructions, loci, theorems, riders and trigonometry, with worked examples from a full revision assignment.

p: Skills: bisecting lines and angles; constructing 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°; copying an angle; constructing triangles and quadrilaterals; use only a ruler and compasses. The four basic loci: a fixed distance from a point gives a circle; equidistant from two points gives a perpendicular bisector; a fixed distance from a line gives two parallel lines; equidistant from two lines gives an angle bisector.

Know the proofs that the angles of a triangle add up to 180° and that an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Know the toolbox: parallel line angles (alternate, corresponding, co-interior), polygons (n − 2) × 180°, congruence (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS), parallelogram properties. In every rider, give a reason for each step.

SOH CAH TOA: sin = O/H, cos = A/H, tan = O/A. Use them to find sides and angles. Special angles: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; sin 45° = cos 45° = √2/2, tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3. Elevation (looking up) and depression (looking down) are equal for the same line of sight. ASTC tells which ratios are positive in each quadrant. The sine and cosine graphs have period 360° and tangent has period 180° with asymptotes.

Construct triangle ABC with AB = 8 cm, angle A = 60° and angle B = 45°. Draw AB = 8 cm. At A construct 60°. At B construct 90° and bisect it to get 45°. The lines meet at C. Then construct L₁, the perpendicular bisector of AB, and L₂, the bisector of angle BAC. The point P where L₁ and L₂ meet is equidistant from A and B, and from lines AB and AC. Measure AP with your ruler.
A regular polygon has 10 sides. Exterior angle = 360° ÷ 10 = 36°. Interior angle = 180° − 36° = 144°. Check: (10 − 2) × 180° = 1440° and 1440° ÷ 10 = 144°.

Prove that opposite angles of a parallelogram ABCD are equal. AD is parallel to BC, so angle A + angle B = 180° (co-interior angles). AB is parallel to DC, so angle B + angle C = 180° (co-interior angles). So angle A + angle B = angle B + angle C, and so angle A = angle C. In the same way angle B = angle D. Q.E.D.
From the top of a building 50 m high, the angle of depression of a car on the ground is 60°. How far is the car from the base? tan 60° = 50/d, so √3 = 50/d, d = 50/√3 = 50√3/3 = 28.87 m.
If cos θ = −0.5 and 0° < θ < 180°, then θ is in Quadrant II with reference angle 60°. So θ = 180° − 60° = 120°.

units.title: The Circle: Parts and the Length of an Arc
units.summary: Revision of the circle (radius, diameter, circumference, area), the parts of a circle (arc, chord, sector, segment) and how to find the length of an arc.

p: Mensuration is the part of mathematics that measures lengths, areas and volumes of shapes. This term we begin with the circle. The Babylonians used 3.125 for π and the Egyptians used 3.16. The Greek mathematician Archimedes (about 287 to 212 BC) found π very accurately. We use π ≈ 22/7 or 3.142.

The radius r is the distance from the centre to the edge. The diameter d = 2r goes across the circle through the centre. The circumference (the distance round the circle) is C = 2πr = πd. The area is A = πr².

An arc is any part of the circumference. A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle (the diameter is the longest chord). A sector is a slice of the circle bounded by two radii and an arc, like a slice of pizza. A segment is the region between a chord and its arc: the 'crust' of the pizza. The smaller region is the minor segment and the larger is the major segment.

img.alt: A circle showing the centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc, a shaded sector and a shaded segment
img.cap: Parts of a circle: a sector (slice) and a segment (between a chord and its arc).

p: An arc is a fraction of the circumference. The fraction depends on the angle θ that the arc makes (subtends) at the centre. A full circle is 360°, so the fraction is θ/360.
Length of arc = (θ / 360°) × 2πr.
So a 180° arc is half the circumference (πr), a 90° arc is a quarter (πr/2) and a θ° arc is (θ/360) × 2πr.

Example 1: a circle has radius 21 cm. Find the length of an arc that subtends 60° at the centre. (π = 22/7.) Arc = (60/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 21 = (1/6) × 132 = 22 cm. Check: the circumference is 2 × 22/7 × 21 = 132 cm and 60° is 1/6 of 360°, so 132 ÷ 6 = 22 cm.
Example 2: an arc of length 11 cm is on a circle of radius 7 cm. What angle does it subtend at the centre? 11 = (θ/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 7 = (θ/360) × 44. So θ = 11 × 360 ÷ 44 = 90°.
Example 3: a circle has radius 10 cm. The arc that subtends 90° has length (90/360) × 2π × 10 = 5π cm.
Example 4: a bicycle wheel has radius 35 cm. Its circumference is 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm. After 100 turns the bicycle has moved 22,000 cm = 220 m.
Example 5: the minute hand of a clock is 10 cm long. In 20 minutes it turns through 120° (20/60 of 360°). The tip travels (120/360) × 2π × 10 = 20π/3 ≈ 20.9 cm.

units.title: The Perimeter of a Sector
units.summary: How to find the perimeter of a sector from its arc and two radii, with worked examples and a problem where the perimeter is given.

sections.h: What is the perimeter of a sector?
p: The perimeter is the total distance around the edge of a shape. A sector has three edges: the curved arc and two straight radii. So perimeter of a sector = arc length + 2r = (θ/360) × 2πr + 2r.

A sector has radius 14 cm and angle 120°. Find its perimeter. (π = 22/7.) Arc = (120/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 14 = (1/3) × 88 = 88/3 = 29.33 cm. Two radii = 2 × 14 = 28 cm. Perimeter = 29.33 + 28 = 57.33 cm (exactly 172/3 cm).
A sector has radius 5 cm and arc length 10 cm. Its perimeter = arc + 2r = 10 + 2 × 5 = 20 cm.

The perimeter of a sector of radius 7 cm is 25 cm. (a) Find the arc length. Perimeter = arc + 2r, so 25 = arc + 14 and arc = 11 cm. (b) Find the angle θ. Arc = (θ/360) × 2 × (22/7) × 7 = (θ/360) × 44 = 11. So θ = 11 × 360 ÷ 44 = 90°.
Do not forget to add the two radii. The arc length alone is not the perimeter of a sector. Also remember that the perimeter is a length (cm), while area is in square units (cm²).

units.activity: A sector has a radius of 6 cm and an angle of 60°. Find its perimeter, using π = 3.142. (Answer: arc = 6.284 cm; perimeter = 18.284 cm.)

units.title: Area of a Sector and Area of a Segment
units.summary: The area of a sector as a fraction of the circle, the area of a segment as sector minus triangle, and the triangle formula ½ r² sin θ.

p: Like arc length, the area of a sector is a fraction of the whole circle's area. The fraction is θ/360. Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr². A 180° sector is half the circle, a 90° sector is a quarter, and a θ° sector is (θ/360) × πr².

Find the area of a sector of radius 10 cm and angle 135°. (π = 3.142.) Area = (135/360) × 3.142 × 10² = 0.375 × 314.2 = 117.825 cm², or 117.83 cm² to 2 decimal places. Check: the full circle is 314.2 cm² and 135/360 = 3/8 = 0.375, so 0.375 × 314.2 = 117.825.
A segment is the 'crust': the part of the sector outside the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord. So area of segment = area of sector − area of triangle.
The triangle has two sides of length r with the angle θ between them. Using area = ½ ab sin C, the triangle area is ½ r² sin θ. So area of segment = (θ/360) × πr² − ½ r² sin θ.

A chord subtends an angle of 90° at the centre of a circle of radius 14 cm. Find the area of the minor segment. (π = 22/7.) Area of sector = (90/360) × (22/7) × 14² = (1/4) × (22/7) × 196 = (1/4) × 616 = 154 cm². Area of triangle = ½ × 14² × sin 90° = ½ × 196 × 1 = 98 cm². Area of segment = 154 − 98 = 56 cm².
Arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr. Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr². Perimeter of sector = arc + 2r. Area of triangle in the sector = ½ r² sin θ. Area of segment = area of sector − area of triangle.

units.activity: Find the area of a sector of radius 7 cm and angle 90° (π = 22/7), and the area of the minor segment cut off by the chord. (Answers: 38.5 cm² and 14 cm².)

units.title: From a Sector to a Cone
units.summary: How a flat sector folds into a cone: slant height, base circumference and curved surface area, and the formula CSA = πrl.

p: If you cut a sector from paper and fold it so the two straight edges meet, you get a cone. This shows how a flat shape and a 3D shape are linked.

(1) The radius of the sector becomes the slant height l of the cone. (2) The arc length of the sector becomes the circumference of the cone's base, which is 2πR where R is the base radius of the cone. (3) The area of the sector becomes the curved surface area (CSA) of the cone.

img.alt: A flat sector with radius l folding into a cone with slant height l, base radius R and height h
img.cap: A sector folds into a cone: the sector's radius is the slant height.

p: Area of sector = (θ/360) × πl². The arc of the sector equals the base circumference: (θ/360) × 2πl = 2πR. Divide both sides by 2πl: θ/360 = R/l. Now put this into the area: CSA = (R/l) × πl² = πRl. So the curved surface area of a cone is CSA = πRl.

sections.h: Example: a sector folded into a cone
p: A sector of radius 15 cm and angle 216° is folded into a cone. Find (a) the base radius R and (b) the vertical height h.
(a) Arc length = base circumference: (216/360) × 2π(15) = 2πR. Divide both sides by 2π: (216/360) × 15 = R. 216/360 = 3/5, so R = 3/5 × 15 = 9 cm.

(b) The slant height is l = 15 cm. The cone's height h, radius R and slant height l form a right-angled triangle: l² = R² + h². So 15² = 9² + h², 225 = 81 + h², h² = 144 and h = 12 cm. (This is the 9, 12, 15 triangle, a multiple of 3, 4, 5.)
The curved surface area of this cone is πRl = π × 9 × 15 = 135π cm², which is about 424 cm². This is also the area of the original sector: (216/360) × π × 15² = 0.6 × 225π = 135π.

units.activity: A sector of radius 10 cm and angle 144° is folded into a cone. Find its base radius and its height. (Answers: R = 4 cm; h = √84 ≈ 9.17 cm.)

units.title: Surface Area of Solids: Cube, Cuboid and Cylinder
units.summary: What surface area and a net are, and the formulas and worked examples for the total surface area of a cube, a cuboid and a cylinder.

p: The surface area (SA) of a solid is the total area of all its faces. Imagine opening a box and laying it flat. The flat shape is called the net, and its area is the surface area. It is measured in square units such as cm² or m².
Surface area is needed for painting (how much paint to buy), packaging (how much material to wrap a product), manufacturing (how much metal sheet), and building (how much roofing).

img.alt: Six solids: cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, square-based pyramid and triangular prism
img.cap: Common solids used in mensuration.

p: A cube has 6 equal square faces. If the side is l, one face has area l², so the total surface area is TSA = 6l². Example: a cube of side 5 cm has TSA = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².

A cuboid has 6 rectangular faces in 3 pairs. With length l, width w and height h: the top and bottom have area 2lw, the front and back have area 2lh, and the left and right have area 2wh. So TSA = 2(lw + lh + wh).
Example: a cuboid with l = 8 cm, w = 5 cm and h = 4 cm. TSA = 2(8 × 5 + 8 × 4 + 5 × 4) = 2(40 + 32 + 20) = 2 × 92 = 184 cm².
Example: a room 10 m long, 8 m wide and 3 m high. The four walls and the ceiling (no floor): walls = 2(10 + 8) × 3 = 108 m², ceiling = 10 × 8 = 80 m². Total = 188 m².

A cylinder has two circular ends and one curved side. If you unroll the curved side it is a rectangle with height h and width equal to the circumference 2πr. So CSA = 2πrh. The two circles have area 2 × πr². The total surface area is TSA = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr(r + h).

Example: a closed tin with r = 7 cm and h = 10 cm (π = 22/7). TSA = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × (7 + 10) = 44 × 17 = 748 cm². Check: two circles 2 × (22/7) × 49 = 308 cm², curved part 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 10 = 440 cm², and 308 + 440 = 748.
Example: a cylinder of radius 5 cm has CSA = 100π cm². Then 2π × 5 × h = 100π, so h = 10 cm. Its TSA = 100π + 2π × 25 = 150π cm².

units.activity: Find the total surface area of a cuboid 6 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. (Answer: 2(24 + 18 + 12) = 108 cm².) Then find the total surface area of a closed cylinder with r = 7 cm and h = 3 cm (π = 22/7). (Answer: 440 cm².)

units.title: Surface Area of Solids: Cone, Prism and Pyramid
units.summary: The total surface area of a cone, a prism and a square-based pyramid, with the 'slant height' and worked examples.

p: A cone has one circular base and one curved side. With base radius R and slant height l: area of base = πR²; curved surface area (CSA) = πRl; total surface area TSA = πR² + πRl = πR(R + l).
The vertical height h, the base radius R and the slant height l form a right-angled triangle, so l² = h² + R². Example: R = 3 and h = 4 gives l = √(9 + 16) = 5.

Example: find the TSA of a cone with R = 5 cm and h = 12 cm (leave π). First find l: l² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169, so l = 13 cm. TSA = π × 5 × (5 + 13) = π × 5 × 18 = 90π cm² (about 282.74 cm²). (The numbers 5, 12 and 13 form a famous Pythagorean triple.)
Example: a cone with slant height 10 cm and base radius 6 cm. The height h = √(100 − 36) = 8 cm. TSA = π × 6 × (6 + 10) = 96π cm².

A prism is a solid with the same cross-section all the way along its length (a cylinder is a circular prism). The total surface area is TSA = 2 × (area of the cross-section) + (perimeter of the cross-section × length). The two ends are the cross-sections, and the side faces unroll into one big rectangle of width equal to the perimeter and height equal to the length.

Example: a triangular prism with a right-angled triangle end with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm and length 10 cm. The area of one end = ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 cm². The perimeter of the end = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 cm. TSA = 2 × 6 + 12 × 10 = 12 + 120 = 132 cm².

A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces that meet at a point (the apex). For a square-based pyramid with base side l, there is one square base and four triangular faces. If s is the slant height of a triangle face (not the vertical height h), the area of one face is ½ × l × s. So TSA = l² + 4 × ½ × l × s = l² + 2ls.
Example: a square pyramid with base side 10 cm and slant height 12 cm. TSA = 10² + 2 × 10 × 12 = 100 + 240 = 340 cm².

sections.h: Do not mix up the two heights
p: The slant height s (or l) is measured along a sloping face. The vertical height h is measured straight up from the base centre to the apex. Use the right-angled triangle to link them: s² = h² + (half the base)² for a square pyramid, and l² = h² + R² for a cone.

units.activity: Find the total surface area of a cone with R = 3 cm and h = 4 cm. (Answer: l = 5 cm; TSA = π × 3 × (3 + 5) = 24π cm².)

units.title: Volume of Prisms: Cube, Cuboid, Cylinder and Triangular Prism
units.summary: What volume means, the rule volume of a prism = base area × height, and the formulas and examples for the cube, cuboid, cylinder and triangular prism.

p: Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up, or how much it can hold: water, sand, air or grain. It is measured in cubic units such as cm³ or m³. Area covers a surface in square units; volume fills space in cubic units. Volume is needed for concrete in a foundation, medicine doses, recipes, shipping containers, grain stores and fuel tanks.

A prism has the same cross-section all along its length. If you slice it anywhere along its length, the slice looks the same as the base. The volume of a prism = area of the base (cross-section) × height (or length). V = A × h. Imagine a stack of identical slices: the area of each slice multiplied by how many slices tall.
Cube of side l: the base is l² and the height is l, so V = l³. Example: l = 3 cm gives V = 27 cm³.
Cuboid: the base is l × w and the height is h, so V = lwh. Example: l = 4, w = 3, h = 2 gives V = 24 cm³.
Cylinder: the base is πr² and the height is h, so V = πr²h. Example: r = 7 cm and h = 10 cm (π = 22/7) gives V = (22/7) × 49 × 10 = 1540 cm³.
Triangular prism: the base is a triangle with area ½bH and the length is L, so V = ½bH × L. Example: b = 6, H = 4 and L = 10 gives V = (½ × 6 × 4) × 10 = 12 × 10 = 120 cm³.

1 cm³ = 1 millilitre (ml) and 1000 cm³ = 1 litre. 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ = 1000 litres. So a tank of volume 1540 cm³ holds 1.54 litres of water. Always make sure all lengths are in the same unit before you multiply.

units.title: Volume of Pyramids and Cones
units.summary: The one-third rule for pyramids and cones, why you must use the vertical height, and worked examples including finding a missing radius or height.

p: A pyramid has a polygon base and rises to a point (the apex). A cone is a pyramid with a circular base. The volume of any pyramid or cone is exactly one third of the volume of the prism with the same base and the same height. So V = ⅓ × base area × vertical height.

Square-based pyramid: V = ⅓ l² h. Cone: V = ⅓ πr² h. Example: l = 6 and h = 9 gives V = ⅓ × 36 × 9 = 108 cm³. A cone and a cylinder with the same radius and height: the cone is exactly one third of the cylinder. If the cylinder's volume is 30 m³ the cone's is 10 m³.

The height h in the volume formula is the vertical height from the base to the apex, never the slant height. If you are given the slant height, use Pythagoras to find h first. For a cone: l² = h² + r². For a square pyramid with base l: s² = h² + (l/2)².

sections.h: Example 1: a cone with given slant height
p: A cone has radius 7 cm and slant height 25 cm. Then h = √(25² − 7²) = √(625 − 49) = √576 = 24 cm. V = ⅓ × (22/7) × 49 × 24 = ⅓ × 22 × 7 × 24 = 1232 cm³.

A cone has volume 110 cm³ and height 21 cm. Find its base radius. (π = 22/7.) V = ⅓πr²h, so 110 = ⅓ × (22/7) × r² × 21 = 22 × r². So r² = 110 ÷ 22 = 5 and r = √5 ≈ 2.24 cm. Check: ⅓ × (22/7) × 5 × 21 = 110. ✓

sections.h: Example 3: pyramid with a slant height
p: A square-based pyramid has base side 10 cm and slant height 13 cm (the height of a triangular face). Find the volume. First find the vertical height: the right-angled triangle uses half the base (5 cm), the vertical height h and the slant height 13. 13² = h² + 5², so h² = 169 − 25 = 144 and h = 12 cm. V = ⅓ × 10 × 10 × 12 = 400 cm³.
More: a square pyramid with base 18 cm and vertical height 12 cm has V = ⅓ × 324 × 12 = 1296 cm³.
A cylindrical oil drum has radius 0.7 m and height 1.5 m. How many litres can it hold? (π = 22/7; 1 m³ = 1000 litres.) V = (22/7) × 0.7² × 1.5 = (22/7) × 0.49 × 1.5 = 2.31 m³ = 2310 litres.
A cylinder 20 cm deep holds 3.08 litres. Its volume is 3080 cm³, so πr² × 20 = 3080, which gives r² = 49 and r = 7 cm.

units.activity: Find the volume of a cone with radius 3 cm and vertical height 4 cm (leave π). (Answer: ⅓ × π × 9 × 4 = 12π cm³.)

units.title: The Frustum: Volume and Surface Area
units.summary: What a frustum is, finding the missing height using similar triangles, and the 'large cone minus small cone' method for volume and surface area.

p: A frustum is what is left when you cut off the top of a cone or pyramid with a cut parallel to the base. A bucket, a flower pot, a lampshade, a drinking cup and a trash can are frustums. The method is always: large cone (or pyramid) minus small cone (or pyramid).

img.alt: A large cone with its top cut off by a cut parallel to the base, leaving a frustum of height h_f, with the small cone of radius r and height h_s removed
img.cap: Frustum = large cone − small cone.

p: Let R be the radius of the large base (bottom), r the radius of the small top, H the height of the whole original cone, h_s the height of the cone that was removed and h_f the height of the frustum, so H = h_s + h_f. The small cone and the large cone are similar, so r/R = h_s/H = h_s/(h_s + h_f). Solve this to find h_s.

sections.h: Volume and surface area of a frustum
p: Volume of frustum = volume of large cone − volume of small cone = ⅓πR²H − ⅓πr²h_s. The same idea works for a pyramid: ⅓ × (large base area) × H − ⅓ × (small base area) × h_s.
Curved surface area = πRL − πrl, where L and l are the slant heights of the large and small cones. Total surface area = πr² (top) + πR² (bottom) + π(RL − rl).
A bucket is 28 cm high. Its bottom radius is R = 15 cm and its top radius is r = 10 cm. Find its volume (π = 22/7). Treat it as a frustum with the small cone removed from the top.
Step 1: r/R = h_s/(h_s + 28). So 10/15 = h_s/(h_s + 28), that is 2/3 = h_s/(h_s + 28). Cross-multiply: 2(h_s + 28) = 3h_s, so 2h_s + 56 = 3h_s and h_s = 56 cm. Then H = 56 + 28 = 84 cm.

A frustum of a cone has top radius 5 cm, bottom radius 10 cm and vertical height 12 cm. Find h_s: 5/10 = h_s/(h_s + 12), so 1/2 = h_s/(h_s + 12), giving h_s + 12 = 2h_s, so h_s = 12 and H = 24 cm. Volume = ⅓π(10² × 24 − 5² × 12) = ⅓π(2400 − 300) = 700π cm³ = 2200 cm³ (π = 22/7).

A frustum of a square pyramid has bottom side 15 cm, top side 5 cm and height 6 cm. Ratio: 5/15 = 1/3 = h_s/(h_s + 6), so h_s + 6 = 3h_s, h_s = 3 and H = 9 cm. Volume = ⅓ × 15² × 9 − ⅓ × 5² × 3 = 675 − 25 = 650 cm³.

units.activity: A frustum of a cone has bottom radius 6 cm, top radius 3 cm and height 8 cm. Find the height of the cone that was cut off. (Answer: 3/6 = h_s/(h_s + 8), so h_s = 8 cm.)

units.title: Compound Shapes and the Sphere
units.summary: Volumes and surface areas of solids made by joining others (cone on cylinder, hemisphere on cylinder), the volume of a sphere and hemisphere, and how to handle hidden faces.

p: A compound shape is a solid made by joining two or more simple solids, for example a cone on a cylinder (a pencil or a rocket), a hemisphere on a cylinder (a capsule, a water tank), or a pyramid on a cube (a hut).

Volume: find the volume of each part and add them. Surface area: find the surface area of each part and add them, but take away any faces that are hidden by the join. For a cone sitting on a cylinder, do not count the cone's base or the cylinder's top. For a hemisphere on a cylinder, do not count the cylinder's top circle or the flat face of the hemisphere. Count only the surfaces you can see.
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³ and surface area = 4πr². Hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr³ and curved surface area = 2πr² (the flat circular face has area πr² if it is exposed).
A hemisphere of radius 7 cm sits on top of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Find the total volume (π = 22/7).
A solid is a cylinder of height 10 cm and radius 3 cm with a hemisphere of radius 3 cm on top. Find (a) the volume and (b) the total surface area.
(a) Cylinder: π × 9 × 10 = 90π cm³. Hemisphere: (2/3)π × 27 = 18π cm³. Total volume = 108π cm³.

(b) Visible surfaces: the curved side of the cylinder 2π × 3 × 10 = 60π cm², the circular base of the cylinder π × 9 = 9π cm², and the curved surface of the hemisphere 2π × 9 = 18π cm². Total surface area = 60π + 9π + 18π = 87π cm².

units.activity: A cone of radius 3 cm and height 4 cm sits on top of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 5 cm. Find the total volume in terms of π. (Answer: ⅓π × 9 × 4 + π × 9 × 5 = 12π + 45π = 57π cm³.)

units.title: Statistics: Collecting and Classifying Data
units.summary: What statistics is, population and sample, primary and secondary data, qualitative and quantitative data, and discrete and continuous data.

p: Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, analysing and interpreting data so that we can make good decisions. It is used in social media, medical research, election polls, business, climate science, education and the economy. The steps of a statistical study are: collect data, organise it in tables, present it in graphs, analyse it with calculations, interpret the results, and make decisions.

Data are facts, figures or information, such as test scores, heights or colours. Meaningful data are relevant to the problem you are studying. The population is the whole group you are interested in (for example all SS1 students in Nigeria). A sample is a small, fair part of the population that you study when the population is too big. A good sample represents the whole population.

Primary data are collected by you, first-hand, using questionnaires, interviews, experiments or observation. Pros: it fits your question exactly, it is up to date and you control its quality. Cons: it takes time, can be expensive and may need a large sample.

Secondary data were collected by someone else: textbooks, government reports (such as the National Bureau of Statistics), company records, websites and newspapers. Pros: cheap, quick and often a lot of data. Cons: it may be out of date, may not fit your needs and may be biased.
Qualitative (categorical) data describe a quality or category and are not numbers: favourite food, gender, colour of a car, state of origin, blood group.

Quantitative (numerical) data are numbers. They are of two kinds. Discrete data are counted and take separate values, usually whole numbers: number of students, shoe size, goals scored, number of children. You cannot have 5.3 students. Continuous data are measured and can take any value in a range: height, temperature, time, weight, distance. Their precision depends on the measuring tool.
