units.title: Frequency Tables for Raw Data
units.summary: What raw data are, how to use tally marks, how to build a frequency table, and how to find the mode and range.

sections.h: From raw data to a table
p: Raw data are data that have just been collected and are in no particular order. They are messy and hard to read. Tabulation means organising them into a frequency distribution table. Tally marks help to count: one stroke for each item, with the fifth stroke crossing the four before it, so groups of five are easy to count. The frequency f is the total count for each value, and Σf (the sum of the frequencies) is the total number of items.

Here are the shoe sizes of 20 students: 7, 8, 9, 7, 8, 10, 6, 8, 9, 7, 8, 8, 7, 6, 8, 9, 7, 8, 10, 8. The smallest size is 6 and the largest is 10. Go through the list and make a tally mark for each value, then count the tallies.

img.alt: A bar chart of shoe sizes 6 to 10 with frequencies 2, 5, 8, 3 and 2, with gaps between the bars
img.cap: Bar chart of the shoe-size data: note the gaps between the bars.

p: The table is much clearer than the raw list. We can see that size 8 is the most common (8 students). This most frequent value is called the mode. Sizes 6 and 10 are the least common (2 students each). The total is 20. The range is the largest value minus the smallest: 10 − 6 = 4.

Frequency table: mark 4 has f = 2; mark 5 has f = 4; mark 6 has f = 5; mark 7 has f = 9; mark 8 has f = 5; mark 9 has f = 4; mark 10 has f = 1. The total is 2 + 4 + 5 + 9 + 5 + 4 + 1 = 30. The modal score is 7, because it has the highest frequency (9).
They are easy to read, show patterns clearly, show the most and least common values, take little space, are ready for graphs and are easy to use to calculate statistics.

units.title: Grouped Data: Class Intervals, Boundaries and Midpoints
units.summary: Why we group data, the class interval, class boundaries, class width and class midpoint, and how to build a grouped frequency table.

p: If we have 100 different heights, a list of every value is too long and hides the pattern. If we group them into ranges, the pattern is clear: for example 150–154 cm: 15 people; 155–159 cm: 25 people; 160–164 cm: 35 people; 165–169: 20 people; 170–174: 5 people.

A class interval is a range of values, such as 10–19, 20–29, 30–39. The class boundaries remove the gaps between classes: subtract 0.5 from the lower limit and add 0.5 to the upper limit. So 10–19 has boundaries 9.5–19.5, 20–29 has 19.5–29.5, and 30–39 has 29.5–39.5. A value such as 19.5 now has a place.

The class width (class size) = upper boundary − lower boundary. For 10–19, the width is 19.5 − 9.5 = 10. The class midpoint (or class mark) = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2. For 10–19 the midpoint is (10 + 19)/2 = 14.5. For 20–29 it is 24.5. For 30–39 it is 34.5.

Group the 30 quiz marks from the last unit into classes 4–5, 6–7, 8–9 and 10–11. Count how many marks fall in each class: 4–5: 2 + 4 = 6; 6–7: 5 + 9 = 14; 8–9: 5 + 4 = 9; 10–11: 1. The total is 6 + 14 + 9 + 1 = 30.

Ages of 30 people at a party, grouped with classes 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39, 40–44 and 45–49: 3, 4, 8, 6, 4, 4 and 1. The total is 30. The modal class is 25–29, because it has the highest frequency (8).
Use classes of equal width. Choose between about 5 and 10 classes. Make sure every value belongs to exactly one class and that the classes cover the smallest and largest values.

units.title: Bar Charts, Line Graphs and Histograms
units.summary: When to use a linear graph, a bar chart and a histogram, and how to draw a histogram with class boundaries.

p: A linear (line) graph joins plotted points by lines. It is used to show trends over time: the temperature during a day, a company's profit over five years, the number of students in each year, or the price of a share.

A bar chart is used for qualitative or discrete data. The bars have gaps between them, they all have the same width, the x-axis lists the categories or values, and the y-axis shows frequency. The bars can be vertical or horizontal. The gaps show that the categories are separate. The bar chart in the previous unit shows the shoe-size data.

A histogram is used for continuous grouped data. The bars touch (there are no gaps) because the data are continuous. The x-axis shows the class boundaries, and the y-axis shows frequency (when the classes have equal widths). The tallest bar shows the modal class.
Bar chart: discrete or qualitative data; gaps; categories or values on the x-axis. Histogram: continuous grouped data; no gaps; class boundaries on the x-axis.
The table shows the heights of 50 SS1 students. Draw a histogram.

Step 1: find the class boundaries: 149.5–154.5, 154.5–159.5, 159.5–164.5, 164.5–169.5, 169.5–174.5. Step 2: set up the axes: the y-axis is frequency from 0 to 20, and the x-axis is height in cm marked with the boundaries. Step 3: draw each bar from the lower boundary to the upper boundary, with a height equal to the frequency. Step 4: label the axes and give the graph a title.

units.title: Pie Charts
units.summary: What a pie chart shows, the formula angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, and how to draw one, with worked examples.

p: A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors. Each sector shows the share of the whole that belongs to one item. The whole circle (360°) stands for the total frequency (or 100%). It is best for showing market share, percentages, budgets and survey results: parts of a whole.
Angle of a sector = (frequency of the item ÷ total frequency) × 360°. After you work out all the angles, check that they add up to 360°.

In an SS1 class of 80 students, 30 are in Arts, 40 are in Science and 10 are in Commercial. Total = 80. Arts: 30/80 × 360° = 135°. Science: 40/80 × 360° = 180°. Commercial: 10/80 × 360° = 45°. Check: 135 + 180 + 45 = 360°.

img.alt: A pie chart with sectors for Arts (135 degrees), Science (180 degrees) and Commercial (45 degrees)
img.cap: Pie chart of the streams in an SS1 class of 80.

sections.h: How to draw a pie chart
p: Draw a circle with compasses and draw one radius. Use a protractor to measure the first angle from the radius and draw the next radius. Continue with each angle, and the last sector should close the circle. Label each sector with its name (and angle or percentage), colour the sectors differently, and give the chart a title.
If a sector shows 20 people out of 80, its angle is 20/80 × 360° = 90°. If 'Food' takes up 120° of a budget, it is 120/360 = 1/3, or about 33.3% of the budget.

A family spends its monthly income as follows: food ₦30,000, rent ₦20,000, school fees ₦15,000, transport ₦10,000, savings ₦15,000. The total is ₦90,000. The angles are: food 30/90 × 360° = 120°; rent 20/90 × 360° = 80°; school fees 15/90 × 360° = 60°; transport 10/90 × 360° = 40°; savings 15/90 × 360° = 60°. The sum is 120 + 80 + 60 + 40 + 60 = 360°.

units.title: Frequency Polygons
units.summary: What a frequency polygon is, how to find class midpoints, how to ground the polygon, and how to draw one from a table or a histogram.

p: A frequency polygon is a line graph made by joining the midpoints of the tops of the bars of a histogram. It shows the shape of the distribution more clearly and is good for comparing two sets of data on the same graph. On the x-axis we put the class midpoints (marks) and on the y-axis the frequency.
To close the shape into a polygon, add an imaginary class with zero frequency before the first class and after the last class. Join the first and last points to the x-axis. This is called grounding.

Use the heights of 50 students. Class midpoints: 150–154 gives (150 + 154)/2 = 152; 155–159 gives 157; 160–164 gives 162; 165–169 gives 167; 170–174 gives 172. Add grounding points: before the first class, 145–149 with midpoint 147 and f = 0; after the last class, 175–179 with midpoint 177 and f = 0.

p: The polygon starts and ends at the ground (zero). It peaks at 162 cm, which is the midpoint of the modal class 160–164. It shows that most heights are close to the middle and that fewer students are very short or very tall.

Both are made from the same data. The histogram shows amounts with bars (using class boundaries on the x-axis). The polygon shows the trend or shape with a line (using class midpoints on the x-axis). When comparing two data sets, two polygons can be drawn on the same axes, which is hard to do with two histograms.

units.title: Revision of Third Term Mathematics
units.summary: A formula sheet for mensuration, a process sheet for statistics, worked revision questions and examination tips.

p: Circle: circumference 2πr; area πr²; arc (θ/360) × 2πr; sector area (θ/360) × πr²; perimeter of sector = arc + 2r; segment = sector − ½r² sin θ. Sector to cone: radius of sector = slant height l; arc = 2πR; sector area = CSA = πRl; (θ/360) × 2πl = 2πR.

Surface area: cube 6l²; cuboid 2(lw + lh + wh); cylinder CSA 2πrh and TSA 2πr(r + h); cone CSA πRl and TSA πR(R + l) with l² = h² + R²; prism 2 × base + perimeter × length; pyramid base + triangular faces.
Volume: cube l³; cuboid lwh; cylinder πr²h; prism base area × h; pyramid ⅓ × base × h; cone ⅓πr²h; sphere (4/3)πr³; hemisphere (2/3)πr³; frustum = large cone − small cone (use r/R = h_s/H).

Data types: qualitative (categories); quantitative: discrete (counted) and continuous (measured). Sources: primary (you collect) and secondary (collected by others). Graphs: bar chart (discrete or qualitative, gaps), histogram (continuous grouped, no gaps, class boundaries), pie chart (parts of a whole, angle = frequency/total × 360°), frequency polygon (class midpoints, grounded).
A solid cylinder has height 10 cm and radius 7 cm. TSA = 2πr(r + h) = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 17 = 748 cm². Volume = πr²h = (22/7) × 49 × 10 = 1540 cm³.

sections.h: Worked question 3: a cone from a sector
p: A cone is made by folding a sector with angle 120° and radius 18 cm. (a) Base radius: (120/360) × 2π × 18 = 2πR, so R = (1/3) × 18 = 6 cm. (b) Height: l² = h² + R², so 18² = h² + 6², h² = 324 − 36 = 288 and h = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 cm. (c) Volume = ⅓πR²h = ⅓ × (22/7) × 36 × 16.97 ≈ 640 cm³.

Mensuration: write what is given and what is needed, draw clear diagrams, check whether you need the slant or vertical height, use Pythagoras for heights, remember that a cone is one third of a cylinder with the same base and height, and show all working.

Statistics: decide the data type first, choose the right graph, use boundaries for histograms and midpoints for polygons, check that pie angles add to 360°, label the axes, give titles, and show calculations.
